title: Lecture 4 — Beginner tutorial
text:
Based on Lec 04.


See the formula
\[P_X(x) = P(\{\omega : X(\omega) \le x\})\]
on a tiny example (coin), then estimate a CDF from samples.
Run with Shift+Enter.




import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print('Ready')




Fair coin:

Omega = {H, T}
P({H}) = P({T}) = 1/2
Random variable X: X(H)=1, X(T)=0


Omega = {"H", "T"}

def P(event):
    event = set(event)
    return sum(0.5 for o in event if o in Omega)

def X(omega):
    return 1.0 if omega == "H" else 0.0

print("P({H}) =", P({"H"}))
print("X(H), X(T) =", X("H"), X("T"))




For a number x, look at the event {omega : X(omega) <= x}, then apply P.
That is exactly P_X(x) from the lecture.

def P_X(x):
    """CDF / distribution function of X at real number x."""
    event = {omega for omega in Omega if X(omega) <= x}
    return P(event)

for x in [-1, 0, 0.5, 1, 2]:
    print(f"P_X({x}) = P(X <= {x}) = {P_X(x)}")




For x < 0: nothing maps to <= x → probability 0

For 0 <= x < 1: only T (value 0) → probability 1/2

For x >= 1: both outcomes → probability 1

That step function is the pushforward / distribution of X.




In ML we rarely know P. We observe many values of X (range samples) and estimate.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 5000
# simulate abstract outcomes, push through X (like a sensor)
samples = np.array([X(o) for o in rng.choice(["H", "T"], size=n)])

xs = np.linspace(-0.5, 1.5, 200)
# empirical CDF: fraction of samples <= x
ecdf = np.array([(samples <= x).mean() for x in xs])
true = np.array([P_X(x) for x in xs])

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.step(xs, true, where="post", label="true P_X (from Omega)")
plt.plot(xs, ecdf, label="empirical CDF from samples")
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("P(X <= x)")
plt.title("Pushforward distribution of coin RV X")
plt.legend()
plt.show()





# Exercise A: unfair coin P(H)=0.7, same X coding.
# Recompute P_X at x = -1, 0, 0.5, 1.

def P_unfair(event, p_h=0.7):
    event = set(event)
    mass = {"H": p_h, "T": 1 - p_h}
    return sum(mass[o] for o in event)

def P_X_unfair(x):
    event = {o for o in Omega if X(o) <= x}
    return P_unfair(event)

for x in [-1, 0, 0.5, 1]:
    print(x, P_X_unfair(x))


# Exercise B: die, X(omega)=omega.
# What is P_X(3.5)? (should equal P(X <= 3.5) = P({1,2,3}) = 3/6)

Omega_die = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}

def P_die(event):
    return len(set(event) & Omega_die) / len(Omega_die)

def P_X_die(x):
    event = {o for o in Omega_die if o <= x}
    return P_die(event)

print("P_X(3.5) =", P_X_die(3.5))







Lecture idea
In this notebook




Inverse image
{omega : X(omega) <= x}


Pushforward / P_X
P of that event


Work with samples
empirical CDF approximates P_X


Course goal
estimate distributions from range samples



Next: several random variables, conditioning, then ML as distribution learning.

title: Lecture 2 — Beginner tutorial
text:
Based on Lec 02.


Feel these ideas with tiny examples:

Random experiment → you choose what it is
Sample space Ω → all outcomes
Events → subsets of Ω
Probability measure P → numbers in [0,1] with simple rules

Run cells top to bottom with Shift+Enter.




import numpy as np

print("Ready")




Lecture point: the experiment is your design choice.
We take: one fair coin toss.
Outcomes are not numbers yet — just labels.

Omega = {"H", "T"}  # sample space
print("Sample space Ω =", Omega)
print("Number of outcomes =", len(Omega))







Event (English)
As a set




Heads
{H}


Tails
{T}


Anything
{H, T} = Ω


Impossible
empty set = ∅




event_heads = {"H"}
event_tails = {"T"}
event_anything = Omega
event_impossible = set()

print("Heads event:", event_heads)
print("Impossible event:", event_impossible)




For a fair coin:

P({H}) = P({T}) = 1/2
P(Ω) = 1
P(∅) = 0

Check lecture properties: non-negative, P(Ω)=1, disjoint additivity.

def P_fair_coin(event):
    """Probability of an event for a fair coin (event subset of {H,T})."""
    event = set(event)
    if not event.issubset(Omega):
        raise ValueError("Event must be a subset of Omega")
    # fair: each singleton outcome has mass 1/2
    return sum(0.5 for outcome in event)

print("P(H) =", P_fair_coin({"H"}))
print("P(T) =", P_fair_coin({"T"}))
print("P(Omega) =", P_fair_coin(Omega))
print("P(empty) =", P_fair_coin(set()))

# Disjoint additivity: H and T do not overlap
print("P(H)+P(T) =", P_fair_coin({"H"}) + P_fair_coin({"T"}))




Same physical coin, new experiment: toss twice.
Ω₂ = {HH, HT, TH, TT}
This matches the lecture: you choose the experiment.

Omega2 = {"HH", "HT", "TH", "TT"}
print("Two-toss sample space:", Omega2)

# Event: exactly one head
exactly_one_head = {o for o in Omega2 if o.count("H") == 1}
print("Exactly one head:", exactly_one_head)

# Fair independent tosses -> each of 4 outcomes has probability 1/4
P_exact = len(exactly_one_head) / len(Omega2)
print("P(exactly one head) =", P_exact)




Lecture: when physics is hard, repeat observations and use statistics.
Simulate many fair tosses; the fraction of heads should approach 1/2.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 10_000
tosses = rng.choice(["H", "T"], size=n)
frac_heads = np.mean(tosses == "H")

print(f"In {n} tosses, fraction of heads ≈ {frac_heads:.3f}")
print("True P(H) for fair coin = 0.5")





# Exercise A: unfair coin with P(H)=0.7

def P_unfair(event, p_heads=0.7):
    event = set(event)
    mass = {"H": p_heads, "T": 1 - p_heads}
    return sum(mass[o] for o in event)

print("Unfair P(H) =", P_unfair({"H"}))
print("Unfair P(T) =", P_unfair({"T"}))
print("Unfair P(Omega) =", P_unfair({"H", "T"}))


# Exercise B: die Omega = {1,...,6}, fair — what is P(even)?

Omega_die = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
even = {2, 4, 6}
P_even = len(even) / len(Omega_die)
print("P(even) =", P_even)

In this notebook

coin once / twice / die


Sample space Ω

Event
subset


Probability measure
function → [0,1] with rules


Statistical view
simulate many tosses

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Big idea in one line
Part 1 explained why GateKeeper looks the way it does.
Part 2 turns that into a buildable shape: monorepo modules, roles/tenants, dynamic routes, the gateway request pipeline, and how MySQL / MongoDB / Redis / Kafka plug in.
Monorepo
├── smart-gateway-service      (data plane)
├── api-management-service     (control plane)
├── analytics-service          (observability path)
├── catalog-service            (demo target)
└── order-service              (demo target)

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 1 — Monorepo + Initializr workflow

Practical setup

Create a parent folder gatekeeper/

Generate each Spring Boot app (Maven, Jar, Java version matching the course)

Keep one port per app (example teaching ports—adjust as in the video):




Service
Example port




Smart Gateway
8080 (public entry)


API Management
8081


Analytics
8082


Catalog
8083


Order
8084




Run apps independently first (health check) before wiring Redis/Kafka.

Why monorepo: one place to navigate shared ideas; still separate deployable Boot apps (not one giant WAR of everything).

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 2 — Multi-tenant thinking (roles)
GateKeeper-style platforms usually separate who administers the platform from who administers one tenant’s APIs.
Platform admin  → manage the platform itself
Tenant admin    → manage routes/policies for one tenant
API caller      → call routes with a JWT under that tenant’s rules
Plain words:

Not every authenticated user is an admin

Route policies can require roles (ROLE_ADMIN, tenant roles, …)

Management APIs are themselves protected (JWT + roles)

Exact role names follow the lecture’s code—learn the idea: platform vs tenant vs caller.

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 3 — Dynamic routing (config, not if-else)
Hard-coding targets in Java:
if (path.startsWith("/catalog")) ...
else if (path.startsWith("/orders")) ...
…does not scale.
Dynamic route (stored by Management, loaded by Gateway) roughly includes:



Field
Meaning




Path pattern
What URL matches


Methods
GET/POST/…


Target base URL
Where to proxy


Auth required?
Anonymous vs JWT


Roles allowed
Authorization


Rate limit
Redis window/limit


Timeout
Fail slow targets


Path rewrite / header rules
Transform at the edge


Active flag
Enable/disable without redeploy



Admin updates route in Management
  → save MySQL + version
  → Kafka config event
  → Gateway fetches latest
  → memory registry updated
  → next requests use new rules

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 4 — Live request pipeline (Gateway)
Think in ordered stages (filters / interceptors / services—same story):
1. Correlation ID     (create or propagate X-Correlation-Id)
2. Route match        (memory registry)
3. JWT validate       (local signature + claims)
4. Role check         (route policy)
5. Rate limit         (Redis atomic)
6. Idempotency        (Redis; mainly configured POSTs)
7. Transform          (path rewrite, header add/remove)
8. Proxy forward      (HTTP to target + timeout)
9. Access event       (publish to Kafka)
10. Return response / gateway error
If a stage fails → consistent gateway error (do not leak stack traces to clients).

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 5 — API Management responsibilities (hands-on view)
Management is not on the hot path for every forward, but it is critical for:

Register / login → issue JWTs

CRUD for routes and policies

Versioning config

Auditing admin actions (AOP is a good fit: “when admin changes route, write audit row”)

Publishing configuration events

MySQL tables (conceptual): users, roles, routes, policy settings, versions, audits.
Other services must not UPDATE Management tables directly.

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 6 — Analytics & observability path
Gateway ──access event──► Kafka topic (e.g. gateway-access-events)
                              │
                              ▼
                         Analytics service
                              │
                              ▼
                           MongoDB
Useful fields: eventId, correlationId, route, method, outcome, duration, rate-limited?, idempotent-replay?
Queries you want later:

requests per route

error rate

slow routes

rate-limit rejections

Dedup: consumers can see duplicates after retries → use unique eventId.
correlationId ties work for one client request; it is not the dedup key.

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 7 — Demo targets (Catalog / Order)
Keep them small on purpose:

A few REST endpoints

Optionally check a business rule the gateway cannot know

Observe path rewrite + header propagation (X-Correlation-Id)

Use for timeout / idempotency demos

They prove the pipe, not a full e-commerce domain.

title: Lecture 42 — GateKeeper project #2
text:
Topic 8 — Practice lab (IDE checklist)

A — Skeleton

Create the five Boot modules

Hit each /actuator/health or custom /health

Commit locally only if you want (this agent will not commit)



B — Management first

User entity + JWT login (reuse skills from lectures 36–38)

Route entity + admin-only CRUD

Return route list API the Gateway can call on refresh



C — Gateway pipeline

In-memory RouteRegistry

Load routes at startup from Management

Filter/interceptor chain for correlation → auth → Redis → proxy

Use WebClient or RestClient/RestTemplate for forwarding (course choice)



D — Redis

Run Redis locally (Docker is fine)

Implement rate limit with atomic ops / Lua as shown in the video

Prove two rapid requests → second blocked when over limit



E — Kafka + Analytics

Topic for access events

Gateway publisher

Analytics consumer → MongoDB document

Confirm client still gets a fast response if Analytics is slow



F — End-to-end demo script

Admin creates /catalog/** route → target catalog:8083

Caller JWT without role → 403

Caller with role → 200 from catalog through gateway

Burst traffic → 429 / rate-limit style response

Check Analytics for the access trail

Monorepo of Boot apps, separate ports

title: Lecture 41 — GateKeeper project #1
text:
Big idea in one line
When one backend becomes many services, clients should not know every host and repeat the same security/rate-limit code.
GateKeeper is a teaching project: a custom API gateway plus management and analytics services using Spring Boot, Redis, and Kafka.
Client
  │
  ▼
Smart Gateway  ──policies──► Redis (rate limit / idempotency)
  │            ──events───► Kafka ──► Analytics (MongoDB)
  │
  ├──► Catalog / Order (demo targets)
  │
  └── config loaded from API Management (MySQL) via notifications

title: Lecture 41 — GateKeeper project #1
text:
Topic 1 — Why an API gateway?
Without a gateway, every client must know:

which service owns which URL

how to validate tokens everywhere

how to apply shared limits and correlation IDs

Gateway jobs:



Job
Meaning




Routing
Choose the target service for this request


Policy enforcement
AuthN/AuthZ, rate limits, idempotency, …


Reverse proxying
Forward HTTP and return the response



Forward proxy  → helps clients reach the internet
Reverse proxy  → sits in front of your servers
API gateway    → reverse proxy + API policies
Boundary rule: gateway handles entry rules. Target services still enforce business rules (who may change this order).

title: Lecture 41 — GateKeeper project #1
section: Topic 2 — What GateKeeper is (and is not)
text:
Topic 2 — What GateKeeper is (and is not)
Educational, scoped gateway platform—not a replacement for Kong / Spring Cloud Gateway / commercial products.

Main apps








App
Plane
Purpose




Smart Gateway Service
Data plane
Live request path


API Management Service
Control plane
Users, routes, policies, JWT issue


Analytics Service
Side path
Consume access events → stats


Catalog / Order demos
Targets
Prove routing & policies





Intentionally out of scope (examples)
Spring Cloud Gateway / Eureka / Config Server, service mesh, circuit breakers as a product feature, TLS termination productization, billing/API keys product, body transforms as a general engine, …
You build enough to see the insides.

title: Lecture 41 — GateKeeper project #1
section: Topic 3 — Data plane vs control plane
text:
Topic 3 — Data plane vs control plane
Control plane (API Management)
  define routes, roles, limits
  store durable config in MySQL
  publish "config changed" events

Data plane (Smart Gateway)
  keep active routes in MEMORY
  validate JWT locally
  talk to Redis for shared counters
  forward to targets
  publish access events (async)
If Management is temporarily down, already loaded routes can still serve traffic. New admin changes wait until Management returns.

title: Lecture 41 — GateKeeper project #1
text:
Topic 4 — Latency design
A gateway always adds a hop. GateKeeper avoids extra synchronous calls:








Work
Where
Why




Route match
Gateway memory
No DB hit per request


JWT validate
Gateway process
No auth-service round trip each time


Rate limit / idempotency
Redis
Shared, fast state


Analytics store
Kafka → Analytics
Off the live response path



BAD:  every request → Management + Auth + Analytics + DB + target
GOOD: memory + local JWT + Redis if needed + target
      (+ Kafka fire-and-forget style analytics)

title: Lecture 41 — GateKeeper project #1
section: Topic 5 — Redis vs Kafka (do not mix them up)
text:
Topic 5 — Redis vs Kafka (do not mix them up)








Question
Redis here
Kafka here




Job
Immediate shared state
Durable async events


Examples
Rate-limit counters, idempotency keys
Access events, config notifications


Retention
Short TTL
Topic retention policy


On request path?
Yes, when policy needs it
Publish; client does not wait for Analytics



Rate limiting: atomic increment + limit check + TTL window.
Idempotency (POST): same key → return saved success instead of repeating a write.
Access events: never log passwords, JWTs, or Authorization headers.

text:
Topic 6 — Ownership map



Store
Owner
Holds

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Video: OAuth 2.0 Masterclass | Google Login, OIDC & PKCE | Full Course #39
Playlist index: 39
Builds on: Lecture 38 (tokens & trust)

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Big idea in one line
“Login with Google” does not mean users type their Google password into your app.
Google authenticates them; your app receives permission (and identity) through a standard protocol: OAuth 2.0 (+ OpenID Connect for “who is this user?”).
User → Your app → redirect → Google login + consent
                         ← redirect back with code
Your app ↔ Google        exchange code → tokens
Your app                 create local session / your JWT

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
section: Topic 1 — Why not collect Google passwords?
text:
Topic 1 — Why not collect Google passwords?
If users gave you their Google password, you could open Drive, Photos, Mail, …
Nobody should do that. OAuth exists so Google stays the identity provider; you only get scoped access the user approved.

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Topic 2 — Main actors







Actor
Plain role




Resource owner
The user


Client
Your application


Authorization server
Google (login + consent + codes/tokens)


Resource server
Google APIs (Calendar, …) when you call them with an access token

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Topic 3 — Scope and consent
Scope = what you ask for (openid, email, profile, or API scopes like calendar read).
Consent = Google shows the user a screen: “Allow this app to …?”
Ask fewer scopes → easier consent → less risk
Ask powerful scopes → user may refuse

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Topic 4 — OAuth vs OpenID Connect (OIDC)









OAuth 2.0
OpenID Connect




Main job
Authorization — allow access to resources
Authentication — prove who logged in


Typical token
Access token
ID token (+ often access token too)


Question answered
“What may this client do?”
“Who is the user?”



For “Sign in with Google,” you want OIDC (login), not only “call Google Calendar.”
ID token     → for your app (identity claims: sub, email, …)
Access token → for calling Google APIs (if scopes allow)

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:
Topic 5 — Authorization Code flow (browser apps)
Common happy path:

User clicks “Continue with Google”

Browser redirects to Google with client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state, …

User logs in + consents

Google redirects to your redirect_uri with an authorization code (+ state)

Your backend exchanges the code for tokens (server-side, with client secret when using confidential clients)

You create your own logged-in state (session or your JWT)

state parameter: random value you send and verify on return → helps stop CSRF on the redirect.

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
section: Topic 6 — PKCE (why mobile / public clients need it)
text:
Topic 6 — PKCE (why mobile / public clients need it)
PKCE (“pixy”) protects the authorization code when a client cannot keep a secret safe (SPA / mobile).
Before redirect:
  create code_verifier (random)
  create code_challenge = hash(verifier)
  send challenge to Google

Token exchange:
  send code + code_verifier
  Google checks verifier matches earlier challenge
Even if an attacker steals the redirect code, they lack the verifier → exchange fails.

title: Lecture 39 — OAuth 2.0, OIDC & PKCE
text:

(Exact property names follow Boot’s OAuth2 client registration format.)


Step 4 — Security config
http
  .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
      .requestMatchers("/", "/error").permitAll()
      .anyRequest().authenticated()
  )
  .oauth2Login(Customizer.withDefaults());


Step 5 — Test

Run app → open a protected URL

Redirect to Google → login → consent

Land back authenticated

Inspect principal / attributes (email, sub) in a controller



Step 6 — Connect to your own JWT (optional bridge)
Many APIs still issue your JWT after Google login succeeds, so mobile clients talk to you the same way as password login.

Topic 8 — Safety checklist







Do
Don’t




Use HTTPS in real environments
Put client secrets in front-end JS


Verify state
Ask for every Google scope “just in case”


Store secrets in env / secret manager
Log ID tokens / access tokens


Understand redirect URI must match exactly

text:

OAuth 2.0  → authorization (access token + scopes + consent)
OIDC       → authentication (ID token = who)
Auth code  → browser redirect dance
PKCE       → protect public clients during code exchange
Spring     → oauth2Login + client registration for Google

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Video: Spring JWT Authentication | JWT Internals & Stateless Security | Full Course #38
Playlist index: 38
Builds on: Lecture 37

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Big idea in one line
HTTP requests do not remember each other.
Stateful apps remember you with a server session. Stateless JWT apps remember you by sending a signed token on every request—and the server rebuilds Authentication from that token.
STATEFUL                         STATELESS (JWT)
────────                         ───────────────
login → create session           login → create JWT
cookie: session id               client stores token
next request: cookie             next request: Authorization: Bearer <jwt>
server loads session context     server verifies signature → builds Authentication

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Topic 1 — Why sessions feel “sticky”
After form/basic login with sessions:

Server stores security info (or a pointer to it)
Browser sends session cookie automatically
Scale-out needs sticky sessions or shared session store

That works. APIs and mobile clients often prefer tokens instead.

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Topic 2 — What a JWT is
JWT = JSON Web Token (often said “jot”).
Three parts separated by dots:
header.payload.signature







Part
Holds




Header
Algorithm + type (e.g. HS256, JWT)


Payload
Claims (sub, roles, exp, …) — readable (Base64), not secret


Signature
Proves the payload was not tampered with (needs server secret/key)



Anyone can decode payload
Only someone with the key can forge a valid signature
Important: default signed JWT is not encryption. Do not put passwords or secrets inside claims.
Related ideas (names only):

JWS — signed token (common API JWT)
JWE — encrypted token (different goal)

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Topic 4 — Custom JWT filter (idea)
Place a filter before username/password filters:
Request
  → JwtAuthFilter
       if Bearer token present:
         parse + verify
         build Authentication
         SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(...)
  → rest of chain
  → controller
If no token and URL is public → continue.
If token invalid → 401.
If valid → authorization rules use the authorities from the token/DB policy you chose.

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Topic 5 — Practice lab (IDE)

Step 1 — Dependencies

Spring Web, Spring Security, JPA (as before)
A JWT library commonly used in courses (e.g. JJWT) — add matching version for your Boot/Java



Step 2 — JwtService responsibilities
Keep it small:

generateToken(username, roles) → string
extractUsername(token)
isValid(token, username) / check expiry

Use a long random secret from config (application.properties), never hard-code in git for real apps.


Step 3 — Login endpoint
@PostMapping("/login")
public Map<String, String> login(@RequestBody LoginRequest req) {
    authenticationManager.authenticate(
        new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(req.username(), req.password())
    );
    String token = jwtService.generateToken(req.username());
    return Map.of("token", token);
}
Only issue a token after authentication succeeds.


Step 4 — Security config

Stateless sessions
CSRF disabled for token API demos
Permit /register, /login
Add JWT filter into the chain
anyRequest().authenticated()



Step 5 — Postman flow

Register user

Login → copy token

Call /api/secure with header Authorization: Bearer <token>

Tamper one character of the token → should fail signature check

Wait until exp passes → should fail as expired

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Topic 6 — Design trade-offs (honest)







Topic
Note




Logout
Server cannot “delete” a pure JWT easily; use short expiry + refresh strategy / blocklist if needed


Secret leak
Attacker can forge tokens until you rotate keys


Fat tokens
Huge payloads waste bandwidth; keep claims small


Revocation
Not free in pure stateless design

title: Lecture 38 — JWT authentication
text:
Short map to keep
JWT = header.payload.signature
Payload is readable → signature is the trust
Login verifies password → issues JWT
Each request: Bearer token → verify → SecurityContext
SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS for token APIs

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Video: Spring Security Authentication Internals | Complete Login Flow | Full Course #37
Playlist index: 37
Builds on: Lectures 35–36

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Big idea in one line
You should not reinvent login as a random controller method.
Spring Security already has a pipeline: filter → AuthenticationManager → AuthenticationProvider → UserDetailsService → PasswordEncoder → SecurityContext.
POST credentials
      │
      ▼
UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter (or your equivalent)
      │  builds Authentication (not yet trusted)
      ▼
AuthenticationManager
      │
      ▼
DaoAuthenticationProvider
      │  loadUserByUsername + password matches
      ▼
Authenticated Authentication
      │
      ▼
SecurityContextHolder  (saved for this request / session)

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 1 — Stop hand-rolled “fake login”
In earlier practice you may have written something like “check username/password in /login yourself.”
Problems:

Easy to forget hashing rules
Easy to forget setting SecurityContext
Easy to disagree with the rest of the filter chain (CSRF, session, logout, …)

Better: let Security’s authentication architecture own the verify step; your code supplies UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder + URL rules.

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 2 — AuthenticationManager and providers
AuthenticationManager
   └── delegates to one or more AuthenticationProvider
            └── DaoAuthenticationProvider  (username/password + UserDetailsService)
DaoAuthenticationProvider (the one you use for DB login):

Call UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername
Use PasswordEncoder.matches
Check account flags (enabled, locked, …)
Return a fully authenticated Authentication with authorities

You rarely call the provider yourself. The manager does.

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 3 — UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken
Two common states of the same class:







State
Meaning




Unauthenticated token
principal = username, credentials = password


Authenticated token
principal = UserDetails, credentials cleared/null, authorities set



That is how a “claim” becomes a “verified identity.”

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 4 — Filter chain groups (mental model)
You do not memorize every filter name on day one. Group them:
1) Exploit protection   → CSRF, headers, …
2) Authentication       → prove identity / read credentials
3) Authorization        → allow or deny based on authorities
4) Misc / special       → logout, anonymous, exception translation, …
Request walks the chain. Fail early when needed. Success → controller.
CSRF note: browser form/session apps care a lot; pure Bearer-token APIs often disable CSRF when sessions are not used (JWT lecture next). Know why before copying a snippet.

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 5 — What “login success” stores
After success:

Authenticated Authentication is created

Placed into SecurityContext

For stateful apps, the context is tied to an HTTP session (cookie) so the next request remembers you

Stateful:
  login once → session id cookie → later requests reuse SecurityContext

Next lecture (JWT):
  login once → token to client → each request sends token → rebuild Authentication

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Topic 6 — Practice lab (IDE)

Step 1 — Keep DB user setup from lecture 36
User entity, repository, CustomUserDetails, CustomUserDetailsService, BCryptPasswordEncoder.


Step 2 — Security filter chain
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()) // OK for simple API demos; revisit for browsers+sessions
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/register", "/login").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated()
        )
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults());
        // or .formLogin(...) for browser form login
    return http.build();
}


Step 3 — Optional: expose AuthenticationManager
Useful when you later issue tokens after verifying credentials:
@Bean
AuthenticationManager authenticationManager(AuthenticationConfiguration config) throws Exception {
    return config.getAuthenticationManager();
}


Step 4 — Trace a login in the debugger (best learning step)

Set breakpoints in CustomUserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername

Call a secured endpoint with Basic Auth (or hit form login)

Watch: service loads user → password check → context filled

In a controller, print SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getAuthorities()



Step 5 — Fail paths to try



Try
Expect




Unknown username
401 / bad credentials


Wrong password
401 / bad credentials


Valid user, missing role for URL
403 if you add hasRole rules



Example role rule:
.requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
section: Topic 7 — How to reason when login breaks
text:
Topic 7 — How to reason when login breaks
Ask in order:

Is UserDetailsService a Spring bean?

Is the password in DB really BCrypt (not plain)?

Are you encoding again on login by mistake?

Is the URL permitted or secured as you think?

Did the Authentication land in SecurityContext after success?

title: Lecture 37 — Authentication internals
text:
Short map to keep
Filter receives credentials
  → AuthenticationManager
  → DaoAuthenticationProvider
  → UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder
  → authenticated Authentication
  → SecurityContext ( (+ session if stateful) )
  → Authorization filters / method security
  → Controller

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
text:
Video: Spring Security DB Authentication & Password Security | Full Course #36
Playlist index: 36
Builds on: Lecture 35

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
text:
Big idea in one line
Spring Security does not talk to your User entity directly.
You load users from the DB, wrap them as UserDetails, and store only hashed passwords (usually BCrypt).
Your table: users (id, username, password_hash, roles, …)
                │
                ▼
        UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(...)
                │
                ▼
           UserDetails   ← what Security understands
                │
                ▼
     PasswordEncoder matches raw password vs hash

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
section: Topic 1 — Why not store plain passwords?
text:
Topic 1 — Why not store plain passwords?
If the DB leaks and passwords are plain text → every account is stolen.
Even “fast hashes” are weak against modern cracking (GPUs + rainbow tables of common passwords).
Need:

One-way hash (cannot reverse to the original password)
Slow enough on purpose (limits guessing speed)
Salt (same password → different hash for different users)

BCrypt does slow hashing + salting for you.

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
text:
Topic 2 — PasswordEncoder
Spring Security’s interface:
@Bean
PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
}



Method
When you use it




encode(raw)
Register / change password → store the result


matches(raw, encoded)
Login → compare typed password to DB hash



Never write your own “encrypt password with Base64.” That is encoding, not security.
Register:
  "secret123" ──encode──► "$2a$10$...."  ──save──► DB

Login:
  typed "secret123" + DB hash ──matches?──► true / false

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
text:
Topic 3 — UserDetails (Security’s user shape)
Security expects a UserDetails with roughly:

username
password (the hash)
authorities / roles
flags: account enabled? locked? expired? credentials expired?

Your JPA entity can stay as User.
You build a bridge (wrapper / adapter) that implements UserDetails and reads from that entity.
Entity User  ──wrap──►  CustomUserDetails implements UserDetails
Plain words: map your world to Security’s world.

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
text:
Topic 6 — Common mistakes







Mistake
Fix




Save plain password
Always encode on register


Double-encode on login
Login uses matches, not encode again for storage


Role without ROLE_ prefix when using hasRole
Be consistent: hasRole("USER") expects ROLE_USER


Forgetting unique username
Add DB unique constraint

title: Lecture 36 — DB authentication & password security
text:
Short map to keep
Register → encode(password) → save hash
Login    → load UserDetails → matches(raw, hash)
UserDetailsService → bridge DB → Security
BCrypt → slow hash + salt

title: Lecture 35 — Spring Security basics
text:
Video: Spring Security | Authentication, Authorization & SecurityContext | Full Course #35
Playlist index: 35
Builds on: Web apps, filters, and REST controllers from earlier lectures

title: Lecture 35 — Spring Security basics
text:
Big idea in one line
Never trust the client.
Spring Security sits in front of your controllers, checks who you are (authentication) and what you may do (authorization), and stores that answer in a SecurityContext.
Client (browser / Postman / mobile)
        │
        ▼
   Tomcat / servlet container
        │
        ▼
   Spring Security filter chain   ← decide: allow / deny / challenge
        │
        ▼
   DispatcherServlet → Controllers

title: Lecture 35 — Spring Security basics
section: Why security is a server job
text:
Why security is a server job
A trust boundary is crossed when a request leaves one world and enters another (internet → your app).
Front-end tricks are not security:

Hide an “Admin” button in HTML → a user can still call /api/admin with Postman or curl
Client-side checks are UX, not protection

Rule: every protected action must be enforced on the server.

title: Lecture 35 — Spring Security basics
text:
Topic 1 — Authentication vs authorization








Word
Plain meaning
Guard analogy




Authentication
“Prove who you claim to be”
Show your employee ID at the gate


Authorization
“Are you allowed to do this?”
ID accepted, but you still cannot sit in the CEO office



Claim: "I am Aditya"
   │
   ├─ proof (password, token, Google login, …)
   ▼
Authentication OK  →  principal known
   │
   ▼
Authorization      →  roles / authorities checked for this URL or method

Authentication factors (quick map)



Factor
Meaning
Example




Something you know
Secret knowledge
Password, PIN


Something you have
Physical / device
Phone OTP, hardware key


Something you are
Biometric
Fingerprint, face



MFA = use more than one factor.

title: Lecture 35 — Spring Security basics
section: Topic 2 — Core objects you must know
text:
Topic 2 — Core objects you must know
SecurityContextHolder
        │  getContext()
        ▼
   SecurityContext          ← “who is current for this thread?”
        │  getAuthentication()
        ▼
   Authentication           ← principal + credentials + authorities + authenticated?

Authentication
Holds:

principal — who (often a username or user object)
credentials — proof (password / token); often cleared after success
authorities — permissions / roles (ROLE_USER, ROLE_ADMIN, …)
authenticated flag — claim verified or not yet

You will see two “modes” of the same idea:

Request — username/password just arrived (not verified yet)
Result — verified principal with authorities filled in



SecurityContext
A small container that holds the current Authentication.


SecurityContextHolder
Static helper that gives you that context (usually via ThreadLocal, so one request thread → one user).
Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
String name = auth.getName();
Any layer can ask “who is calling?” without passing the user through every method by hand.

title: Lecture 35 — Spring Security basics
text:
Topic 3 — Where Security runs (filters)
Spring Security plugs into the filter layer between the servlet container and DispatcherServlet.
Request
  → Filter1 (e.g. CSRF / headers)
  → Filter2 (authentication)
  → Filter3 (authorization)
  → …
  → Servlet / Controller
If authentication fails → response stops early (401 / login redirect).
If authorization fails → 403 Forbidden.
Boot + spring-boot-starter-security auto-configures a default filter chain and a default user (until you customize it).

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Topic 1 — Default behaviour (refresh)
Typical Boot defaults you feel in practice:

Propagation: REQUIRED

Rollback on runtime exceptions

Isolation: database default (often READ_COMMITTED)

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Topic 2 — Propagation cheat sheet



Mode
If TX already exists
If none




REQUIRED
Join it
Create one


REQUIRES_NEW
Suspend it; start new
Create one


SUPPORTS
Join it
Run with no TX


MANDATORY
Join it
Throw


NOT_SUPPORTED
Suspend; run without TX
Run without TX


NEVER
Throw
Run without TX


NESTED
Savepoint inside current
Create one



REQUIRED (default) — “be part of the caller’s unit of work”
REQUIRES_NEW       — “commit/rollback myself even if outer fails later”
NESTED             — “partial rollback via savepoint” (DB support matters)

Mental pictures
Outer REQUIRED
  └─ Inner REQUIRED     → same TX

Outer REQUIRED
  └─ Inner REQUIRES_NEW → inner commits alone; outer can still roll back its own work
Use REQUIRES_NEW for things like audit logs that must persist even when the business TX fails — carefully.

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Topic 3 — Commit / rollback attributes







Attribute
Use




rollbackFor
Also roll back for these exception types (e.g. checked)


noRollbackFor
Do not roll back for these


readOnly
Hint: reads only (optimizations / intent)


timeout
Fail if TX runs too long (seconds)



@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
public void importFile() throws Exception {
    // checked exceptions also roll back
}

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Topic 4 — Isolation levels (why they exist)
Concurrent transactions can cause:



Phenomenon
Plain meaning




Dirty read
See another TX’s uncommitted change


Non-repeatable read
Re-read a row; committed data changed


Phantom read
Re-query a range; new matching rows appear



Isolation ↑  →  fewer surprises, often more locking / less concurrency
Isolation ↓  →  more concurrency, more anomaly risk

Common levels







Level
Rough protection




READ_UNCOMMITTED
Allows dirty reads


READ_COMMITTED
No dirty reads (common default)


REPEATABLE_READ
Same row reads stay stable (phantoms depend on DB)


SERIALIZABLE
Strongest; transactions feel almost one-at-a-time



@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ)
public void reportBalances() { }
Exact behaviour is database-specific. Always verify with your DB docs when tuning.

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Topic 5 — Choosing attributes (practical)
Ask:

Should this method share the caller’s success/failure? → REQUIRED

Must this succeed independently? → REQUIRES_NEW

Is this read-mostly reporting? → readOnly = true (+ isolation if needed)

Do checked exceptions mean business failure? → rollbackFor

Do not crank isolation to SERIALIZABLE everywhere “to be safe.” Measure need vs throughput.

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Practice lab

Outer service method REQUIRED calls inner REQUIRED; throw in outer after inner write — both roll back.

Change inner to REQUIRES_NEW; throw in outer after inner returns — inner changes remain.

Call a MANDATORY method with no outer TX — expect failure.

Add rollbackFor = Exception.class and throw a checked exception — confirm rollback.

(Optional) Two threads: demonstrate why isolation matters with concurrent updates (keep the demo small).

title: Lecture 34 — Propagation & isolation
text:
Short map to keep
@Transactional
  propagation → join / new / nested / none / reject
  isolation   → how much concurrent visibility
  rollbackFor → which exceptions undo work
  readOnly / timeout → intent & limits

title: Lecture 33 — Spring transactions
text:
Big idea in one line
A transaction is one business unit of work.
All steps succeed together, or none stick. Spring’s @Transactional marks that boundary so you do not hand-write begin/commit/rollback every time.
Transfer ₹1000 A → B
  UPDATE A  -1000
  UPDATE B  +1000
Must be ONE transaction (not half a transfer)

title: Lecture 33 — Spring transactions
text:

Letter
Meaning




A Atomicity
All or nothing


C Consistency
Valid state → valid state (rules/constraints hold)


I Isolation
Concurrent TXs do not corrupt each other carelessly


D Durability
After commit, result survives crash



Isolation details deepen in lecture 34.

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1
text:

Playlist index: 31
Builds on: 30 — JPA relationships

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1
text:
Big idea in one line
Three separate knobs:

Cascade — if I persist/delete parent, should children follow?

Fetch type — load related data now or later?

Fetch plan per query — for this use case, what graph do I need? (EntityGraph / join fetch)

Cascade  ≠  ownership (mappedBy / JoinColumn)
Lazy     ≠  "never load"
EAGER    ≠  guaranteed single JOIN SQL

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1
text:
Topic 1 — Cascading
Cascade = propagate a persistence operation along a relationship.
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
private List<OrderItem> items = new ArrayList<>();
order.addItem(item1);
order.addItem(item2);
em.persist(order); // also persists item1, item2 if PERSIST cascade

Cascade types



Type
Propagates




PERSIST
persist


MERGE
merge


REMOVE
remove


REFRESH
refresh


DETACH
detach


ALL
all of the above



Not on by default. Add only when lifecycles truly belong together (order + order lines). Avoid REMOVE on shared many-to-many (deleting a student must not delete a shared course).
Helper still required for owning side:
public void addItem(OrderItem item) {
    items.add(item);
    item.setOrder(this);
}

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1
text:
Topic 2 — Lazy vs Eager



Fetch
Meaning




LAZY
Load association when first needed (hint)


EAGER
Association must be available when entity is loaded




JPA defaults



Relationship
Default




@ManyToOne / @OneToOne
EAGER


@OneToMany / @ManyToMany
LAZY



Practical habit: make to-one LAZY too, then fetch explicitly per use case.
@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinColumn(name = "department_id")
private Department department;
find(Student)
  SELECT student columns...
  department = proxy (not loaded)

student.getDepartment().getName()
  SELECT department...   ← triggered now

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1
text:
Topic 3 — N+1 problem
Pattern:

1 query loads N parents

Loop touches a lazy association → up to N more queries

List<Student> students = // findAll students
for (Student s : students) {
    System.out.println(s.getDepartment().getName()); // may query each time
}
SELECT * FROM student;                 -- 1
SELECT * FROM department WHERE id=?;   -- +1 per distinct miss
...
L1 cache can reduce duplicates (100 students, 3 departments → maybe 1+3), but the design smell remains: relationship access hides SQL.
Same idea for collections:
SELECT * FROM department;                      -- 1
SELECT * FROM student WHERE department_id=1;   -- N times
Lazy is not the enemy. Missing a fetch plan for a known use case is.
Switching mapping to EAGER is a blunt fix: loads association even when unused, and may still use extra selects.

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1
text:
Topic 4 — Detect with SQL logging
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG
Run the loop. Count statements. If you see repeats inside a for-loop, you found N+1.

title: Lecture 31 — Cascading, lazy loading & N+1

text:
Practice lab

@ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) on Student.department.

findAll students; loop print department names; count SQL.

Add @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "department") on a query method.

Repeat loop; SQL count should drop.

Add cascade = PERSIST on Order.items; persist order with two new items in one call.

text:
Short map to keep
Cascade:  parent op → child ops (lifecycle)
Lazy:     load later when touched
N+1:      1 + N hidden queries in a loop
Fix:      EntityGraph / join fetch per use case

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Big idea in one line
EntityManager is not “just a SQL helper.”
It holds a persistence context: a short-lived workspace of managed entities for one unit of work (usually one transaction).
@Service method (@Transactional)
        │
        ▼
 persistence context (1st-level cache)
   map of managed entities
        │
        ▼
 flush → SQL to DB
        │
        ▼
 commit → DB transaction ends

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 1 — Spec vs provider (again, sharper)
JPA annotations + EntityManager API
              │
              ▼
        Hibernate Session
              │
              ▼
             JDBC
You code to JPA. Hibernate tracks state, builds SQL, caches entities in the persistence context.

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 2 — Persistence context
Plain meaning: Hibernate’s memory of entities it is currently managing.







Question
Answer




Where do managed entities live?
Persistence context


How long?
Typically for the transaction


What is first-level cache?
That same context (per persistence context, not app-wide)



Student a = em.find(Student.class, 1L);
Student b = em.find(Student.class, 1L);
// a == b  (same managed instance) inside same context
Second find often hits L1 cache → no second SELECT for same id.

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 3 — Entity lifecycle states
          persist()
 transient ───────► managed ◄──── merge() (returns managed copy)
                       │  ▲
              remove() │  │ refresh / find again in new context...
                       ▼  │
                    removed    detached
                                 ▲
                                 │ clear() / transaction end / em.close()



State
Meaning




Transient
New Java object, not known to Hibernate yet


Managed
Tracked by persistence context; changes can auto-flush


Detached
Was managed; context no longer tracks it


Removed
Scheduled for DELETE on flush



Important: managed ≠ “SQL already ran.” Inserts/updates often wait until flush.

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 4 — Dirty checking & flush
@Transactional
public void rename(Long id, String name) {
    Student s = em.find(Student.class, id); // managed
    s.setName(name);                        // dirty
} // end → flush → UPDATE → commit
Dirty checking: compare current field values to loaded snapshot
Flush:          push pending SQL to the database
Commit:         finish the DB transaction



Myth
Reality




Setter runs UPDATE immediately
Usually waits until flush


flush() == commit()
Flush writes SQL; commit ends transaction


detach() deletes the row
No — only stops tracking



Manual flush (rare in normal apps):
em.flush();  // SQL now, transaction still open
Batch tip: after many inserts, flush() + clear() keeps memory small.

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 5 — Why @Transactional on the service
Spring starts a transaction, binds an EntityManager/Session to that work, then commits or rolls back.
Controller
   → Service proxy (@Transactional)
        begin TX + persistence context
        → repository / EntityManager calls
        flush + commit (or rollback)
Self-invocation note (same as AOP): calling this.method() inside the same class may skip the proxy → no new transaction boundary. Prefer calling through another Spring bean.

Which ops need a transaction?



Operation
Usually needs TX?




find (simple)
Often works read-only / auto


persist / merge / remove / flush
Yes



Put write methods in @Transactional service methods.

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 6 — First-level cache limits
L1 helps same id lookups in one persistence context.
It does not:

Share across HTTP requests / different transactions by default

Automatically make every JPQL query use the cache the same way as find

Replace a second-level cache (separate topic)

Request A TX          Request B TX
 context A            context B
 (own L1)             (own L1)

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Topic 7 — Handy EntityManager methods



Method
Plain use




persist
New entity → managed (insert later)


find
Load by PK (uses L1)


remove
Managed entity → delete later


merge
Copy detached state into a managed instance


flush
Sync SQL now


clear
Detach all (empty L1)


detach
Detach one


refresh
Reload from DB (overwrite memory)


contains
Is this instance managed here?

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Practice lab

In one @Transactional method: find the same id twice; print a == b.

Change a field; enable show-sql; confirm UPDATE timing (end of method).

Call em.flush() mid-method; watch SQL appear earlier.

After commit, in a new transaction, find again — new managed instance.

Try modifying a detached entity outside a context; notice no automatic UPDATE.

title: Lecture 29 — Hibernate internals
text:
Short map to keep
@Transactional service
   persistence context = L1 cache
   entities: transient → managed → detached/removed
   setters on managed → dirty → flush SQL → commit

title: Lecture 28 — Hibernate fundamentals
text:
Big idea in one line
ORM maps objects ↔︎ tables.

Your code (Student objects)
        │

title: Lecture 28 — Hibernate fundamentals
text:
Topic 1 — Why ORM after JDBC?
With JDBC / Spring JDBC you always:

Write INSERT/SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE text

Bind params in order

Map columns → fields by hand

That grows painful with many entities and relationships.
Object-relational impedance mismatch: Java thinks in objects/references; DB thinks in tables/keys/joins. ORM is the translator.

title: Lecture 28 — Hibernate fundamentals
text:
Topic 2 — JPA vs Hibernate (simple)







Name
Role




JPA / Jakarta Persistence
Spec / interfaces / annotations (@Entity, EntityManager)


Hibernate
Popular implementation (does the real work)



List  → ArrayList
JPA   → Hibernate
In Boot you usually import jakarta.persistence.*. Runtime engine is still Hibernate when JPA starter is used.

text:

Property
Plain meaning

Hibernate may create/alter tables from entities (ok for learning)

HikariCP is Boot’s default pool when JDBC starter is present.



Idea

Pool size
How many connections sit ready


Borrow
Get one for your work


Return

title: Lecture 24 — Pointcuts & proxy types
text:
Big idea in one line
Pointcuts choose which methods get advice.
Proxy type chooses how Spring wraps the bean (interface-based JDK proxy vs subclass-based CGLIB) — and that affects what can be intercepted.
Pointcut expression ──► matching methods
Spring wraps bean ────► JDK proxy OR CGLIB proxy
Caller uses proxy ────► advice runs

title: Lecture 24 — Pointcuts & proxy types
text:
Topic 1 — execution pointcut (most common)
Shape:
execution( modifiers? return-type declaring-type? method-name(params) throws? )
Examples:
// any method in a package
execution(* com.example.demo.service.*.*(..))

// any public method named save
execution(public * save(..))

// ProductService only
execution(* com.example.demo.service.ProductService.*(..))

// one arg
execution(* com.example.demo.service.*.*(*))

// starts with get
execution(* com.example.demo.service.*.get*(..))



Piece
Meaning




* return
any return type


.. in params
any number of args (including 0)


* in params
exactly one arg of any type


* in name/package
wildcard segment

title: Lecture 24 — Pointcuts & proxy types
Lecture 24 — Pointcuts & proxy types
Lecture 24 — Pointcuts & proxy types
section: Topic 4 — JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB
text:
Topic 4 — JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB
Bean implements an interface?
  │
  ├─ YES (classic Spring default story)
  │     JDK dynamic proxy
  │     - implements the same interface(s)
  │     - cast to interface type works
  │     - cast to concrete class may fail
  │
  └─ NO  (class only)  OR Boot often prefers CGLIB anyway
        CGLIB proxy
        - subclass of the concrete class
        - works without an interface

Practical rules

Prefer injecting the interface type (OrderService) not the impl class when you have one.

Final classes / methods are hard or impossible for CGLIB to override — advice may not apply.

Private methods are not advised by Spring AOP (only public calls through the proxy on Spring beans).

Self-invocation: this.helper() inside the same class bypasses the proxy → no advice on helper().

Wrong (self-call)                 Right
─────────────────                 ─────
@Service                          @Service
class S {                         class S {
  void a(){ this.b(); }             void a(){ other.b(); } // or inject self carefully
  void b(){ ... }  // no advice     ...
}                                 }

Step 4 — Self-invocation surprise

From method a(), call this.b() where b matches the pointcut.

Move the call to another bean (or redesign) and see advice return.



Step 5 — Final method experiment (optional)
Make a matched method final and see whether advice still applies with CGLIB (often breaks). Restore after learning.

title: Lecture 22 — AOP basics
text:
Big idea in one line
AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming) lets you keep shared behavior — logging, timing, transactions, security checks — in one place (aspect), and apply it to many methods without copy-paste.
Spring usually does this with a proxy around your bean.
Without AOP                         With AOP
───────────                         ────────
OrderService.place()                OrderService.place()  ← clean business
  log...                              │
  time...                             ▼
  business                            Proxy
  log...                                ├─ log / time / security
                                        └─ real OrderService.place()

title: Lecture 22 — AOP basics
text:
Topic 1 — Cross-cutting concerns
A concern is “cross-cutting” when it cuts across many classes:



Concern
Shows up in




Logging
almost every service method


Timing
APIs / slow use-cases


Transactions
many service methods (@Transactional is AOP!)


Security
methods that need roles



Filters/Interceptors help for HTTP.
AOP helps for any Spring bean method (service layer especially).

title: Lecture 22 — AOP basics
text:
Topic 2 — Core vocabulary (simple)
Aspect     = the class that holds the extra behavior (@Aspect)
Advice     = the actual code that runs (@Before, @Around, ...)
Join point = a moment you could plug into (method call in Spring AOP)
Pointcut   = expression choosing which join points
Proxy      = wrapper bean clients actually call
Mindmap:
          @Aspect
             │
     ┌───────┴────────┐
 Pointcut          Advice
 "which methods?"  "what to run?"
             │
          Proxy applies both
             │
          Your @Service

title: Lecture 22 — AOP basics
text:
Topic 3 — Why proxies?
You ask Spring for OrderService.
If an aspect applies, Spring may give you a proxy object that implements the same API:
Client → orderService.place()
           │
           ▼
         Proxy
           ├─ run advice
           └─ call target.place() on real bean
Important limitation (preview): self-calls inside the same class (this.otherMethod()) do not go through the proxy, so advice may not run. Call through the injected bean/proxy instead. More in lecture 24.

title: Lecture 21 — Interceptors
text:
Big idea in one line
An Interceptor is Spring MVC middleware around the handler (controller method).
It is not a servlet Filter: it runs inside Spring, knows which controller method was chosen, and has three clear hooks.
Filter(s)
  → DispatcherServlet
      → Interceptor.preHandle
          → Controller
      → Interceptor.postHandle
      → Interceptor.afterCompletion
  ← response

title: Lecture 21 — Interceptors
text:
Filters vs Interceptors (keep this table)









Filter
Interceptor




API
Servlet (Filter)
Spring MVC (HandlerInterceptor)


Knows controller method?
No
Yes (handler argument)


Runs if no handler mapped?
Can still run
Tied to MVC handler execution


Typical use
Auth gate, encoding, raw logging
Audit handler name, MVC-specific checks, model tweaks



Use both in real apps: Filters for servlet-wide concerns; Interceptors when you need Spring MVC context.

title: Lecture 21 — Interceptors
Lecture 21 — Interceptors
Lecture 21 — Interceptors
Lecture 21 — Interceptors
text:
Topic 4 — Order of multiple interceptors
registry.addInterceptor(A);
registry.addInterceptor(B);

Incoming:  A.preHandle → B.preHandle → Controller
Outgoing:  B.postHandle → A.postHandle
Then:      B.afterCompletion → A.afterCompletion  (reverse for completion too)
Registration order matters.

title: Lecture 20 — Filters advanced
text:
Big idea in one line
Sometimes a Filter must change what controllers see (headers, parameters, body) or change what the client gets back.
Raw HttpServletRequest / HttpServletResponse are mostly read-once — so you wrap them with wrapper classes, then pass the wrappers down the chain.
Request  → wrap → chain.doFilter(wrappedReq, wrappedRes)
Response ← read from wrapper (body/headers you captured or changed)

title: Lecture 20 — Filters advanced
text:
Why wrappers?







Goal
Problem without wrapper




Read JSON body for logging
Input stream can be read only once — controller gets empty body


Add a custom header for downstream code
Hard to “inject” without wrapping


Change response body / add header after controller
Need to capture output, then write final bytes



Spring/servlet API gives:

HttpServletRequestWrapper

HttpServletResponseWrapper

helpers like ContentCachingRequestWrapper / ContentCachingResponseWrapper (Spring)

title: Lecture 20 — Filters advanced
Lecture 20 — Filters advanced
section: Topic 2 — Response headers after the controller

title: Lecture 20 — Filters advanced
Lecture 20 — Filters advanced
Lecture 20 — Filters advanced
text:
Picture: wrap → chain → unwrap
Filter.doFilter
  ├─ wrap request  (optional)
  ├─ wrap response (optional)
  ├─ chain.doFilter(wrappedReq, wrappedRes)
  │     └─ controller writes JSON into wrapper buffer
  ├─ inspect / tweak buffered response
  └─ copyBodyToResponse()  // send real bytes to client

title: Lecture 20 — Filters advanced
text:
Topic 5 — Practical caution

Do not log secrets (passwords, tokens) from bodies in production.

Large file uploads: caching whole body can blow memory — skip or limit paths.

Only wrap when you need to; plain logging of URL/status does not need body wrappers.

Order matters: body-caching filters usually sit early so later filters/controllers read through the same wrapper.

title: Lecture 20 — Filters advanced
text:
Practice lab (IDE steps)

Step 1 — Request id header

Build a request wrapper that adds X-Request-Id.

Pass wrapper into chain.doFilter.

In a controller, read request.getHeader("X-Request-Id") and return it in JSON.

Call the API → you should see a UUID you did not send.



Step 2 — Response header
After chain.doFilter, set X-Elapsed-Ms.
Check Postman headers tab.


Step 3 — Log response body

Wrap with ContentCachingResponseWrapper.

Call chain, print body, then copyBodyToResponse().

Remove copyBodyToResponse() once on purpose → empty client body (then put it back).



Step 4 — Log request JSON on POST
Use ContentCachingRequestWrapper, POST a JSON DTO, print body after the chain.
Confirm the controller still receives the DTO (body not consumed away).

title: Lecture 20 — Filters advanced
text:
Short map to keep
Need to change/read stream twice? → Wrapper
Request wrapper  → fake/extra headers, replay body
Response wrapper → capture body, then copyBodyToResponse()
Never forget copy for caching response wrappers

title: Lecture 19 — Filters basics
text:
Video: Spring Boot Filters | FilterChain, Logging, Auth & Request Flow | Spring Boot Full Course #19
Playlist index: 19
Builds on: Spring MVC request flow (DispatcherServlet)

title: Lecture 19 — Filters basics
text:
Big idea in one line
A Filter is servlet-level middleware: it can run before and after your Spring MVC stack, for logging, simple auth checks, timing, CORS headers, and blocking bad requests — without stuffing that into every controller.
Request
  → Filter 1
    → Filter 2
      → DispatcherServlet
        → Controller
      ← response
    ← Filter 2 (after)
  ← Filter 1 (after)
Response

title: Lecture 19 — Filters basics
text:
Why Filters? (cross-cutting for HTTP)
Cross-cutting = the same concern on many endpoints:

log method + URL + status

measure time taken

require an Authorization header

reject requests early

If you copy that into 20 controllers, you will miss endpoints. Filters sit outside controllers once.

title: Lecture 19 — Filters basics
section: Topic 1 — Where Filters sit in the flow
text:
Topic 1 — Where Filters sit in the flow
Client
  │
  ▼
Servlet container (Tomcat)
  │
  ├─ Filters  ◄── YOU ARE HERE (javax/jakarta.servlet.Filter)
  │
  ▼
DispatcherServlet (Spring MVC front controller)
  │
  ▼
HandlerMapping → Controller → View/JSON
Key: Filters see the raw HttpServletRequest / HttpServletResponse.
They run even for paths that later 404 inside MVC (depending on mapping), and they are older servlet API — not Spring MVC-specific.

title: Lecture 19 — Filters basics
Lecture 19 — Filters basics
Lecture 19 — Filters basics
Lecture 19 — Filters basics
text:
Topic 5 — What to log / check (practical)
Safe, useful request facts:

HTTP method

request URI / query string

client IP (req.getRemoteAddr() — proxies need extra headers later)

selected headers (never log raw passwords or full tokens in prod logs)

response status + duration

title: Lecture 19 — Filters basics
text:
Practice lab (IDE steps)

Step 1 — Add LoggingFilter

@Component class implementing Filter.

Log method + URI before chain.doFilter.

Log status + time after.

Hit any controller endpoint → see logs wrap the call.



Step 2 — Add AuthFilter with @Order

Higher order number than logging (runs after logging on the way in).

If header X-API-KEY != secret, return 401 JSON and return without chain.doFilter.

Postman without header → 401, controller never runs.

With header → controller runs.



Step 3 — Limit URL pattern (optional)
Register with FilterRegistrationBean for /api/* only.
Call /hello outside /api → auth filter should not block it.


Step 4 — Confirm order
Swap @Order values and watch which log line appears first.

title: Lecture 19 — Filters basics
section: When Filters are a good fit
text:
When Filters are a good fit







Use a Filter
Prefer something else




Logging every HTTP call
Method-level logging inside services → AOP later


Early reject before MVC
Business validation of body → @Valid


Servlet-level headers
Spring MVC model tweaks → Interceptor (next lecture)

title: Lecture 19 — Filters basics
text:
Short map to keep
Filter = servlet middleware
doFilter = your code around chain.doFilter
call chain   → continue
skip chain   → you own the response
@Order / FilterRegistrationBean = ordering + URL patterns
Runs BEFORE DispatcherServlet

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
text:
Video: Spring Boot Profiles & YAML Explained | Dev vs Prod Configuration | Spring Boot Full Course #18
Playlist index: 18
Builds on: application.properties / @Value from lecture 10

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
text:
Big idea in one line
Same app, different environments.
Use profiles (dev, prod, …) and optionally YAML so port, DB URL, logging, and feature flags change without editing Java.
application.yml          ← shared defaults
application-dev.yml      ← local/dev overrides
application-prod.yml     ← production overrides

spring.profiles.active=dev   ← which override pack is on

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
text:
Why profiles?



Environment
Typical needs




dev
H2 or local Postgres, verbose logs, maybe fake mail


prod
real DB, less noisy logs, real secrets from env



Hard-coding localhost in Java breaks the day you deploy. Profiles keep environment details in config files.

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
text:
Topic 1 — YAML vs properties (same idea)
Both are Spring config. YAML is nested and often easier to read:
properties
server.port=8080
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:demo
YAML
server:
  port: 8080
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:demo
Indentation matters in YAML. Wrong spaces = startup fail.
You can keep .properties if you prefer. Profiles work with both:

application-dev.properties / application-dev.yml

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
text:
Topic 2 — Profile-specific files
src/main/resources/
  application.yml           # always loaded
  application-dev.yml       # when profile "dev" is active
  application-prod.yml      # when profile "prod" is active
Example application.yml:
spring:
  application:
    name: demo-api

server:
  port: 8080
Example application-dev.yml:
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:devdb
  jpa:
    show-sql: true

logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.example: DEBUG
Example application-prod.yml:
server:
  port: 80

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db.example.com:5432/app
  jpa:
    show-sql: false

logging:
  level:
    root: WARN
Merge rule (simple mental model): base file loads first; active profile file(s) override matching keys.

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
section: Topic 3 — How to activate a profile
text:
Topic 3 — How to activate a profile

A) Inside config (good for local default)
spring:
  profiles:
    active: dev


B) IDE run configuration
IntelliJ / Eclipse: VM option or program arg:
-Dspring.profiles.active=dev
or
--spring.profiles.active=dev


C) Command line when running the jar
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod


D) Environment variable
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
Practical tip: do not bake prod as the only default in the repo. Prefer dev locally; set prod on the server.

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML

Boot starts
  │
  ├─ load application.yml
  ├─ see active profile = dev
  ├─ load application-dev.yml (overrides)
  ├─ create only @Profile("dev") beans
  └─ app runs with merged Environment

title: Lecture 18 — Profiles & YAML
text:
Practice lab (IDE steps)

Step 1 — Switch to YAML (optional)

Rename application.properties → application.yml (or add YAML beside it).

Move server.port and app name into YAML.

Run — app should still start.



Step 2 — Add profile files
Create application-dev.yml and application-prod.yml with different ports, e.g. 8081 vs 8082, and different logging.level.


Step 3 — Activate dev
Set spring.profiles.active=dev (file or IDE).
Run → confirm the dev port.


Step 4 — Switch to prod in the IDE
Change active profile to prod, run again → prod port / logging should apply.


Step 5 — Profile-only bean
Add a @Component @Profile("dev") that prints "Dev bean loaded" in @PostConstruct.
Run with dev → see message. Run with prod → bean absent.

text:
Short map to keep
application.yml        = shared
application-{name}.yml = overrides for that profile
spring.profiles.active = which override pack
@Profile("dev")        = create this bean only when dev is on
YAML ≈ nested properties (watch indentation)

title: Lecture 17 — Exception handling
text:
Video: Spring Boot Exception Handling: Make Your APIs Professional | Spring Boot Full Course #17
Playlist index: 17
Builds on: 16 — DTOs & Validations

title: Lecture 17 — Exception handling
text:
Big idea in one line
Controllers should not be full of try/catch.
Throw meaningful exceptions from services; catch them in one global handler and return a clear JSON error body + HTTP status.
Service throws ResourceNotFoundException
        │
        ▼
@RestControllerAdvice
  @ExceptionHandler(...)
        │
        ▼
JSON { message, status, ... } + 404

title: Lecture 17 — Exception handling
text:
Why central exception handling?
Without it:







What clients see
Why it is bad




Default Whitelabel / stack-ish error
Ugly, inconsistent, sometimes leaks internals


Different controllers invent different error JSON
Front-end cannot rely on one shape


try/catch copy-paste
Business code gets noisy



With a global handler: one error contract for the whole API.

title: Lecture 17 — Exception handling
Lecture 17 — Exception handling
Lecture 17 — Exception handling
Lecture 17 — Exception handling
Lecture 17 — Exception handling
Lecture 17 — Exception handling
text:
Picture: request with an error
POST /users  (invalid email)
  → Controller (@Valid fails)
  → MethodArgumentNotValidException
  → GlobalExceptionHandler
  → 400 + { field messages }

GET /products/999
  → Service throws ResourceNotFoundException
  → GlobalExceptionHandler
  → 404 + { message }

title: Lecture 17 — Exception handling
text:
Practice lab (IDE steps)

Step 1 — Add exceptions + ApiError
Create exception package with ResourceNotFoundException and ApiError record/class.


Step 2 — Throw from service
In getById / update / delete, use orElseThrow(...) instead of returning null.


Step 3 — Global handler
Add GlobalExceptionHandler with handlers for:

ResourceNotFoundException → 404

MethodArgumentNotValidException → 400

(optional) generic Exception → 500



Step 4 — Test in Postman

GET a missing id → 404 JSON with your shape

POST invalid DTO → 400 with field messages

Confirm happy path still returns 200/201



Step 5 — Confirm controllers stayed clean
No try/catch needed in controller methods for these cases.

title: Lecture 17 — Exception handling
text:
Short map to keep
Service throws domain exception
Controller stays clean
@RestControllerAdvice catches
  → pick HTTP status
  → build ApiError JSON
Validation failures = MethodArgumentNotValidException

title: Lecture 16 — DTOs & Validations
text:
Video: DTOs & Validations in Spring Boot | Make Your REST API Professional | Spring Boot Full Course #16
Playlist index: 16
Builds on: REST controllers + entities from earlier CRUD lectures

title: Lecture 16 — DTOs & Validations
text:
Big idea in one line
Do not expose your database entity as the API contract.
Use a DTO (Data Transfer Object) for what goes in/out of the HTTP layer, and validate that DTO before your service runs.
Client JSON
    │
    ▼
Request DTO  (+ @Valid rules)
    │
    ▼
Service maps DTO ↔ Entity
    │
    ▼
DB / Entity
    │
    ▼
Response DTO → JSON to client

title: Lecture 16 — DTOs & Validations
text:
Why DTOs? (plain problem)
If the controller accepts the Entity directly:







Risk
What goes wrong




Extra fields
Client can send id, role, createdAt and overwrite things


Leakage
Response may show password hashes, internal flags, relations


Coupling
Changing DB columns instantly changes your public API



DTO fix: the API shape is a separate class. The entity stays an internal detail.

section: Topic 1 — Request DTO vs Response DTO

title: Lecture 16 — DTOs & Validations
section: Topic 2 — Map Entity ↔︎ DTO (no magic required)

title: Lecture 16 — DTOs & Validations
text:

Step 1 — Project

Open your existing Boot Web + JPA product/user app (or a tiny new one from Initializr: Web + Validation + H2/JPA).
Confirm spring-boot-starter-validation is in the POM.



Step 2 — Create DTO package
Create dto package:

CreateProductRequest
ProductResponse



Step 3 — Annotate + map
On request fields use @NotBlank, @Positive (for price), @Size as needed.
In service: map request → entity → save → map entity → response.


Step 4 — Controller uses DTO only
Replace @RequestBody Product product with @Valid @RequestBody CreateProductRequest request.
Return ProductResponse, not the entity.


Step 5 — Break it on purpose (Postman)
Send invalid JSON:
{ "name": "", "price": -5 }
Expected: request fails validation (400). Controller method should not reach service save logic.
Send a valid body → 200/201 + response without internal-only fields.

Entity  = DB shape (internal)
DTO     = API shape (public)
@Valid  = "check annotations before method runs"
starter-validation = brings Hibernate Validator

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Video: Spring MVC Architecture | DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping & JSP Flow | Full Course #15
Playlist index: 15
Builds on: Lecture 14 · Lectures 11–13

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Big idea in one line
Spring MVC is still servlet-based.
One front controller — DispatcherServlet — receives every request, finds the right controller method, and builds the response (JSON or a JSP page).
Client → Tomcat → DispatcherServlet → Controller method → Response
Boot makes this easy. This lecture shows what Boot was hiding.

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
section: Topic 1 — Spring MVC vs Spring Boot
text:
Topic 1 — Spring MVC vs Spring Boot







Piece
Role




Spring MVC (spring-webmvc)
Web framework: mapping, controllers, views, JSON


Spring Boot
Auto-configures MVC + embedded Tomcat + Jackson for you



Boot does not replace MVC. Your @GetMapping methods are MVC features.
Without Boot you would manually:

start Tomcat

create Spring web context

register DispatcherServlet

enable WebMvc / component scan

add Jackson

With Boot + spring-boot-starter-web, most of that appears automatically.

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Topic 2 — Why DispatcherServlet?
Pure servlet style: one servlet per URL family.
/student/create → CreateStudentServlet
/student/get    → GetStudentServlet
/student/update → UpdateStudentServlet
Each servlet repeats parsing, routing ideas, response writing…
Spring MVC idea:

One central servlet receives everything, then dispatches to the correct handler method.

That central servlet is DispatcherServlet. It is still a normal servlet Tomcat can call.
Traditional:  URL → YourServlet
Spring MVC:   URL → DispatcherServlet → @Controller method

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Topic 3 — High-level request flow
Client HTTP request
        │
        ▼
Tomcat receives it
        │
        ▼
Tomcat calls DispatcherServlet
        │
        ▼
HandlerMapping: "which controller method?"
        │
        ▼
HandlerAdapter: "invoke that method"
        │
        ▼
Args resolved (@PathVariable, @RequestBody, …)
        │
        ▼
Controller → Service → Repository (your layers)
        │
        ▼
Return value handled
  ├─ REST: object → JSON (message converter)
  └─ MVC page: view name → ViewResolver → JSP
        │
        ▼
Client gets response
DispatcherServlet coordinates. Other components do specialized jobs.



Component
Job




DispatcherServlet
Front controller / coordinator


HandlerMapping
Map request → handler method


HandlerAdapter
Actually call the method


Argument resolvers
Fill method parameters


HttpMessageConverter
JSON ↔︎ Java (often Jackson)


ViewResolver
Logical view name → real page (JSP)

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Topic 4 — HandlerMapping
DispatcherServlet does not hardcode “GET /students/1 means getStudent.”
At startup:

Component scan finds @RestController / @Controller

HandlerMapping reads @GetMapping, @PostMapping, …

Builds an internal table

GET    /students/{id}  → StudentController.getStudent
POST   /students       → StudentController.createStudent
PUT    /students/{id}  → StudentController.updateStudent
DELETE /students/{id}  → StudentController.deleteStudent
At runtime it looks up that table.
Same path + different HTTP method can mean different handlers (GET list vs POST create).

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Topic 5 — HandlerAdapter
HandlerMapping finds the method.
HandlerAdapter runs it (prepare args, invoke, handle return).
DispatcherServlet
   asks Mapping  → "getStudent"
   asks Adapter  → "please call getStudent properly"

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
section: Topic 6 — How data reaches method parameters
text:
Topic 6 — How data reaches method parameters

Path variable
GET /students/10 + @GetMapping("/{id}") + @PathVariable Integer id → id = 10


Query param
GET /students?name=Rohit + @RequestParam String name → name = Rohit


Request body
POST JSON + @RequestBody Student student → Jackson fills the object.
JSON bytes → HttpMessageConverter (Jackson) → Student
Student return value → converter → JSON response
No-arg constructor on the model helps Jackson construct objects.

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
section: Topic 7 — Manual Spring MVC lab (no Boot)

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Practice lab (pick a path)

Path A — REST mental model (Boot project you already have)

Hit GET /api/students/1

Narrate: Tomcat → DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → controller → JSON



Path B — Manual App (follow the video)

Add webmvc + embed tomcat + jackson

Path C — JSP hello

@Controller returning "home"

InternalResourceViewResolver

home.jsp under WEB-INF/views

Open /home in a browser

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
section: How to reason when something fails
text:
How to reason when something fails

404 with Boot REST? Mapping/path/method mismatch — HandlerMapping found nothing.

Manual app: Tomcat up but Spring silent? DispatcherServlet not registered/mapped, or context not started with config.

JSON null / fail? Missing Jackson, missing getters, or no no-arg constructor.

JSP 404? ViewResolver prefix/suffix wrong, or file not under WEB-INF/views.

Returns literal "home" as text? You used @RestController instead of @Controller for a view.

title: Lecture 15 — Spring MVC architecture
text:
Short map to keep
Tomcat calls DispatcherServlet (front controller)
  → HandlerMapping picks @RequestMapping method
  → HandlerAdapter invokes it
  → converters / view resolvers finish the response

Boot = same MVC, less wiring
REST = @RestController + JSON
Pages = @Controller + ViewResolver + JSP
