title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Video: How Java Web Apps Actually Work | Servlets, Tomcat & WAR Files | Full Course #14
Playlist index: 14
Builds on: Lecture 2 · Lectures 11–13 (you already used HTTP APIs)

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Big idea in one line
Browsers speak HTTP, not Java.
Tomcat (a servlet container) receives HTTP and calls your Java servlet. Spring Boot embeds Tomcat so main() starts the server for you.
Browser ──HTTP text──► Tomcat ──calls──► Your Servlet (doGet/doPost/…)

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
section: Why this lecture after Boot CRUD?
text:
Why this lecture after Boot CRUD?
You already wrote @RestController methods. Under the hood, something still:

Listens on a port

Parses HTTP

Calls Java code

Writes an HTTP response

That “something” is the servlet world. Spring MVC sits on top of it (next lecture).

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 1 — Browser only sends HTTP
Opening http://localhost:8080/hello does not call HelloServlet.java directly.
The browser sends text roughly like:
GET /hello HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080
Java classes do not magically receive that. A server process must be listening on the port.

Could you use raw sockets?
Yes — ServerSocket on 8080. Then you manually parse URLs, headers, bodies, status codes, threads… forever.
Servlets exist so developers write business logic, not HTTP plumbing.
Without servlet container:
  Browser → raw socket code → you parse HTTP → you route → you write response

With servlet container:
  Browser → Tomcat → HttpServletRequest/Response → your Servlet class

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 2 — Static vs dynamic



Kind
Behavior




Static
Server returns an existing file (HTML/CSS/image)


Dynamic
Response depends on logic / DB / input (/user?id=101)



Dynamic needs Java (or another language). The missing link: how does HTTP enter Java? → Servlet.

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 4 — Tomcat = Servlet Container
Tomcat is a Java server. More precisely: a Servlet Container.
“Container” means it creates, manages, and controls objects — like Spring’s IoC container manages beans.
Tomcat manages:

servlet creation

init / service / destroy

request & response objects

threads

URL mapping

sending the response


Inversion of control (again)



Style
Who is in charge




Normal Java
You new the object and call methods


Servlet world
Tomcat creates and calls


Spring world
Spring container creates and injects



Same IoC idea. Different container.

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 5 — Request path through Tomcat
GET /myapp/hello
        │
        ▼
Tomcat: which app? → myapp
        which URL? → /hello
        which servlet? → HelloServlet
        which method? → doGet
        │
        ▼
helloServlet.doGet(request, response)
HttpServletRequest gives method, path, params, headers, body access.
HttpServletResponse lets you write status, headers, body.

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 6 — Servlet lifecycle
create object → init() → service() → doGet/doPost/… → destroy()



Method
When
Typical use




init()
Once after creation
One-time setup


service()
Every request
HttpServlet routes to doXxx


doGet / doPost / …
Matching HTTP verb
Your logic


destroy()
Once before removal
Close resources



Default: servlet often loads on first request (then reused).
One servlet object usually serves many requests — be careful with mutable instance fields under concurrency.
First  GET /lifecycle → constructor, init, service, doGet
Second GET /lifecycle → service, doGet   (no second init)
Stop Tomcat           → destroy

title: Lecture 14 — Servlets, Tomcat & WAR files
text:
Topic 7 — External Tomcat + WAR
Traditional flow:
Install Tomcat
  → build myapp.war
  → copy WAR into tomcat/webapps/
  → start Tomcat
  → app runs
Mental model: application goes inside Tomcat.

What is a WAR?
WAR = Web Application Archive. Packaged web app (classes, web.xml, static files, libs).
External Tomcat knows how to explode/run WARs under webapps/.
One Tomcat can host many apps:
/app1/hello  → servlet in app1
/app2/login  → servlet in app2


Start / stop (idea)



OS
Start
Stop




Windows
bin\startup.bat
bin\shutdown.bat


Mac/Linux

title: Lecture 10 — Application properties, @Value & runners
text:
Big idea in one line
Do not hardcode changeable values in Java.
Put them in config. Inject them into beans. Run startup code with a runner — not by hand from main.
Hardcoded Java values          Externalized config
─────────────────────          ───────────────────
provider = "Razorpay"   →      payment.provider=Razorpay
retry = 3               →      payment.retry-count=3

Change value? edit Java,       Change value? edit config
recompile, rebuild             (same code can stay)

title: Lecture 10 — Application properties, @Value & runners
text:
Why configuration files?
Tomorrow you may switch Razorpay → Stripe, or change retry count per environment.
If those values live inside a class:

Edit Java

Recompile

Rebuild

Redeploy

Painful for settings that change often.
Better place for them:

payment provider name

retry / timeout

feature flags

database URL / username

server port

Keep business logic in Java. Keep settings outside.

title: Lecture 10 — Application properties, @Value & runners
text:
Topic 1 — application.properties
Spring Boot loads this file by convention from:
src/main/resources/application.properties
Example:
payment.provider=Razorpay
payment.retry-count=3
payment.enabled=true
payment.timeout=5000
YAML works too (application.yml). Same idea, different writing style:
payment:
  provider: Razorpay
  retry-count: 3
  enabled: true
  timeout: 5000

Is this “external”?
The file inside src/main/resources is packaged into the JAR. Changing only that source file still needs a rebuild.
But Boot also reads overrides from outside the JAR:

environment variables

command-line args

system properties

external config files

Plain words: keep settings out of business methods so environments can differ without rewriting logic.
Dev:  payment.provider=TestProvider
Prod: payment.provider=Razorpay
Same PaymentService code in both places.

title: Lecture 10 — Application properties, @Value & runners
Lecture 10 — Application properties, @Value & runners
Lecture 10 — Application properties, @Value & runners
text:
Topic 4 — Why runner interfaces?
This lecture often uses Boot without Web. There is no controller endpoint to hit.
You still need code to run after the container is ready.
Options:

Manually call getBean from main (works, but feels like Core homework)

Let Boot call a runner bean automatically

Web style:     request → controller → service
No-web style:  startup → CommandLineRunner / ApplicationRunner → service

Why not call beans from main?
var context = SpringApplication.run(App.class, args);
PaymentService pay = context.getBean(PaymentService.class);
pay.pay();
Works. But you are back to manual “fetch bean, call method.”
Prefer: Spring creates a runner bean; Boot invokes it after startup.

title: Lecture 10 — Application properties, @Value & runners
Lecture 10 — Application properties, @Value & runners

text:
Startup flow (short map)
main()
  → SpringApplication.run

  → ApplicationContext created
  → @SpringBootApplication (scan + auto-config)
  → beans created + injected
  → context ready
  → CommandLineRunner / ApplicationRunner.run(...)
  → app ready
Configuration is loaded before your beans need those values.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
text:
Video: Spring Boot Core | @SpringBootApplication, Auto Configurations | Full Course #9
Playlist index: 9
Builds on: Lectures 05–08

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
text:
Big idea in one line
Spring Boot is still Spring.
It does not replace the IoC container. It starts the container for you and turns on smart defaults based on what JARs are on your classpath.
Spring Core (what you already learned)
  create context → scan components → make beans → inject deps

Spring Boot
  same steps
  + less startup code
  + "starters" (ready dependency packs)
  + auto-configuration (Boot adds useful beans when it makes sense)

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
text:
Why Boot after Core?
In Core you kept writing the same startup again and again:

Make ApplicationContext
Point it at a config class / XML
Put @ComponentScan (or list beans in XML)
Call getBean(...) yourself

That is fine for learning. In real apps it gets boring and easy to get wrong.
Boot’s job: keep the useful Spring Core behavior, remove the repeated setup.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
section: Picture: Core startup vs Boot startup
text:
Picture: Core startup vs Boot startup
SPRING CORE                              SPRING BOOT
────────────                             ───────────
main                                     main
  │                                        │
  ├─ new AnnotationConfig...               ├─ SpringApplication.run(App.class, args)
  │    (AppConfig.class)                   │
  ├─ @Configuration                        ├─ @SpringBootApplication on App
  ├─ @ComponentScan                        │     (includes scan + config + auto-config)
  ├─ beans created                         ├─ beans created (yours + Boot’s)
  └─ you call getBean / business code      └─ app keeps running (web server if web starter)
Same engine. Shorter ignition key.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
text:
Topic 1 — Make a Boot project (hands-on)

Option A (recommended): Spring Initializr

Open start.spring.io
Maven · Java · a stable Boot version · packaging Jar
Add dependency: Spring Boot Starter is enough for this lecture (no Web yet)
Generate → unzip → open in IDE



Option B: empty Maven + parent
If you build by hand, your pom.xml needs at least:

a spring-boot-starter-parent parent (versions)
a spring-boot-starter dependency (core Boot on the classpath)

You already saw Initializr do this in lecture 02. Today we explain why those lines exist.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
text:
Topic 2 — spring-boot-starter-parent (simple meaning)
Problem: many libraries must use matching versions.
If Web is version A and JDBC is version B, things break. Checking that by hand is painful.
Fix: Boot gives you a parent POM.
<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version><!-- Boot version --></version>
</parent>

What the parent does for you







Without parent
With parent




You pick versions for every Spring-related dependency
Parent already knows a tested set of versions


Easy to mix incompatible JARs
Add starters without writing <version> most of the time



Plain words: the parent is a “version menu” Boot maintains so you do not fight dependency hell.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
text:
Topic 3 — spring-boot-starter (simple meaning)
A starter is a ready-made dependency pack.







Starter
Rough meaning




spring-boot-starter
Core Boot support (logging, auto-config engine, …)


spring-boot-starter-web
Web apps + embedded Tomcat + Spring MVC


spring-boot-starter-test
Testing tools



When you only add spring-boot-starter (no web), Tomcat does not start.
That is normal. Boot only pulls Tomcat when a web starter puts those classes on the classpath.
Remember: starters change what is available. Auto-config decides what Boot creates from that.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
section: Topic 6 — Auto-configuration (the part that feels like magic)
text:
Topic 6 — Auto-configuration (the part that feels like magic)

Plain explanation

You add a starter → JARs appear on the classpath

Boot has a list of “if you have X, I can set up Y” rules

For each rule, Boot asks: should I turn this on?

If yes, Boot adds beans into the same IoC container as your beans

Classpath has Jackson?  ──yes──► maybe create JSON-related beans
Classpath has Tomcat + web? ──yes──► start embedded server setup
You already defined MyService? ──yes──► skip Boot’s default MyService


Two conditions you should know by name







Annotation
Plain meaning




@ConditionalOnClass
“Only if this class exists on the classpath”


@ConditionalOnMissingBean
“Only if you did not already define this bean”



Why @ConditionalOnMissingBean matters:
Boot gives defaults. You can override them by declaring your own @Bean / @Component of the same type. Boot then steps aside.
You define DataSource bean  → Boot’s default DataSource auto-config backs off
You define nothing          → Boot may create a default (when DB starter is present)


Your beans vs Boot’s beans








Kind
Who wrote the class
How it got into the container




App beans
You
@Component / your @Bean


Auto-config beans
Spring Boot / libraries
Enabled by @EnableAutoConfiguration + conditions



Same container. Different authors.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
section: Topic 7 — Why no Tomcat without Web?
text:
Topic 7 — Why no Tomcat without Web?
Common surprise:

“I run Boot, but there is no Tomcat on 8080.”

Because:

Auto-config looks at the classpath

Without spring-boot-starter-web, Tomcat / web MVC pieces are not there (or not selected)

So Boot does not start a web server

Add Web starter → Tomcat-related auto-config can turn on → you see a port again (like lecture 02).
Takeaway: Boot is not “always a web framework.” It becomes a web app when you pull web dependencies.

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
section: How to reason when something fails
text:
How to reason when something fails
Ask in this order:

Is the class under the main package (or a sub-package)? → component scan

Is the starter on the classpath? → check pom.xml

Did I already define my own bean that blocks Boot’s default? → @ConditionalOnMissingBean

Am I expecting a web server without the web starter? → add Web or stop expecting port 8080

This is how you debug Boot without calling it “magic.”

title: Lecture 9 — Spring Boot core
text:
Short map to keep
pom parent     → compatible versions
starters       → which libraries exist
@SpringBootApplication
   ├─ configuration (your @Bean allowed on main)
   ├─ component scan (your @Component)
   └─ enable auto-config (Boot’s conditional beans)
SpringApplication.run → start container + apply all of the above

Why learn XML if Boot uses annotations?
Finish this motivation fully — it is the point of the lecture:







Reason
What it buys you




Legacy codebases
Many enterprise apps still declare beans in XML; you must read and change them


Mental model
XML makes bean definitions visible as documents — same blueprints annotations build invisibly


Same container
ApplicationContext does not care whether metadata came from XML, @Configuration, or stereotypes



Do not memorize every tag. Learn the mapping: each XML construct ↔︎ the annotation / Java-config idea you already know. Syntax is searchable; reasoning is not.
                    configuration metadata
                 ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                 ▼          ▼          ▼
            XML files   @Configuration  @Component scan
                 \          |          /
                  \         |         /
                   ▼        ▼        ▼
                 BeanDefinition(s) in the IoC container
                              │
                              ▼
                    create · inject · lifecycle

text:
Topic 7 — XML autowiring modes (complete)
Instead of writing every ref, you can ask Spring to guess:
<bean id="orderService"
      class="com.example.xmlLab.OrderService"
      autowire="byType"/>








Mode
Behavior
Failure mode




no (default)
Only explicit ref / value
You forgot a dependency → null / missing ctor arg


byName
Match property name to bean id
Rename breakages


byType
Match property/ctor type to a unique bean
Ambiguity if 2 beans of that type


constructor
Like byType on constructor args
Same ambiguity risk



Teaching judgment: Autowiring reduces XML noise but hides the wiring graph. Explicit ref is clearer for learning and for tricky graphs. Modern annotation config has the same tradeoff (@Autowired by type vs @Qualifier).

title: Lecture 8 — Spring XML configuration
text:
Topic 8 — Scopes in XML (complete)
<!-- default -->
<bean id="orderService" class="..." scope="singleton"/>

<bean id="userService"
      class="com.example.xmlLab.UserService"
      scope="prototype"/>
Same semantics as lecture 6:








Scope
Instances
Destroy callbacks




singleton
one per definition
yes on context close


prototype
new each request
no container @PreDestroy / destroy-method for handed-out instances



var a = context.getBean("userService", UserService.class);
var b = context.getBean("userService", UserService.class);
System.out.println(a == b); // false for prototype
Optional: lazy-init="true" on a singleton ↔︎ @Lazy.

Create package com.example.xmlLab and src/main/resources/beans.xml.

After the lab you should be able to open a foreign applicationContext.xml and answer: What beans exist? How are they wired? What scope? What runs on startup/shutdown?

title: Lecture 8 — Spring XML configuration
text:
Reasoning toolkit (teach / review)
When reading XML config, walk this checklist:

Which context class loads it? (ClassPathXmlApplicationContext vs annotation)

List every <bean id> — those are your definitions

For each dependency: is it value or ref?

Constructor-arg or property? (required timing differs)

Any duplicate types without explicit ref / with autowire="byType"?

Scope + lazy-init?

init/destroy method names?

Imports — is this file the root or a fragment?


Robust-app notes

Prefer constructor injection in XML and in annotations

Prefer explicit ref over clever autowire while learning

Keep XML modules small (import) so ownership is clear

Never assume prototype destroy-method runs

Treat XML as documentation of the object graph — that skill transfers to Boot auto-config debugging

title: Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
section: Why this lecture matters (not syntax tourism)
text:
Why this lecture matters (not syntax tourism)
If you only memorize annotations, you will still get lost when:

A dependency is null in a constructor but fine later
Resources leak on shutdown (DB pools, file handles, threads)
A prototype bean’s cleanup “never runs”
A @Lazy bean hides a wiring bug until production traffic hits it

Target outcome: you can draw the lifecycle from memory, predict when each line of your code runs, and choose init/destroy hooks the way you would when teaching or reviewing a PR.

title: Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
text:
Master mindmap — singleton bean (default path)
Read this top-to-bottom. Every practice below hangs off this map.
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. IoC container starts                                     │
│    new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class)  │
│    (or SpringApplication.run …)                             │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. Read configuration metadata (reflection)                 │
│    @Configuration · @ComponentScan · @Bean methods          │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 3. Build ALL bean definitions FIRST                         │
│    Blueprint per type: name, class, scope, lazy flag,       │
│    dependency list — NO business objects yet for lazy/proto │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 4. Instantiate non-lazy singletons (dependency order)       │
│    constructor runs here                                    │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 5. Populate remaining DI (setter / field if any)            │
│    (constructor DI already happened in step 4)              │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 6. Aware callbacks (optional)                               │
│    BeanNameAware · ApplicationContextAware · …              │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 7. Initialization callbacks                                 │
│    @PostConstruct → InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()   │
│    → @Bean(initMethod=…)                                    │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 8. Bean ready — your app calls business methods             │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 9. Destruction callbacks (on context.close / shutdown)      │
│    @PreDestroy → DisposableBean.destroy()                   │
│    → @Bean(destroyMethod=…)                                 │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                            ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 10. Bean destroyed / removed from active use                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Variants (same map, different cut-points):
@Lazy singleton
  steps 1–3 always
  steps 4–8 deferred until first getBean / first injection use
  steps 9–10 still apply when context closes (if bean was created)

prototype
  steps 1–3 always
  steps 4–7 when requested
  then Spring HANDS OBJECT TO CLIENT and stops managing it
  ⇒ steps 9–10 DO NOT run for that instance

title: Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
text:
Topic 1 — Container start & configuration (complete)

What “passing AppConfig.class” actually means
You do not pass an AppConfig instance into the container. You pass class metadata. Spring uses Java reflection to discover:

annotations on the class (@Configuration, @ComponentScan)
@Bean methods
which packages to scan

var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);


Minimal config you already know
@Configuration
@ComponentScan // same package as AppConfig if no basePackages given
public class AppConfig {
}


Reasoning checkpoint







Question
Answer you should be able to give




Why reflection?
Container must discover annotations without you calling every setter by hand


When does scanning happen?
During context refresh / construction — before you call business methods


Is AppConfig itself a bean?
Yes — @Configuration is a @Component; Spring needs an instance to invoke @Bean methods



Do not leave this half-baked: until the context exists and config is read, no @PostConstruct on your services can run.

title: Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
text:
Topic 2 — Bean definition phase (complete)

What a bean definition is
A bean definition is the container’s blueprint for a bean — metadata before (or independent of) creating the instance:



Metadata
Examples




Bean name
default: camelCase class name (orderService)


Type
OrderService.class


Scope
singleton / prototype / …


Lazy flag
default false for singleton


Dependencies
constructor args, @Autowired points





Critical ordering rule
Spring builds definitions for all managed types first, then decides which objects to instantiate now.
Why?

Prototype → must not create at startup
@Lazy singleton → must not create at startup
Dependency graph → must know “Order needs Payment” before creating Order

Scan components
      │
      ▼
Create definitions for OrderService AND PaymentService
      │
      ▼
Only THEN instantiate the eager singletons (in dependency order)


Instantiation order is dependency-aware
Not random. If OrderService’s constructor needs PaymentService, Spring creates Payment first, then Order — even if scan discovered Order first.

section: Topic 4 — Aware interfaces (complete, including when not to use)

title: Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
text:
Topic 6 — Ready / use phase (complete)
After init callbacks, the bean is in the singleton registry (for singletons) and ready.
CartService cart = context.getBean(CartService.class);
System.out.println(cart.getValue(1)); // Aditya
This is the phase of normal application traffic: controllers call services, services call repositories, etc.
Mental model: steps 1–7 are “Spring assembling the machine.” Step 8 is “you driving it.”

title: Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
text:
Topic 8 — @Lazy singleton (complete variant)
Eager singleton:  definition → create now → … → ready at startup
Lazy singleton:   definition → WAIT → create on first use → … → ready
@Component
@Lazy
public class CartService { /* same as above */ }
Experiment

Mark CartService @Lazy.
Start context but do not getBean(CartService.class).
Observe: no constructor / @PostConstruct logs.
Then getBean → full remaining lifecycle runs.
context.close() → @PreDestroy runs if the bean was created.

When it is justified

Expensive bean rarely touched
Breaking a circular dependency with a lazy proxy (workaround — redesign still better)

When it is dangerous

Hides misconfiguration until first request (fails late)
“Make everything lazy for performance” is not a strategy

title: Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
text:
Topic 9 — Prototype scope (complete variant)
import org.springframework.beans.factory.config.ConfigurableBeanFactory;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Scope;

@Component
@Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
public class CartService { /* ... */ }

Lifecycle difference — finish this idea fully
Prototype request:
  create → inject → Aware → @PostConstruct → HAND OVER TO YOU
                                              │
                                              ▼
                         Spring forgets this instance
                         (no @PreDestroy from container)
Why? If Spring kept every prototype forever to call @PreDestroy later, it would retain references and risk memory leaks. So Spring initializes prototypes, then releases ownership.



Callback
Singleton
Prototype




Constructor
yes
yes (each instance)


@PostConstruct
yes
yes (each instance)


@PreDestroy
yes (on context close)
no (you clean up)



Robust-app rule: if a prototype holds a file/socket/pool, you must close it in your code (try-with-resources, explicit close(), custom tracking). Do not expect @PreDestroy.
Prove it in the lab: add @PreDestroy logging, use prototype scope, getBean twice, context.close() — destroy log should not appear for those instances.

title: Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
Lecture 7 — Bean lifecycle
text:
Reasoning toolkit (teach / review mode)
When you see a Spring class, ask in order:

Scope? singleton or prototype (or web scope)?
Lazy? created at startup or on demand?
How are deps injected? constructor (safe in ctor) vs field/setter (wait for @PostConstruct)?
What must run once after wiring? → @PostConstruct
What resource must be released? → @PreDestroy only if Spring still manages this instance
Is this prototype? → plan manual cleanup


Robust application checklist

Stateless services → singleton; no request-specific mutable fields
Constructors stay light
Init that needs deps → @PostConstruct
Every acquired resource has a matching release path
Prototypes: document who closes what
@Lazy used deliberately, not as default cargo-cult

title: Lecture 6 — Circular dependency, bean scope, lazy & eager
text:
Concepts

Circular dependency
OrderService  ──needs──►  PaymentService
     ▲                         │
     └──────── needs ──────────┘
Spring creates beans in dependency order. With constructor injection on both sides, neither bean can finish constructing → typically BeanCurrentlyInCreationException (or a clear circular-reference error at context startup).








Approach
What happens
Verdict




Redesign (extract third type / events / break the cycle)
No cycle
Preferred


@Lazy on one constructor parameter
Injects a lazy proxy; real bean created later
Workaround


Setter / field injection
Partial object published, then wired
Workaround; hides design smell



Constructor injection is not “wrong” here — it surfaces the cycle early. That is a feature.


Side note from the lecture: @Configuration is a component
@Configuration is meta-annotated with @Component. The config class itself becomes a bean so Spring can invoke your @Bean methods. Component scanning + @Bean factories both live in the same container world you started in lecture 5.


Bean scope
Scope = how many instances Spring creates for a bean definition, and when.








Scope
Instances
Typical use




singleton (default)
One per bean definition
Stateless services


prototype
New instance every time the bean is requested
Stateful / per-use objects


request / session / application
Web-aware (later)
HTTP request/session lifetime









ImportantInterview-depth point



Singleton does not mean “only one object in the whole JVM / container.”
It means one instance per bean definition.
Two @Bean methods that both return OrderService → two singleton definitions → two instances, each reused when you ask for that definition.




Eager vs lazy initialization









Eager
Lazy




When created
When the container starts (for singletons by default)
On first request / first use


Default
Singleton → eager
Prototype → effectively lazy (created when asked)


Fail-fast
Config errors show at startup
Errors may hide until first use


Annotation
(default)
@Lazy on a bean or on an injection point



Tradeoff: eager = slower startup, faster discovery of broken wiring; lazy = faster startup, later failures.

title: Lecture 5 — Spring IoC container
text:
Goal
Take the manual DI idea from lecture 4 and let Spring create and wire objects.
You will practice two registration styles:

Stereotype + component scan — @Component (and friends)
Java config — @Configuration + @Bean

And you will inject collaborators with constructor injection (@Autowired when needed).






TipProject setup for this lab



Create a small Spring project (not full Boot web app required):

Initializr: Maven, Java 21, dependency Spring Boot is fine even with no Web — or add only what you need
Or a plain Spring Core app with spring-context on the classpath

Package example: com.example.ioclab
If you use Spring Boot, @SpringBootApplication already includes component scanning from its package downward. For a pure Spring demo, you will use AnnotationConfigApplicationContext as shown below.

title: Lecture 5 — Spring IoC container
text:
Concepts

Bean
A bean is an object created and managed by the Spring IoC container.
Not every Java object is a bean — only the ones the container knows about.


What the container does (replaces main wiring)
You declare types + relationships
            │
            v
   Spring IoC container
     • instantiate beans
     • inject dependencies
     • manage lifecycle
            │
            v
   Your code calls business methods


Two ways to tell Spring about beans








Approach
How you mark types
Typical use




Component scanning
@Component / @Service / @Repository / @Controller
Your own app classes


@Bean methods
Methods inside @Configuration
Third-party types, explicit factory setup



@Service, @Repository, @Controller are specializations of @Component (same scanning idea; clearer intent).


@Autowired
Asks Spring: “find a bean that matches this dependency and inject it.”

Match is usually by type
On a single constructor, Spring Boot / modern Spring can inject without writing @Autowired
If multiple constructors exist, mark the one Spring should use
If multiple beans of the same type exist, resolve with @Primary / @Qualifier (see exercises)



Component scan
Spring looks in configured packages for stereotype annotations.
Boot: scanning starts from the package of the @SpringBootApplication class — keep your components in that package or subpackages.

Mistake

title: Lecture 4 — Dependency Injection & IoC
text:
Video: Dependency Injection & IoC Explained | Loose Coupling | Full Course #4
Playlist index: 4

title: Lecture 4 — Dependency Injection & IoC
text:
Goal
Implement the lecture’s Order / Notification example yourself in plain Java (no Spring yet).
By the end you will have felt:

Tight coupling pain (new EmailService() inside business code).
Programming to an interface.
Dependency Injection via constructor and setter.
Why this is called Inversion of Control — and what Spring will automate next lecture.







ImportantHow to use this page



Do not only watch. Create a simple Maven (or plain Java) project named e.g. di-lab and type each stage. Keep stages in git commits or separate packages (stage1, stage2, …) so you can compare.

title: Lecture 4 — Dependency Injection & IoC
text:
Concepts

Dependency
If OrderService needs EmailService to finish placeOrder(), then EmailService is a dependency of OrderService.


Tight coupling (the problem)
OrderService ──creates──► EmailService
Problems:

Cannot switch to SMS/Popup without editing OrderService
Hard to unit-test without sending real emails
OrderService does two jobs: business logic and object creation (SRP smell)



Loose coupling via interface
OrderService ──depends on──► NotificationService (interface)
                                      ▲
                      EmailService / SmsService / …
Still incomplete if OrderService itself does new EmailService().


Dependency Injection (DI)
Someone outside creates the dependency and passes it in (constructor or setter).
OrderService only uses NotificationService; it does not create it.


Inversion of Control (IoC)
Control of creating and wiring objects moves from the class to an external assembler (main today, Spring container tomorrow).
Rough relationship used in the lecture:







Term
Role




IoC
The broader idea — control of wiring is inverted


DI
A practical technique to achieve IoC


Spring IoC container
Automates creation, wiring, lifecycle of beans





Injection styles (this lecture)







Style
Idea




Constructor injection
Pass dependency in constructor (preferred for required deps)


Setter injection
setX(...) after construction


Field injection
Annotate fields — meaningful with Spring; deferred

text:
What Spring will replace next
Today main is the IoC “container”:

Create objects
Wire dependencies
Call business methods

Lecture 5: Spring’s IoC container does (1) and (2). Your code declares what depends on what; the container builds the graph.

title: Lecture 3 — Master Apache Maven
text:
Goal
After this lecture you can:

Read a pom.xml and explain groupId, artifactId, version.
Add a dependency and know where Maven downloads it from.
Run key lifecycle phases (clean, compile, package) and know what target/ is.

Maven is how almost every Spring Boot project is built. Tracking Boot code without Maven literacy is painful.

title: Lecture 3 — Master Apache Maven
text:
Concepts

Why Maven exists
Hand-managing JARs does not scale:

Wrong versions
Missing transitive libraries
“Works on my machine” classpath chaos

Maven is a build + dependency + project tool. It downloads libraries, compiles, tests, and packages your app using a standard layout.


Standard project layout
my-app/
  pom.xml
  src/
    main/
      java/          ← application code
      resources/     ← application.properties, etc.
    test/
      java/          ← tests
  target/            ← build output (generated; do not edit)


Coordinates (GAV)
Every artifact is identified by:



Field
Example
Meaning




groupId
com.example
Organization / namespace


artifactId
demo
Project name


version
0.0.1-SNAPSHOT
Release version



Together: com.example:demo:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.


POM (Project Object Model)
pom.xml is the project’s declaration: coordinates, packaging (jar/war/pom), dependencies, plugins, Java version, parent BOM (Spring Boot parent often manages versions for you).


Repositories







Repo
Role




Maven Central
Public default remote repository


Local ~/.m2/repository
Cache of downloaded artifacts on your machine



First build downloads; later builds reuse the local cache.


Super POM vs effective POM

Super POM: Maven’s built-in defaults.
Your POM: What you write.
Effective POM: Merged result (your POM + parents + Super POM).
Inspect with: mvn help:effective-pom



Build lifecycle (default)
Important phases (in order):
validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy



Phase
What it roughly does




compile
Compile main sources


test
Run unit tests


package
Build the JAR/WAR in target/


install
Put the artifact into your local .m2


clean
Delete target/ (separate clean lifecycle)



Running a phase runs all previous phases in that lifecycle too (package implies compile + test, unless you skip tests).

title: Lecture 3 — Master Apache Maven
section: Practice — hands-on in your editor / terminal
text:
Practice — hands-on in your editor / terminal
Use either:

The Spring Boot project from lecture 02, or
A fresh Maven project from Initializr (Maven + Java, even without Web)


Step 1 — open and read pom.xml
Find and write down (in your notes):

groupId
artifactId
version
parent (if present — Boot projects usually inherit spring-boot-starter-parent)
One <dependency> block (e.g. spring-boot-starter-web)



Step 2 — confirm Maven works
In the project root (folder that contains pom.xml):
mvn -v
If the IDE bundles Maven, you can use the IDE’s Maven tool window instead of the CLI.


Step 3 — compile
mvn compile
Confirm target/classes appears with .class files.


Step 4 — package
mvn package
Find the JAR under target/ (name includes artifactId + version).
For Boot apps this is often an executable “fat” JAR.


Step 5 — clean
mvn clean
target/ should be removed (or emptied). Run package again to regenerate it.


Step 6 — see the effective POM (optional but useful)
mvn help:effective-pom > effective-pom.xml
Skim it: notice how much configuration came from the parent, not your short pom.xml.


Step 7 — add a dependency deliberately

Pick a small library on Maven Central (or Maven Repository), e.g. a JSON helper you are curious about.
Copy the <dependency>…</dependency> snippet into your pom.xml <dependencies> section.
Reload Maven in the IDE / run mvn compile.
Confirm the JAR appears under External Libraries (IDE) or in ~/.m2/repository/....

Then remove the dependency if you do not need it — the point is learning the workflow.

title: Lecture 3 — Master Apache Maven
section: How this connects to Spring Boot
text:
How this connects to Spring Boot
When Initializr added Spring Web, it added a dependency like spring-boot-starter-web to the POM. That starter pulls Tomcat, Spring MVC, Jackson, etc. Maven resolved that graph; Boot did not magically invent JARs on disk.

Video: Build Your First Spring Boot Application | REST API | Full Course #2

title: Lecture 2 — First Spring Boot application
text:
Goal
Build a tiny Spring Boot app that responds to:
GET http://localhost:8080/hello  →  Hello World
You will type every step in your IDE. Pause the video and implement here — that is the point of these notes.

title: Lecture 2 — First Spring Boot application
text:
Concepts you need while coding

Localhost, IP, and port







Idea
Plain meaning




IP address
Unique address of a machine on a network


localhost / 127.0.0.1
“This same computer”


Port
Number that routes traffic to one process on that machine (Chrome, Spotify, your app…)


Default Spring Boot port
8080 (changeable)



On the public internet, browsers often hit 443 (HTTPS). A reverse proxy may forward that to your app’s internal port (e.g. 8080). Locally you call the app port directly.


Spring Initializr
start.spring.io generates a ready project skeleton: folders, Java version, Spring Boot version, and pom.xml dependencies — so you are not stuck on setup before writing business code.


Embedded Tomcat
Adding Spring Web pulls in an embedded Apache Tomcat. When you run the main class, Tomcat listens on a port. You do not install Tomcat separately for this hello-world.


Annotations you will use (names only — depth later)







Annotation
Role in this lecture




@SpringBootApplication
On the generated main class — Boot entry point


@RestController
Marks a class as an HTTP API “gateway”


@GetMapping("/hello")
Maps HTTP GET /hello to a method

title: Lecture 2 — First Spring Boot application
section: Practice — build it step by step
text:
Practice — build it step by step

Step 0 — prerequisites

JDK installed
IDE ready
Video paused after the Initializr section if you prefer typing first



Step 1 — generate the project

Open https://start.spring.io
Choose roughly:








Field
Suggested choice




Project
Maven


Language
Java


Spring Boot
A stable release (avoid SNAPSHOT / RC while learning)


Packaging
Jar


Java
21 (or 17+)


Dependencies
Spring Web




Click Generate, unzip the project, open the folder in your IDE.







Note



Exact Boot version numbers change over time. Prefer the newest stable release Initializr offers. Concepts stay the same.




Step 2 — run the skeleton once
Open the generated *Application.java (has public static void main).
Optionally add one line inside main before understanding Boot:
System.out.println("Hello World");
Run the main class. In the console logs you should see something like Tomcat started on port(s): 8080.
Open a browser:
http://localhost:8080
You will likely see a Whitelabel Error Page — that is OK. It proves the server is up, but no endpoint is mapped yet.


Step 3 — create HelloController
In the same package as your main application class (e.g. com.example.demo), create:
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class HelloController {

    @GetMapping("/hello")
    public String hello() {
        return "Hello World";
    }
}
What you are doing

@RestController → “this class exposes HTTP endpoints”
@GetMapping("/hello") → “when someone GETs /hello, run this method”
Returning a String → Spring writes that string as the HTTP response body



Step 4 — verify in the browser

Re-run the application (restart so changes load).
Visit:

http://localhost:8080/hello
Expected: page shows Hello World.


Step 5 — change the port
Open src/main/resources/application.properties and add:
server.port=9090
Restart. Tomcat should start on 9090. Now:
http://localhost:8080/hello   → fails (nothing listening)
http://localhost:9090/hello   → Hello World
Set the port back to 8080 (or delete the line) when you are done experimenting.


Step 6 — second endpoint
Add another method (method name does not have to match the path):
@GetMapping("/bye")
public String greetBye() {
    return "Bye";
}
Restart and test both /hello and /bye.


Step 7 — optional HTML in the response
@GetMapping("/hello")
public String hello() {
    return "<h1>Hello World</h1>";
}
The browser will render the heading. (Real apps usually return JSON and let a frontend render HTML — that comes later.)

title: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text: Video: Tutorial 15 Part 2 — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
crumbs: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs

title: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text:
Learning goals

Stack recurrent layers so layer \(\ell\) reads the sequence of hiddens from layer \(\ell-1\).
Use bidirectional RNNs when the whole sequence is available offline.
Apply depth practically: dropout between layers, gradient clipping, sensible widths.
crumbs: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs

title: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text:
Before this clicks
A single recurrent layer mixes time; depth mixes features at each time. A deep RNN is not “more time steps” — it is several recurrent modules stacked so \(h_t^{(\ell)}\) depends on \(h_t^{(\ell-1)}\) and \(h_{t-1}^{(\ell)}\). Bidirectional models run a forward and a backward recurrent net and concatenate states when future context is allowed (not for strict causal generation).
crumbs: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs

title: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text:
Main ideas

1. Stacked (deep) recurrence
For layer \(\ell=1,\ldots,L\):
\[
h_t^{(\ell)}=\mathrm{RNN}^{(\ell)}\!\bigl(h_t^{(\ell-1)},\,h_{t-1}^{(\ell)}\bigr),
\]
with \(h_t^{(0)}:=x_t\). Each layer has its own weights. Top layer \(h_t^{(L)}\) feeds the task head.
Same stacking works with LSTM or GRU cells instead of vanilla RNN cells.


2. Why go deep?
Lower layers capture short / local patterns; higher layers compose them (analogous to deep CNNs). Empirically, 2–3 recurrent layers often help; extreme depth needs residuals or careful init.


3. Bidirectional RNNs
Forward state \(\overrightarrow{h}_t\) sees \(x_1,\ldots,x_t\); backward \(\overleftarrow{h}_t\) sees \(x_T,\ldots,x_t\). Representation:
\[
h_t=\bigl[\overrightarrow{h}_t;\,\overleftarrow{h}_t\bigr].
\]
Use for labeling, classification of full utterances, offline ASR/NLP — not when you must predict the next token online without peeking ahead.


4. Regularization and training tips



Knob
Role




Dropout between layers / on inputs
Reduce co-adaptation


Gradient clipping
Tame exploding norms


Layer sizes decreasing or constant
Capacity vs compute


Pack padded sequences
Correct batching of variable \(T\)



Deep stacks amplify vanishing issues; prefer LSTM/GRU units when \(T\) or \(L\) grows.


5. Deep + bidirectional
Common pattern: 2 bidirectional LSTM layers, then a dense CRF/softmax head for sequence tagging. Output at each \(t\) uses both past and future context from every layer.
crumbs: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs

title: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text:
Worked mini-example
Sentence of length \(T=4\), embedding size \(4\), two stacked GRUs with hidden size \(8\), then bidirectional on the top layer only.

Layer 1: map \(x_t\in\mathbb{R}^{4}\to h_t^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{8}\) over time.
Layer 2 biGRU: forward and backward each output \(\mathbb{R}^{8}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(h_t\in\mathbb{R}^{16}\).
Token classifier: \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times 16}\) times \(h_t\).

Parameter count grows with \(L\) and direction, not with \(T\) (aside from compute). Batching still uses (batch, time, dim) with masks.
crumbs: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs

title: Tutorial 15B — Deep RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Deep RNN = longer BPTT
Depth is vertical stacking; BPTT length is the time unroll


Bidirectional always better
Illegal for causal next-step prediction


More layers always help
Diminishing returns + harder optimization


Vanilla deep RNN is fine for long \(T\)
Prefer gated cells when depth or length is large

title: Tutorial 15A — RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text: Video: Tutorial 15 Part 1 — RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs

title: Tutorial 15A — RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text:
Learning goals

Write the basic RNN recurrence and see weight sharing across time.
Explain vanishing/exploding gradients as the motive for gated units.
Contrast LSTM and GRU at the level of cell state and gates.

title: Tutorial 15A — RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text:
Before this clicks
A sequence \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\) (tokens, frames, sensor readings) has order that matters. An RNN keeps a hidden state \(h_t\) that summarizes “what happened so far,” updated with the same weights at every \(t\). Training unrolls the graph in time (BPTT). Long unrollings multiply many Jacobians \(\Rightarrow\) gradients can shrink or blow up; LSTMs/GRUs add gates so memory can pass more stably.

title: Tutorial 15A — RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text:
Main ideas

1. Vanilla RNN
\[
h_t=\tanh(W_{xh}x_t+W_{hh}h_{t-1}+b),\qquad
\hat{y}_t=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{hy}h_t+c)
\]
(or a single label from \(h_T\)). Parameters \((W_{xh},W_{hh},\ldots)\) do not depend on \(t\).


2. Batching sequences
Minibatches pad/pack variable lengths. A batch tensor is often (batch, time, features). Masks ignore pad steps in the loss. Teacher forcing (for generation) feeds the true previous token during training.


3. Why gates?
In a deep-in-time tanh RNN, \(\partial h_T/\partial h_1\) is a product of many factors with singular values often \(<1\) \(\Rightarrow\) vanishing gradients; \(>1\) \(\Rightarrow\) exploding (clipping helps explosions; architecture helps vanishing).


4. LSTM (intuition)
Maintain a cell \(c_t\) as a highway for long-range memory, plus gates in \((0,1)\):

Forget \(f_t\): how much of \(c_{t-1}\) to keep.
Input \(i_t\): how much new candidate \(\tilde{c}_t\) to write.
Output \(o_t\): how much of \(c_t\) to expose as \(h_t\).

Schematically:
\[
c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\tilde{c}_t,\qquad
h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t).
\]


5. GRU (intuition)
Fewer tensors than LSTM: a reset gate and an update gate blend previous hidden state with a candidate — no separate cell. Often similar accuracy, cheaper.



Model
Memory path
Gate count (rough)




RNN
\(h_t\) only
none


LSTM
\(c_t\) + \(h_t\)
forget, input, output


GRU
\(h_t\) with update/reset
two

title: Tutorial 15A — RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text:
Worked mini-example
Binary sequence: predict next bit. Tiny RNN with \(h\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\). After seeing 1,0,1, \(h_3\) should differ from \(h_3\) after 0,0,0 if the recurrence mixes past inputs. For a long run of identical bits, a vanilla RNN’s \(\partial L/\partial W_{hh}\) may nearly vanish; an LSTM can keep \(f_t\approx 1\) so \(c_t\) carries the early “I saw a 1” signal forward with less attenuation.

title: Tutorial 15A — RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




RNN = only language
Any ordered sequence; audio, video, time series too


LSTM “solves” all long memory
Helps a lot; still finite capacity; attention/transformers go further


GRU outdated vs LSTM
Often competitive; pick by validation


Batch time axis is optional
Need a clear time (or pack) dimension for recurrence

title: Tutorial 14B — Transfer Learning using CNNs
text: Video: Tutorial 14 Part 2 — Transfer Learning using CNNs

title: Tutorial 14B — Transfer Learning using CNNs
text:
Learning goals

Motivate transfer when your labeled set is small but a related large dataset exists.
Distinguish feature extraction (frozen backbone) from fine-tuning.
Sketch a practical recipe: swap the head, choose learning rates, unfreeze carefully.

title: Tutorial 14B — Transfer Learning using CNNs
text:
Before this clicks
A CNN trained on a huge source task (e.g. ImageNet classification) learns early filters that detect edges and textures useful far beyond that task. Transfer learning reuses those weights as a starting point for a target task with fewer labels, instead of training from random initialization.

title: Tutorial 14B — Transfer Learning using CNNs
text:
Main ideas

1. Backbone + head
Split the net into:

Backbone (conv stack): representation \(h=\phi_\theta(x)\).
Head (last dense layers): maps \(h\) to target labels.

Throw away the source head; attach a new head sized for your classes (or regression outputs).


2. Frozen feature extractor
Fix \(\theta\) (no grad through the backbone). Train only the new head on target data:
\[
\min_{w}\;\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell\bigl(f_w(\phi_\theta(x_i)),\,y_i\bigr).
\]
Cheap, stable, good when target data is tiny and domains are similar.


3. Fine-tuning
Allow some or all backbone weights to update, usually with a smaller learning rate than the head:
\[
\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta_{\mathrm{small}}\nabla_\theta L,\qquad
w\leftarrow w-\eta_{\mathrm{large}}\nabla_w L.
\]
Often: train head first, then unfreeze top conv blocks, then (optionally) more. Over-aggressive fine-tuning on tiny data can forget useful source features.


4. When transfer helps







Situation
Tendency




Related visual domain, few labels
Strong gains


Very different domain (e.g. medical vs natural photos)
Still often helps early layers; fine-tune more


Abundant target labels
From-scratch can compete; transfer still speeds training





5. Practical checklist

Load pretrained CNN; replace final layer.
Preprocess like the source model (resize, normalize).
Freeze backbone; train head.
Unfreeze last blocks; fine-tune with small \(\eta\).
Regularize (weight decay, early stopping, light augmentation).

title: Tutorial 14B — Transfer Learning using CNNs
text:
Worked mini-example
Target: 3 dog-breed classes, \(n=90\) images. Source: ImageNet CNN.

Freeze backbone; train a \(3\)-way logistic head for a few epochs \(\to\) usable baseline.
Unfreeze the last residual/conv stage with \(\eta_{\mathrm{backbone}}=10^{-4}\), \(\eta_{\mathrm{head}}=10^{-3}\).
Validation accuracy typically rises vs training the same CNN from scratch on \(90\) images (scratch overfits almost immediately).

The math is ordinary ERM; the win is the initialization / representation, not a new loss.

title: Tutorial 14B — Transfer Learning using CNNs
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Transfer = knowledge distillation
Distillation trains a student to match a teacher’s outputs; transfer reuses weights/features


Must fine-tune everything
Frozen extractor is a valid, often best first try


Source and target labels must match
Only the input domain should be related enough


Higher LR on backbone is safer
Usually the opposite: small LR on pretrained weights

title: Tutorial 14A — CNNs
text: Video: Tutorial 14 Part 1 — CNNs

title: Tutorial 14A — CNNs
text:
Learning goals

See a CNN as an MLP with local receptive fields and weight sharing.
Compute a tiny 1-D / 2-D convolution and a pooling step by hand.
Name the usual stack: conv \(\to\) nonlinearity \(\to\) pool \(\to\) (repeat) \(\to\) dense head.

title: Tutorial 14A — CNNs
text:
Before this clicks
An image is a grid of numbers (channels \(\times\) height \(\times\) width). A fully connected layer on flattened pixels has one weight per pixel–unit pair — huge, and it ignores that nearby pixels matter more. A filter (kernel) is a small weight patch slid across the grid; the same weights are reused everywhere (parameter sharing). That is the practical heart of a CNN.

title: Tutorial 14A — CNNs
text:
Main ideas

1. Convolution as a local weighted sum
For a 1-D signal \(x\) and filter \(w\) of length \(k\), a valid convolution output at position \(t\) is
\[
z_t=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1} w_j\, x_{t+j}
\]
(plus a bias \(b\) in practice). In 2-D, sum over a \(k\times k\) window (and over input channels). Sliding the window builds a feature map.


2. Why this helps on images







Idea
Plain English




Local connectivity
Each unit sees a patch, not the whole image


Weight sharing
One edge detector is reused at every location


Translation equivariance
Shift the input \(\Rightarrow\) feature map shifts similarly



Fewer parameters than a dense MLP of similar “coverage,” and the inductive bias matches natural images.


3. Nonlinearity and pooling
After conv, apply an elementwise activation (commonly ReLU: \(\max(0,z)\)). Pooling (e.g. max over \(2\times 2\)) downsamples: keeps a strong local response, shrinks spatial size, adds mild translation robustness.


4. Stacking and the classifier head
Early layers tend to pick edges/textures; deeper maps become more abstract. Flatten (or global-pool) the last maps and feed a small MLP for class scores. Training uses the same backprop story as MLPs; gradients flow through the shared filters.


5. Practical batching intuition
A minibatch is a 4-D tensor: (batch, channels, height, width). One forward pass applies the same filters to every sample in the batch. Data augmentation (crops, flips) is common because CNNs still overfit when labels are scarce.

title: Tutorial 14A — CNNs
text:
Worked mini-example
Input row \(x=[1,2,0,3]\), filter \(w=[1,-1]\), bias \(0\), valid conv:
\[
z_0=1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 2=-1,\quad
z_1=1\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0=2,\quad
z_2=1\cdot 0+(-1)\cdot 3=-3.
\]
ReLU \(\Rightarrow\) \([0,2,0]\). Max-pool with width \(2\), stride \(2\) on \([0,2,0]\) (pad or drop the last) \(\Rightarrow\) e.g. \(\max(0,2)=2\). Same arithmetic, in 2-D, is what a first CNN layer does on a tiny patch.

title: Tutorial 14A — CNNs
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Convolution “understands” objects by itself
Filters learn from data; architecture only biases locality/sharing


Pooling is required
Common, not sacred; stride-in-conv can downsample instead


More filters always better
Capacity \(\uparrow\) and overfit risk \(\uparrow\); need data/regularization


CNN \(\neq\) MLP
It is a constrained MLP; the constraints are the point

title: Tutorial 13 — PyTorch: Training the Model
text: Video: Tutorial 13 — PyTorch: Training the Model

title: Tutorial 13 — PyTorch: Training the Model
text:
Learning goals

Wire loss + optimizer to an nn.Module.
Write the canonical train step: zero grad \(\to\) forward \(\to\) loss \(\to\) backward \(\to\) step.
Track a simple train/val metric and switch train() / eval() modes.

title: Tutorial 13 — PyTorch: Training the Model
text:
Before this clicks
Tutorials 11–12 gave you batches and a differentiable model. Training is empirical risk minimization on mini-batches: approximate
\[
\min_\theta\;\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}\big[\ell(f_\theta(x),y)\big]
\]
by stochastic gradient steps. One loop over the training set is an epoch.

title: Tutorial 13 — PyTorch: Training the Model
text:
Main ideas

1. Loss and optimizer
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim

criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()   # classification logits vs class index
# criterion = nn.MSELoss()         # regression
optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
# optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits of shape \((B,C)\) and integer labels of shape \((B,)\) — it applies log-softmax internally. Do not softmax before it.


2. One training step
\[
\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\widehat{\nabla}_\theta L_{\mathrm{batch}}(\theta)
\]
in code:
model.train()
for xb, yb in train_loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    logits = model(xb)
    loss = criterion(logits, yb)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
Order matters: clear old grads, compute loss, backprop, then apply the update.


3. Evaluation
model.eval()
correct, total = 0, 0
with torch.no_grad():
    for xb, yb in val_loader:
        pred = model(xb).argmax(dim=1)
        correct += (pred == yb).sum().item()
        total += yb.size(0)
acc = correct / total
model.eval() changes Dropout / BatchNorm behavior; no_grad skips the graph.


4. Device placement
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model.to(device)
xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
Model and batch must live on the same device.


5. What to log
Per epoch (or every few steps): train loss, val loss/accuracy, learning rate. Overfitting often shows train loss falling while val loss rises.

title: Tutorial 13 — PyTorch: Training the Model
text:
Worked mini-example
Binary-ish 2-class toy with \(B=4\), \(C=2\). Model outputs logits
\[
Z=\begin{bmatrix}2.0&0.1\\0.3&1.5\\1.2&0.8\\0.1&2.2\end{bmatrix},\quad
y=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
CrossEntropyLoss averages \(-\log p_{y_i}\) over the batch after softmax. Predictions via argmax are \([0,1,0,1]\) — accuracy \(1.0\) on this lucky batch. Real training repeats many noisy batches until average loss drops.

title: Tutorial 13 — PyTorch: Training the Model
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Softmax then CrossEntropyLoss
Double softmax path; pass logits instead.


Forget zero_grad
Gradients accumulate; steps become wrong.


model.eval() freezes weights
It only changes layer behavior; weights still change if you call step.


Train accuracy alone
Always check a held-out set.

title: Tutorial 12 — PyTorch: Building MLP and Autograd
text:
Learning goals

Build a small MLP with nn.Linear and nonlinearities inside nn.Module.
Explain what autograd stores and how loss.backward() fills .grad.
Distinguish parameters (requires_grad=True) from plain data tensors.
crumbs: Tutorial 12 — PyTorch: Building MLP and Autograd

title: Tutorial 12 — PyTorch: Building MLP and Autograd
text:
Before this clicks
A multilayer perceptron (MLP) stacks affine maps and elementwise nonlinearities:
\[
h = \sigma(Wx + b).
\]
Training needs \(\partial L/\partial W\) for every weight. Autograd builds a computation graph while you run the forward pass, then applies reverse-mode differentiation (backprop) when you call backward().
crumbs: Tutorial 12 — PyTorch: Building MLP and Autograd

title: Tutorial 12 — PyTorch: Building MLP and Autograd
text:
Main ideas

1. nn.Module skeleton
import torch.nn as nn

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_hid, d_out):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(d_in, d_hid)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(d_hid, d_out)
        self.act = nn.ReLU()
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(self.act(self.fc1(x)))
forward is the math; calling model(x) runs it. Submodules registered in __init__ appear in model.parameters().


2. Affine layer shapes
nn.Linear(d_in, d_out) implements \(y = xW^\top + b\) with
\[
W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}},\quad
b\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}.
\]
If x is \((B,d_{\mathrm{in}})\), output is \((B,d_{\mathrm{out}})\).


3. Autograd in one picture

Forward: compute \(L\) from inputs and parameters.
loss.backward(): autograd walks the graph backward, accumulating \(\partial L/\partial\theta\) into theta.grad.
An optimizer (next tutorial) uses those grads to update \(\theta\).

Enable tracking with requires_grad=True (parameters of nn.Module already have it).
w = torch.tensor([2.0], requires_grad=True)
x = torch.tensor([3.0])
y = w * x          # y = 6
y.backward()       # dy/dw = x = 3
print(w.grad)      # tensor([3.])


4. Gradients accumulate
.grad is additive. Before a new step, call optimizer.zero_grad() (or model.zero_grad()), otherwise you sum gradients across steps by accident.


5. torch.no_grad() for inference
At evaluation, wrap code in with torch.no_grad(): (or model.eval() for dropout/BN behavior) so you do not build a graph you will not differentiate.
crumbs: Tutorial 12 — PyTorch: Building MLP and Autograd

title: Tutorial 12 — PyTorch: Building MLP and Autograd
text:
Worked mini-example
One-hidden-unit network for scalar \(x\):
\[
\hat{y} = w_2\,\mathrm{ReLU}(w_1 x),\quad
L=\tfrac12(\hat{y}-t)^2.
\]
If \(x=2\), \(w_1=1\), \(w_2=3\), \(t=4\), then \(\mathrm{ReLU}(2)=2\), \(\hat{y}=6\), \(L=2\). Autograd yields
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2}=(\hat{y}-t)\cdot\mathrm{ReLU}(w_1 x)=2\cdot 2=4,
\]
and similarly chains into \(w_1\). You write the forward expression; PyTorch fills the grads.
crumbs: Tutorial 12 — PyTorch: Building MLP and Autograd

title: Tutorial 12 — PyTorch: Building MLP and Autograd
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Must code backprop by hand
Autograd does it from the forward ops you used.


backward() updates weights
It only fills .grad; an optimizer applies the update.


Data tensors need requires_grad
Usually only parameters (and sometimes inputs for saliency).


Calling forward twice without zero_grad
Grads accumulate; clear between optimizer steps.

title: Tutorial 11 — PyTorch: Tensors and Data Loaders
text:
Learning goals

Treat a tensor as a multidimensional array that can live on CPU/GPU and (later) track gradients.
Read and reshape shapes like (N, C, H, W) without guessing.
Build a tiny Dataset and wrap it in a DataLoader for mini-batches.
crumbs: Tutorial 11 — PyTorch: Tensors and Data Loaders

title: Tutorial 11 — PyTorch: Tensors and Data Loaders
text:
Before this clicks
NumPy arrays hold numbers. A PyTorch Tensor is the same idea, plus: device placement, dtype control, and optional autograd tracking. Neural nets train on mini-batches — small groups of examples — so you need a pipeline that yields (inputs, labels) repeatedly. That pipeline is Dataset + DataLoader.
crumbs: Tutorial 11 — PyTorch: Tensors and Data Loaders

title: Tutorial 11 — PyTorch: Tensors and Data Loaders
text:
Main ideas

1. Creating tensors
import torch

x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])  # shape (2, 2)
z = torch.zeros(3, 4)                         # shape (3, 4)
r = torch.randn(2, 3)                         # standard normal
Useful attributes: x.shape, x.dtype, x.device. Convert: torch.from_numpy(a) / x.numpy() (careful with shared memory and requires_grad).


2. Shapes and indexing
Think of shape left-to-right as “outer to inner.” For images, a common layout is
\[
(N, C, H, W)
\]
= batch size, channels, height, width. For a batch of feature vectors,
\[
(N, D)
\]
= \(N\) examples, each with \(D\) features.
Operations like view / reshape, permute, and unsqueeze / squeeze change layout without inventing new data (when contiguous rules allow).


3. Elementwise ops vs matmul

+, *, torch.exp act elementwise (with broadcasting).
Matrix multiply: x @ W or torch.matmul(x, W).

If x has shape \((N,D)\) and \(W\) has shape \((D,H)\), then
\[
xW \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times H}.
\]


4. Dataset: one example at a time
Implement __len__ and __getitem__(i):
from torch.utils.data import Dataset

class ToyDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, X, y):
        self.X, self.y = X, y
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.X)
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.X[i], self.y[i]


5. DataLoader: batches and shuffling
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

loader = DataLoader(ToyDataset(X, y), batch_size=32, shuffle=True)
for xb, yb in loader:
    # xb shape (B, ...), yb shape (B,) or (B, ...)
    pass
shuffle=True for training; often False for validation. num_workers speeds I/O on large disks; start with 0 while debugging.
crumbs: Tutorial 11 — PyTorch: Tensors and Data Loaders

title: Tutorial 11 — PyTorch: Tensors and Data Loaders
text:
Worked mini-example
Four points in \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\) with labels:
\[
X=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\\1&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
y=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
DataLoader(..., batch_size=2, shuffle=False) yields two batches of shape \((2,2)\) for \(X\) and \((2,)\) for \(y\). With shuffle=True, which two rows travel together changes each epoch.
crumbs: Tutorial 11 — PyTorch: Tensors and Data Loaders

title: Tutorial 11 — PyTorch: Tensors and Data Loaders
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Tensor = only 2D matrix
Tensors can be 0D–nD; matrices are the 2D special case.


shape order is optional
Order is a contract; permute wrong axes and the model sees garbage.


Dataset must load all data into RAM
__getitem__ can read from disk; the loader only holds the current batch.


Batch dim is always last
In PyTorch vision/NLP, batch is almost always the first axis.

title: Tutorial 10B — Numerical Example on MLE and MAP
text:
Learning goals

Compute a likelihood for IID Uniform\((0,\theta)\) data and find the MLE.
Contrast MLE with MAP under a discrete prior on a coin bias.
Practice turning a posterior odds comparison into a simple counting rule.
crumbs: Tutorial 10B — Numerical Example on MLE and MAP

title: Tutorial 10B — Numerical Example on MLE and MAP
text:
Before this clicks
Likelihood \(L(\theta;\mathcal{D})=p(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)\) (product under IID). MLE \(=\arg\max_\theta L\). MAP \(=\arg\max_\theta p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D})\propto p(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)p(\theta)\). Indicators matter: Uniform\((0,\theta)\) likelihood is zero unless \(\theta\) exceeds every sample.
crumbs: Tutorial 10B — Numerical Example on MLE and MAP

title: Tutorial 10B — Numerical Example on MLE and MAP
text:
Main ideas

1. Uniform\((0,\theta)\) likelihood
Density: \(p(x\mid\theta)=1/\theta\) for \(0\le x\le\theta\) (and \(0\) otherwise), \(\theta>0\).
For IID \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\),
\[
L(\theta;\mathcal{D})
=\theta^{-n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{0\le x_i\le\theta\}
=\theta^{-n}\,\mathbf{1}\{\theta\ge\max_i x_i\}.
\]
So for \(\theta\) below the sample maximum, likelihood is exactly zero.


2. MLE for \(\theta\)
On \(\theta\ge m:=\max_i x_i\), \(L=\theta^{-n}\) is decreasing in \(\theta\). Hence
\[
\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}=m=\max_i x_i.
\]
Tutorial numbers (illustrative): samples like \(1.75,0.5,2.2\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(m=2.2\). Then \(L(10)=(1/10)^3>0\), while \(L(1.9)=0\) because \(1.9<2.2\).


3. MAP for a two-point prior on a Bernoulli bias
Second problem spirit: \(\theta\in\{0.5,0.6\}\) with prior mass \(1/2\) on each (zero elsewhere). Data: \(n\) IID Bernoulli\((\theta)\) trials with \(n_H\) heads.
Posterior odds reduce to a likelihood-ratio test. Taking logs yields a threshold on \(n_H\):
\[
\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MAP}}
=
\begin{cases}
0.6 & \text{if } n_H \gtrsim c\cdot n,\\
0.5 & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\]
with \(c\) from \(\ln\) ratios (tutorial obtained about \(0.55\)). Intuition: you need enough heads before the prior’s \(0.6\) hypothesis wins.


4. Moral
MLE ignores \(p(\theta)\); MAP multiplies by the prior and can shrink / discretize the estimate onto a preferred set. Same theme as regularized ERM later.
crumbs: Tutorial 10B — Numerical Example on MLE and MAP

title: Tutorial 10B — Numerical Example on MLE and MAP
text:
Worked mini-example
Uniform samples \(\{0.5,1.75,2.2\}\):



\(\theta\)
\(L(\theta)\)




\(1.9\)
\(0\) (below max)


\(2.2\)
\((1/2.2)^3\) (MLE)


\(10\)
\((1/10)^3\) (smaller than at \(2.2\))
crumbs: Tutorial 10B — Numerical Example on MLE and MAP

title: Tutorial 10B — Numerical Example on MLE and MAP
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




MLE for Uniform\((0,\theta)\) is the sample mean
No — it is the maximum.


Likelihood can be positive for \(\theta\) inside the data range
Any \(\theta<\max x_i\) is impossible under the model.


MAP always equals MLE
Only if the prior is flat on the relevant set.

title: Tutorial 10A — Numerical Example on Bayes Classifier
text:
Learning goals

Recover the OLS normal equations from matrix ERM with squared loss.
Build a Bayes classifier from class-conditionals, priors, and losses.
See how unequal misclassification costs shift the decision in an overlap region.
crumbs: Tutorial 10A — Numerical Example on Bayes Classifier

title: Tutorial 10A — Numerical Example on Bayes Classifier
text:
Before this clicks
Bayes classifier (0–1 loss, equal priors): pick the class with larger posterior \(P(Y=i\mid x)\), equivalently larger class-conditional times prior. With general losses, compare expected losses, not just posteriors. OLS: linear \(h_\theta(x)=\theta^\top x\) under squared ERM.
crumbs: Tutorial 10A — Numerical Example on Bayes Classifier

title: Tutorial 10A — Numerical Example on Bayes Classifier
text:
Main ideas

1. OLS in matrix form (augmented features)
Stack \(n\) examples into \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times (d+1)}\) (extra column of ones for bias) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\). ERM with squared loss:
\[
\theta^\star=\arg\min_\theta\frac{1}{n}\,\|X\theta-y\|_2^{2}.
\]
Expanding and setting the gradient to zero recovers the normal equations
\[
X^\top X\,\theta^\star = X^\top y
\]
(when \(X^\top X\) is invertible, \(\theta^\star=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\)). Same optimum as the earlier per-example sum form.


2. Two-class Bayes setup (tutorial problem spirit)
Suppose \(Y\in\{1,2\}\) with known (or given) class-conditionals on a feature \(X\) (often uniform / piecewise densities on intervals in the board work), and priors \(P(Y=1),P(Y=2)\).
Under 0–1 loss with equal priors, Bayes compares \(p(x\mid Y=i)\) (or posteriors). Decision regions:

In the exclusive support of class \(1\): predict \(1\).
Exclusive support of class \(2\): predict \(2\).
In the overlap \(S_{12}\): compare weighted conditionals.



3. Unequal costs move the overlap decision
If falsely predicting class \(1\) is much more expensive (tutorial used a large cost factor, e.g. order \(10\)), the Bayes rule in the overlap can flip to the safer class even when raw densities look comparable.
Schematic comparison (equal priors): predict class \(1\) only if
\[
\frac{p(x\mid Y=1)}{p(x\mid Y=2)}
>
\text{(cost-adjusted threshold)}.
\]
In the worked board calculation, the likelihood ratio in the overlap fell below the cost-adjusted threshold, so the entire overlap was assigned to class \(2\).


4. Uniqueness
Bayes decision regions need not be unique if ties occur on sets of measure zero / equal risk alternatives. Different representations of the same partition can look different as formulas (e.g. a linear rule vs a set description) while agreeing almost everywhere — or disagree if the candidate rule is simply not Bayes.
crumbs: Tutorial 10A — Numerical Example on Bayes Classifier

title: Tutorial 10A — Numerical Example on Bayes Classifier
text:
Worked mini-example
Equal priors, 0–1 loss. Supports: class 1 on \([0,4]\), class 2 on \([2,6]\), both uniform on their supports. Overlap \([2,4]\).
Density heights: \(p(x\mid 1)=1/4\) on \([0,4]\), \(p(x\mid 2)=1/4\) on \([2,6]\).
Equal costs \(\Rightarrow\) either class is fine on a measure-zero knife-edge; with a higher cost for calling “1” when truth is “2”, prefer class \(2\) throughout the overlap. Final Bayes-style rule:

\([0,2)\): class \(1\)
\([2,6]\): class \(2\)

(Exact constants in the video follow the problem sheet densities; the logic is identical.)
crumbs: Tutorial 10A — Numerical Example on Bayes Classifier

title: Tutorial 10A — Numerical Example on Bayes Classifier
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




OLS formula needs centering always
Augment with a bias column instead (tutorial’s “augmented data”).


Bayes = compare densities only
Only after priors and losses are plugged in; costs change the threshold.


Any linear separator is Bayes
Must verify risk / posterior comparison; a hand-drawn line can fail in the overlap.
crumbs: Tutorial 10A — Numerical Example on Bayes Classifier

title: Tutorial 9 — MAP Estimate
text: Video: Tutorial 9 — MAP Estimate

title: Tutorial 9 — MAP Estimate
text:
Learning goals

Estimate a Gaussian mean with known variance under a Gaussian prior.
Verify conjugacy and read off the posterior mean/mode.
See MAP as a convex combination of the MLE and the prior mean.

title: Tutorial 9 — MAP Estimate
text:
Before this clicks
MAP: \(\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}=\arg\max_\theta p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D})\propto p(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)p(\theta)\).
Conjugate prior: posterior stays in the same family as the prior.

title: Tutorial 9 — MAP Estimate
text:
Main ideas

1. Setup
Observe \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2\) known. Only \(\mu\) is unknown.
MLE: \(\mu_{\mathrm{ML}}=\bar x=\frac1n\sum_i x_i\).


2. Likelihood as a function of \(\mu\)
\[
p(\mathcal{D}\mid\mu) \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^2\right),
\]
an exponential of a quadratic in \(\mu\). Multiplying by a Gaussian prior \(p(\mu)=\mathcal{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2)\) keeps an exponential-quadratic form \(\Rightarrow\) Gaussian posterior (conjugate).


3. Posterior parameters
Matching quadratics gives posterior \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2)\) with
\[
\frac{1}{\sigma_n^2} = \frac{1}{\sigma_0^2}+\frac{n}{\sigma^2},
\qquad
\mu_n = \sigma_n^2\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2}+\frac{n\bar x}{\sigma^2}\right).
\]
Equivalently, \(\mu_n\) is a precision-weighted average of \(\mu_0\) and \(\bar x\).


4. MAP
For a Gaussian, mean = mode, so \(\mu_{\mathrm{MAP}}=\mu_n\): a convex combination of prior mean and MLE. As \(n\to\infty\), weight on \(\bar x\) dominates \(\Rightarrow\) MAP \(\to\) MLE.
Hyperparameters \((\mu_0,\sigma_0^2)\) play the role Beta’s \((\alpha,\beta)\) played for Bernoulli.

title: Tutorial 9 — MAP Estimate
text:
Worked mini-example
\(\sigma^2=1\), prior \(\mu_0=0\), \(\sigma_0^2=1\), \(n=4\), \(\bar x=2\):
\[
\frac{1}{\sigma_n^2}=1+4=5,\quad \sigma_n^2=\tfrac15,
\quad \mu_n=\tfrac15\bigl(0+4\cdot 2\bigr)=\tfrac85=1.6.
\]
MAP \(=1.6\) sits between \(0\) and \(2\).

title: Tutorial 9 — MAP Estimate
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Prior variance = data variance
\(\sigma_0^2\) is belief about \(\mu\); \(\sigma^2\) is observation noise.


MAP \(\neq\) posterior mean here
For Gaussian posterior they coincide.


Must integrate the evidence \(Z\)
For MAP / mode of a Gaussian, normalizing constant can be ignored.

title: Tutorial 9 — MAP Estimate
text:

NPTEL: 106108841

text: Video: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs
crumbs: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs

title: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs
text:
Learning goals

Write responsibilities \(\gamma_{ij}\) for a GMM.
Derive M-step updates for \(\alpha_j\), \(\mu_j\), \(\Sigma_j\).
See K-means as a hard-assignment limit of spherical GMMs.
crumbs: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs

title: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs
text:
Before this clicks
EM for latent-variable models: E-step sets \(q(z)=p_{\theta^{(t)}}(z\mid x)\); M-step maximizes the expected complete log-likelihood. For GMMs the complete model is “pick component \(j\) with probability \(\alpha_j\), then draw Gaussian \(j\).”
crumbs: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs

title: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs
text:
Main ideas

1. Why not plain MLE?
\[
\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\sum_{j=1}^{M}\alpha_j\,\mathcal{N}(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)
\]
is a log of sums — messy. EM introduces latents.


2. Responsibilities (E-step)
\[
\gamma_{ij} \;=\; P(Z=j\mid x_i;\theta^{(t)})
= \frac{\alpha_j\,\mathcal{N}(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^{M}\alpha_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}
\Big|_{\theta^{(t)}}.
\]
\(\sum_j\gamma_{ij}=1\) for each \(i\).


3. Expected complete log-likelihood (with simplex constraint)
Up to terms independent of \(\theta\), maximize
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\gamma_{ij}\Bigl[\log\mathcal{N}(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)+\log\alpha_j\Bigr]
\]
subject to \(\sum_j\alpha_j=1\) (Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\)).


4. M-step closed forms
Define \(N_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ij}\). Then
\[
\alpha_j^\star = \frac{N_j}{n},
\]
\[
\mu_j^\star = \frac{1}{N_j}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ij}\,x_i,
\]
\[
\Sigma_j^\star = \frac{1}{N_j}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma_{ij}\,(x_i-\mu_j^\star)(x_i-\mu_j^\star)^\top.
\]
(Softly weighted versions of the usual Gaussian MLEs; \(\alpha_j\) from the same constrained discrete MLE pattern as Tutorial 7B.)
Iterate E \(\leftrightarrow\) M until parameters / likelihood stabilize.


5. K-means as a limit
Assume \(\Sigma_j=\sigma^2 I\) for all \(j\) and let \(\sigma^2\to 0\). Responsibilities collapse to a hard assignment: \(\gamma_{ij}\to 1\) for the nearest mean (smallest \(\|x_i-\mu_j\|^2\)) and \(0\) otherwise. Re-estimating means under hard assignments is K-means. Soft GMM assignments harden into cluster indicators.
crumbs: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs

title: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs
text:
Worked mini-example
Two components, one point \(x\) with \(\gamma_{i1}=0.8\), \(\gamma_{i2}=0.2\). That point contributes \(0.8x\) toward \(\mu_1\)’s weighted sum and \(0.2x\) toward \(\mu_2\). After all points, divide by \(N_1\) and \(N_2\).
crumbs: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs

title: Tutorial 8 — Computation of EM for GMMs
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




\(\gamma_{ij}\) are parameters
They are E-step outputs, recomputed each iteration.


Update \(\alpha_j\) without constraint
Must enforce \(\sum\alpha_j=1\) (Lagrange).


K-means = GMM always
Only in the spherical, vanishing-variance hard limit.
