title: Tutorial 7B — MLE for Generalized Discrete Distribution
text:
Learning goals

Represent a categorical random variable with a one-hot vector.
Set up constrained MLE for probabilities \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\).
Recover the intuitive “relative frequency” estimate via a Lagrangian.
crumbs: Tutorial 7B — MLE for Generalized Discrete Distribution

title: Tutorial 7B — MLE for Generalized Discrete Distribution
text:
Before this clicks
A categorical (generalized discrete) RV \(Z\) takes values \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) with probabilities \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\). Constraints: \(p_j\ge 0\) and \(\sum_j p_j=1\). Unconstrained calculus is not enough — use a Lagrange multiplier for the sum-to-one constraint.
crumbs: Tutorial 7B — MLE for Generalized Discrete Distribution

title: Tutorial 7B — MLE for Generalized Discrete Distribution
text:
Main ideas

1. One-hot representation
Map \(Z\) to an \(m\)-vector \(V=(V_1,\ldots,V_m)\) with exactly one \(1\) and the rest \(0\):
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{m} V_j = 1,\qquad V_j\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Then
\[
P(V=v) = \prod_{j=1}^{m} p_j^{v_j}.
\]
(Only the active category contributes.)


2. Log-likelihood for i.i.d. data
Data \(v^{(1)},\ldots,v^{(n)}\). Log-likelihood:
\[
\ell(p) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{m} v^{(i)}_j \log p_j.
\]


3. Constrained optimization
Maximize \(\ell(p)\) subject to \(\sum_j p_j=1\) (nonnegativity left as a check / exercise in class). Lagrangian:
\[
L = \sum_{i,j} v^{(i)}_j\log p_j + \lambda\Bigl(1-\sum_{s=1}^{m} p_s\Bigr).
\]
\(\partial L/\partial p_j=0\) gives
\[
p_j = \frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n} v^{(i)}_j.
\]
Using \(\sum_j p_j=1\) shows \(\lambda=n\), hence
\[
p_j^\star = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} v^{(i)}_j
\]
= fraction of times category \(j\) appears. Matches intuition.
crumbs: Tutorial 7B — MLE for Generalized Discrete Distribution

title: Tutorial 7B — MLE for Generalized Discrete Distribution
text:
Worked mini-example
Three categories, data counts \((n_1,n_2,n_3)=(2,5,3)\), \(n=10\):
\[
p^\star = (0.2,\,0.5,\,0.3).
\]
Same answer from the Lagrangian route.
crumbs: Tutorial 7B — MLE for Generalized Discrete Distribution

text:

Confusion
Clarification




Free \(p_j\in\mathbb{R}\)
Must be a probability vector (simplex).


Softmax needed here
Not for this finite categorical MLE; frequencies already live on the simplex.


One-hot is optional fluff
It makes the likelihood \(\prod p_j^{v_j}\) and the algebra clean.

title: Tutorial 7A — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text: Video: Tutorial 7A — MLE for Gaussian Distribution

title: Tutorial 7A — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text:
Learning goals

Write the Gaussian log-likelihood in 1-D and in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
Derive MLEs for mean and variance / covariance.
See the 1-D “squared residual” become a \(d\)-D outer product.

title: Tutorial 7A — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text:
Before this clicks
Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE): given i.i.d. samples and a parametric density \(p_\theta\), choose \(\theta\) that maximizes \(\prod_i p_\theta(x_i)\), or equivalently the log-likelihood \(\sum_i \log p_\theta(x_i)\). Recipe: differentiate wrt parameters, set gradients to zero.
Useful matrix identities (Matrix Cookbook): cyclic property of trace; derivatives of \(\mathrm{tr}(A\,zz^\top)\) and \(\log\det A\).

title: Tutorial 7A — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text:
Main ideas

1. One-dimensional Gaussian
\[
p(x\mid\mu_i,\sigma_i) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_i}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu_i)^2}{2\sigma_i^2}\right).
\]
For \(n\) samples from one class, the log-likelihood is
\[
\ell = -n\log\sigma_i - \tfrac12 n\log(2\pi) - \sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{(x_j-\mu_i)^2}{2\sigma_i^2}.
\]
Setting \(\partial\ell/\partial\mu_i=0\) and \(\partial\ell/\partial\sigma_i=0\) gives
\[
\mu_i^\star = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_j,\qquad
(\sigma_i^\star)^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(x_j-\mu_i^\star)^2.
\]
(Sample mean and average squared deviation.)


2. Multivariate Gaussian
For \(x,\mu\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and SPD covariance \(\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\),
\[
p(x) = (2\pi)^{-d/2}\,|\Sigma|^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 (x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right).
\]
Sanity check: the quadratic form is a scalar, so the density is a scalar.
Log-likelihood over \(n\) samples involves \(\log|\Sigma|\) and sum of Mahalanobis terms. Differentiating wrt \(\mu\) yields
\[
\mu^\star = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_j.
\]
Differentiating wrt \(\Sigma\) (via \(\partial\log\det\) / trace identities) yields
\[
\Sigma^\star = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(x_j-\mu^\star)(x_j-\mu^\star)^\top.
\]


3. Link 1-D \(\leftrightarrow\) multi-D



1-D
Multi-D




\((x_j-\mu)^2\)
outer product \((x_j-\mu)(x_j-\mu)^\top\)


scalar variance
covariance matrix

title: Tutorial 7A — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text:
Worked mini-example
Data \(\{1,3,5\}\) in 1-D: \(\mu^\star=(1+3+5)/3=3\), variance \((4+0+4)/3=8/3\).
In 2-D with mean \(\mu^\star\) and centered rows \(z_j\), \(\Sigma^\star=\frac1n\sum z_j z_j^\top\) is the empirical covariance.

title: Tutorial 7A — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Divide by \(n-1\)
Classical unbiased sample variance uses \(n-1\); MLE uses \(n\).


\(\Sigma\) can be any matrix
Covariance must be symmetric positive (semi)definite.


Class label ignored
These formulas are for one Gaussian component / one class-conditional.

title: Tutorial 6 — NP Classifier Example and ROC Curve

title: Tutorial 6 — NP Classifier Example and ROC Curve
text:
Learning goals

Specialize the NP rule for 1-D equal-variance Gaussians.
Define false positive / false negative / true positive rates.
Read an ROC curve and interpret AUC.
crumbs: Tutorial 6 — NP Classifier Example and ROC Curve

title: Tutorial 6 — NP Classifier Example and ROC Curve
text:
Before this clicks
A threshold-based binary classifier says “class \(1\)” when a score (here, often just \(x\) itself) exceeds a cutoff \(\tau\). Moving \(\tau\) trades one error type for the other. The ROC curve plots that trade-off.
crumbs: Tutorial 6 — NP Classifier Example and ROC Curve

title: Tutorial 6 — NP Classifier Example and ROC Curve
text:
Main ideas

1. NP example: equal-variance 1-D Gaussians
Assume \(X\in\mathbb{R}\), \(X\mid Y=i\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma^2)\) with \(\mu_0<\mu_1\). The LR test reduces to a threshold on \(x\):
\[
h(x)=1 \quad\text{iff}\quad x > \tau,
\]
where \(\tau\) is chosen so type I error equals \(\alpha\):
\[
\int_{\tau}^{\infty} p(x\mid Y=0)\,dx = \alpha.
\]
That blue right-tail under the class-\(0\) density is exactly the allowed false-positive mass.


2. Four outcomes and two rates
With \(C_1\) = positive, \(C_0\) = negative, and decide \(C_1\) if \(x>\tau\):



Quantity
Probability
Common name




\(E_0\)
\(P(X\le\tau\mid X\in C_1)\)
False negative rate


\(E_1\)
\(P(X>\tau\mid X\in C_0)\)
False positive rate


\(1-E_0\)
\(P(X>\tau\mid X\in C_1)\)
True positive rate (recall)


\(1-E_1\)
\(P(X\le\tau\mid X\in C_0)\)
True negative rate





3. Precision and recall
\[
\mathrm{precision} = \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}},\qquad
\mathrm{recall} = \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}}.
\]
Their harmonic mean is the F1 score (mentioned in class; useful but secondary here).


4. ROC curve
For fixed class-conditionals, vary \(\tau\). Plot the point \((E_1,\,1-E_0)\) = (FPR, TPR) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The path is the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.

You can estimate these rates from training data for each \(\tau\).
Works for any thresholded score, not only Gaussian NP.



5. AUC and the random baseline
Join \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\): the diagonal \(y=x\) is a random coin-flip classifier. A useful ROC should lie above this line.
AUC = area under the ROC curve: a single summary of ranking quality. Larger is better (perfect = \(1\)).


6. Discriminability (equal-variance Gaussians)
With equal variances one finds a \(\tau\)-independent gap
\[
d = \frac{|\mu_1-\mu_0|}{\sigma}
\]
linking the two error rates; larger \(d\) means an easier ROC / smaller Bayes error.
crumbs: Tutorial 6 — NP Classifier Example and ROC Curve

title: Tutorial 6 — NP Classifier Example and ROC Curve
text:
Worked mini-example
Equal priors, equal-variance Gaussians, \(0\text{--}1\) loss: Bayes error is
\[
P_e = \tfrac12\int_{-\infty}^{\tau} p(x\mid Y=1)\,dx + \tfrac12\int_{\tau}^{\infty} p(x\mid Y=0)\,dx,
\]
which evaluates via \(\Phi\). Sweeping \(\tau\) traces the ROC; the Bayes operating point is one point on that curve. If you need FPR \(\le 0.05\), pick the \(\tau\) on the ROC with \(E_1=0.05\) and read off TPR — that is the NP operating point for \(\alpha=0.05\).
crumbs: Tutorial 6 — NP Classifier Example and ROC Curve

title: Tutorial 6 — NP Classifier Example and ROC Curve
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




ROC needs Gaussians
No — any thresholded score yields an ROC.


High AUC means calibrated probabilities
AUC measures ranking / separability, not calibration.


Diagonal ROC is “good enough”
It is chance-level; learn nothing.

title: Tutorial 5 — Neyman–Pearson Classifier
text: Video: Tutorial 5 — Neyman–Pearson Classifier

title: Tutorial 5 — Neyman–Pearson Classifier
text:
Learning goals

Distinguish type I (false positive) and type II (false negative) errors.
State the Neyman–Pearson (NP) design problem.
Recognize that the NP rule is a likelihood-ratio test with threshold set by the allowed type I level \(\alpha\).

title: Tutorial 5 — Neyman–Pearson Classifier
text:
Before this clicks
The Bayes classifier minimizes a weighted sum of all error types (via losses and priors). Sometimes you refuse that trade-off: e.g. in a medical test, you may insist “false alarm rate \(\le \alpha\)” and then make missed detections as rare as possible.

title: Tutorial 5 — Neyman–Pearson Classifier
text:
Main ideas

1. Two error types (binary decision)
Treat class \(1\) as “positive” and class \(0\) as “negative.”








Name
Meaning
Example (COVID test)




Type I / false positive
Predict \(1\) when truth is \(0\)
Healthy person flagged positive


Type II / false negative
Predict \(0\) when truth is \(1\)
Infected person flagged negative





2. NP design problem
Find a classifier \(h_{\mathrm{NP}}\) that

keeps type I error \(\le \alpha\): \[
P\bigl(h(X)=1 \mid X\in C_0\bigr) \;\le\; \alpha,
\]
among all such classifiers, has the smallest type II error: \[
P\bigl(h(X)=0 \mid X\in C_1\bigr)
\] is minimized (equivalently, true-positive rate is maximized).



3. Likelihood-ratio form
The NP classifier compares class-conditionals:
\[
h_{\mathrm{NP}}(x) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \dfrac{p(x\mid Y=1)}{p(x\mid Y=0)} > K, \\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
The threshold \(K\) is chosen so that type I error equals \(\alpha\) (when possible):
\[
P\!\left(\frac{p(X\mid Y=1)}{p(X\mid Y=0)} > K \,\Big|\, Y=0\right) = \alpha.
\]
So NP, like Bayes, needs the ratio of class-conditionals; the difference is how the threshold is set (by \(\alpha\), not by prior\(\times\)loss).


4. Proof sketch (why LR works)

By construction, choosing \(K\) from \(\alpha\) meets the type I constraint.
For any other classifier \(h\) that also meets the type I bound, consider the integral \[
I = \int \bigl(h_{\mathrm{NP}}(x)-h(x)\bigr)\bigl(p(x\mid Y=1)-K\,p(x\mid Y=0)\bigr)\,dx.
\] Split into regions where the LR is above / below \(K\); each piece is nonnegative, so \(I\ge 0\).
Rewriting \(I\ge 0\) in terms of error probabilities shows that \(h_{\mathrm{NP}}\) has higher (or equal) true-positive rate than any competing \(h\) — i.e. least type II error.

title: Tutorial 5 — Neyman–Pearson Classifier
text:
Worked mini-example (conceptual)
Suppose you allow at most \(\alpha=0.05\) false positives. You sweep \(K\) until the fraction of class-\(0\) mass where LR \(>K\) is \(5\%\). That \(K\) defines \(h_{\mathrm{NP}}\). Among all rules with false-positive rate \(\le 5\%\), this one maximizes detection of class \(1\).

title: Tutorial 5 — Neyman–Pearson Classifier
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




NP ignores class-conditionals
It requires them (via the LR), just like Bayes.


NP = Bayes with weird losses
Related family of LR tests, but the constraint \(\alpha\) replaces the usual prior\(\times\)loss threshold.


Smaller \(\alpha\) is always better
Smaller \(\alpha\) forces a harsher \(K\) and usually increases type II error.

title: Tutorial 4 — Minmax Classifier
text: Video: Tutorial 4 — Minmax Classifier

title: Tutorial 4 — Minmax Classifier
text:
Learning goals

Recall the two-class risk integral and how it depends on the prior.
Define the minmax classifier and see why its risk is prior-independent.
For 1-D Gaussian class-conditionals, find the threshold that satisfies the minmax condition.

title: Tutorial 4 — Minmax Classifier
text:
Before this clicks
Risk for a classifier \(h\) is the expected loss under the true joint distribution of \((X,Y)\). For two classes \(Y\in\{0,1\}\) with \(0\text{--}1\)-style losses, risk splits into two pieces: mistakes in region \(S_1(h)\) (where \(h\) says \(1\)) when \(Y=0\), and mistakes in \(S_0(h)\) when \(Y=1\).
The prior \(P(Y=0)\) is how often class \(0\) occurs. The Bayes classifier needs the prior; if the prior is unknown or can change, we may want a different design.

title: Tutorial 4 — Minmax Classifier
text:
Main ideas

1. Risk is linear in the prior (for a fixed classifier)
For a two-class problem, \(P(Y=0)=1-P(Y=1)\). Substituting into the risk integral and rearranging shows:

For any fixed hypothesis \(h\), risk varies linearly with the prior \(P(Y=0)\).

Intuition: one error type is weighted by the prior, the other by \(1-\)prior; fix \(h\) and only those weights move.


2. Definition of the minmax classifier
A classifier \(h_{\mathrm{mm}}\) is called a minmax (or min–max) classifier when the two weighted error contributions match in the sense that the coefficient of the prior vanishes. Concretely (equal-loss case), the condition becomes
\[
\int_{S_1(h)} p(x\mid Y=0)\,dx \;=\; \int_{S_0(h)} p(x\mid Y=1)\,dx.
\]
In words: the probability of saying “\(1\)” when truth is \(0\) equals the probability of saying “\(0\)” when truth is \(1\) (under equal loss magnitudes).
Consequence: risk of \(h_{\mathrm{mm}}\) no longer depends on the prior.


3. Picture: Bayes risk vs fixed \(h\) vs minmax

Bayes risk (best possible for each prior) is typically a U-shaped / quadratic-looking curve vs prior.
Any fixed classifier is a straight line vs prior.
A minmax classifier is a horizontal line (constant risk).

The minmax rule is useful when you distrust the prior or want worst-case-prior robustness.


4. Worked case: 1-D Gaussians, equal losses
Assume one feature \(X\in\mathbb{R}\), class-conditionals
\[
X\mid Y=i \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2),\qquad \mu_0<\mu_1,
\]
and a threshold rule: \(h(x)=0\) iff \(x<a\) (else \(1\)).
The minmax condition becomes equal tail areas:
\[
\int_{a}^{\infty} p(x\mid Y=0)\,dx \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{a} p(x\mid Y=1)\,dx.
\]
Standardizing to \(\Phi\) (standard normal CDF) yields
\[
\Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu_0-a}{\sigma_0}\right) \;=\; \Phi\!\left(\frac{a-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\right),
\]
hence
\[
\frac{\mu_0-a}{\sigma_0} \;=\; \frac{a-\mu_1}{\sigma_1},
\]
and the threshold
\[
a \;=\; \frac{\mu_0\sigma_1 + \mu_1\sigma_0}{\sigma_0+\sigma_1}.
\]


Observations

This minmax threshold is a linear rule in the means/stds; the Bayes threshold for the same Gaussians is generally quadratic (depends on the prior and variances).
If \(\sigma_0=\sigma_1=\sigma\), then \(a=(\mu_0+\mu_1)/2\), which matches the Bayes threshold for equal priors and equal variances.

title: Tutorial 4 — Minmax Classifier
text:
Worked mini-example
Suppose \(\mu_0=0\), \(\mu_1=4\), \(\sigma_0=\sigma_1=1\). Minmax threshold:
\[
a = \frac{0\cdot 1 + 4\cdot 1}{1+1} = 2.
\]
Same as the equal-prior Bayes threshold. If instead \(\sigma_0=1\), \(\sigma_1=2\):
\[
a = \frac{0\cdot 2 + 4\cdot 1}{1+2} = \frac{4}{3}.
\]
The decision boundary shifts toward the tighter class-\(0\) density so the two misclassification areas match.

title: Tutorial 4 — Minmax Classifier
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Minmax = Bayes
No. Bayes minimizes risk for a known prior; minmax makes risk insensitive to the prior.


Minmax ignores losses
Losses still matter; the equal-area form above assumes the relevant loss magnitudes are equal.


Always worse than Bayes
For the true prior, Bayes is best; minmax can be better if the prior you used for Bayes is wrong.

title: Tutorial 4 — Minmax Classifier
text:
References

Course playlist: Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning
NPTEL course page: 106108841
Duda, Hart, Stork, Pattern Classification — classical decision theory (Bayes / minimax)
Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Ch.1 — decision theory overview

title: Tutorial 3 — Risk Minimization Framework
text: Video: Tutorial 3 — Risk Minimization Framework

title: Tutorial 3 — Risk Minimization Framework
text:
Learning goals

Extend Bayes decision theory to \(M\) classes and general losses (including reject options)
Minimize conditional risk pointwise to get the optimal action
Recover the usual “max posterior” rule for \(0\)–\(1\) loss
See that Gaussian class-conditionals yield quadratic (or linear) discriminants

title: Tutorial 3 — Risk Minimization Framework
text:
Before this clicks
Lectures 15–16: risk \(R(h)=\mathbb{E}[L(h(X),Y)]\); binary Bayes under \(0\)–\(1\) loss.
Priors \(P(Y)\), class-conditionals \(p(x\mid Y)\), posteriors \(P(Y\mid x)\).

title: Tutorial 3 — Risk Minimization Framework
text:
Main ideas

1. More general decisions
True labels \(Y\in\{c_0,\ldots,c_{M-1}\}\).
Hypothesis actions \(\alpha\in\{\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{K-1}\}\) — \(K\) need not equal \(M\) (e.g. an extra reject action).
Loss \(\lambda(\alpha_j, c_t)\ge 0\): cost of deciding \(\alpha_j\) when truth is \(c_t\).


2. Conditional risk
\[
R(h)=\mathbb{E}_X\bigl[\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}\bigl[L(h(X),Y)\mid X\bigr]}_{\text{conditional risk } r(h(X)\mid X)}\bigr].
\]
For a fixed \(x\), if \(h(x)=\alpha_i\),
\[
r(\alpha_i\mid x)=\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}\lambda(\alpha_i,c_t)\,P(Y=c_t\mid X=x).
\]
Optimal rule: for each \(x\), choose \(\alpha_i\) with smallest conditional risk (ties arbitrary). That is the general Bayes classifier / Bayes decision rule.


3. Special case: \(0\)–\(1\) loss, actions \(=\) labels
Then \(r(i\mid x)=1-P(Y=c_i\mid x)\), so minimizing conditional risk \(\Leftrightarrow\) maximizing the posterior:
\[
h_B(x)=\arg\max_i P(Y=c_i\mid X=x).
\]
Minimizes probability of misclassification.


4. Two-class unequal losses \(\Rightarrow\) likelihood-ratio test
With actions \(\{0,1\}\) and losses \(\lambda_{01},\lambda_{10}\) for the two error types, the Bayes rule compares posteriors with a threshold involving the loss ratio (odds / likelihood ratio form after Bayes’ rule). Unequal losses matter in medicine: false negative vs false positive need not cost the same.


5. Gaussian class-conditionals \(\Rightarrow\) quadratic discriminant
Assume \(1\)-D (tutorial; \(d\)-D similar) \(X\mid Y=i\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma_i^{2})\). Taking logs of the likelihood-ratio test produces a decision of the form
\[
a x^{2}+b x+c \;\gtrless\; 0
\]
— a quadratic discriminant.
If \(\sigma_0=\sigma_1\), equal priors, equal losses, it collapses to a linear threshold between the means (LDA-style intuition).

title: Tutorial 3 — Risk Minimization Framework
text:
Worked mini-example
Two classes, \(0\)–\(1\) loss, equal priors, \(\sigma_0=\sigma_1=\sigma\), \(\mu_0<\mu_1\). Bayes threshold is the midpoint
\[
x^\star=\frac{\mu_0+\mu_1}{2}.
\]
If instead \(\lambda_{10}\gg\lambda_{01}\) (calling class \(0\) when truth is \(1\) is very costly), the threshold shifts to make “predict \(1\)” more often — same Gaussians, different loss matrix.

Clarification

Reject / other actions allowed; \(K\) may exceed \(M\)


Always threshold at \(1/2\)
Only for equal losses & two classes with symmetric costs

It is just Bayes + Gaussian class-conditionals + algebra


Conditional risk \(=\) true risk
Conditional risk is the inner \(\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid X]\); true risk averages it over \(X\)

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text: Video: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
1. Letters and envelopes — impossible event
Four letters, four envelopes, random permutation. Probability that exactly three are in the correct envelope?
Answer: \(0\). If three are correct, the fourth is forced correct. “Exactly three” cannot occur.
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
2. Two coins + Bayes
Bag: fair coin + double-headed coin. Draw a coin at random, toss.
Prior: \(P(F)=P(B)=1/2\).
Likelihoods: \(P(H\mid F)=1/2\), \(P(H\mid B)=1\).
\[
P(F\mid H)
=\frac{P(H\mid F)P(F)}{P(H\mid F)P(F)+P(H\mid B)P(B)}
=\frac{(1/2)(1/2)}{(1/2)(1/2)+(1)(1/2)}
=\frac{1}{3}.
\]
If the same coin then shows tails, it must be fair: \(P(F\mid H,T)=1\) (double-headed coin cannot produce \(T\)).
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
section: 3. Find \(k\) so a density integrates to 1
text:
3. Find \(k\) so a density integrates to 1
Support \([0,1]\), candidate \(p(x)=k\,x(1-x)\). Need
\[
\int_{0}^{1}k\,x(1-x)\,dx=1
\implies
k\int_{0}^{1}(x-x^{2})\,dx=k\Bigl(\tfrac12-\tfrac13\Bigr)=\frac{k}{6}=1
\implies k=6.
\]
Takeaway: densities normalize by integration over the whole space, not by forcing \(p(x)\le 1\) pointwise.
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
4. Uniform on \([-1,2]\) and \(|X|\)
\(X\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[-1,2]\), so \(p_X=1/3\) on that interval. Let \(Y=|X|\).

\(P(X\le Y)=P(X\le|X|)=1\) (true for every real \(x\)).
\(P(X<Y)=P(X<|X|)=P(X<0)=\int_{-1}^{0}(1/3)\,dx=1/3\).

Takeaway: \(<\) vs \(\le\) can matter when you describe events carefully (here the equality case has positive probability on a continuum? actually \(P(X=|X|)=P(X\ge 0)=2/3\), so the two probabilities differ).
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
5. Discrete expectation
If \(X\) uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,20\}\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{k=1}^{20}k\cdot\frac{1}{20}=\frac{1}{20}\cdot\frac{20\cdot 21}{2}=\frac{21}{2}.
\]
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
6. LOTUS + linearity
\(X\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0,1]\), \(Y=X^{2}+2X+1\).
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[X^{2}]+2\mathbb{E}[X]+1.
\]
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=1/2\), \(\mathbb{E}[X^{2}]=\int_0^1 x^{2}\,dx=1/3\), so \(\mathbb{E}[Y]=7/3\).
LOTUS: \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]=\int g(x)p(x)\,dx\) without finding the law of \(g(X)\) first.
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
7. Standardization
\(Y=(X-\mu)/\sigma\) with \(\mu=\mathbb{E}[X]\), \(\sigma=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[Y]=0\), \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)=1\) (using linearity and \(\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^{2}\mathrm{Var}(X)\)).
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
8. IID binaries — mass of \(Z=X+Y\)
\(X,Y\) i.i.d. Bernoulli(\(p\)). Then \(Z\in\{0,1,2\}\) and
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(Z=0)&=(1-p)^{2},\\
P(Z=1)&=2p(1-p),\\
P(Z=2)&=p^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Independence \(\to\) products; identical laws \(\to\) same \(p\) in each factor. Watch which property you use at each step.
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
10. Covariance without a full density
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[Y]=0\), \(\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathrm{Var}(Y)=1\), \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=\rho\).
\[
\mathbb{E}[(X+Y)^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[X^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]+2\mathbb{E}[XY]=1+1+2\rho=2(1+\rho),
\]
using \(\mathbb{E}[X^{2}]=\mathrm{Var}(X)+(\mathbb{E}[X])^{2}\) and \(\mathbb{E}[XY]=\rho\) when means are zero.
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
11. Conditional expectation under independence
\(X\perp Y\), \(Z=X+Y\). Then
\[
\mathbb{E}[Z\mid Y]=\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]+\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Y]=\mathbb{E}[X]+Y=\mu_1+Y.
\]
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
12. Linear image of joint Gaussians
\(X,Y\) i.i.d. \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), \(Z=3X+4Y\). Then \(\mathbb{E}[Z]=0\), \(\mathrm{Var}(Z)=9+16=25\) (cross term vanishes by independence), so
\[
p_Z(z)=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{z^{2}}{50}\Bigr).
\]
crumbs: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory

title: Tutorial 2 — Simple Problem Solving in Probability Theory
text:
13. Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Every verbally plausible event has positive probability
Logic can force probability zero.


Density value must be \(\le 1\)
Normalization is an integral constraint.


IID used as a vague synonym for “random”
Factor joints; reuse the same parameters.


Need full density for every expectation
Variance / covariance identities often suffice.

title: Lecture 69 — Introduction to Reinforcement Learning (RL)
text: Video: Lec 69 — Introduction to Reinforcement Learning : RL

title: Lecture 69 — Introduction to Reinforcement Learning (RL)
text:
Learning goals

Name the RL loop: agent interacts with an environment via states, actions, and rewards.
Define policy and value at a beginner level.
Contrast RL with supervised learning (no fixed \((x,y)\) dataset of correct actions).

title: Lecture 69 — Introduction to Reinforcement Learning (RL)
text:
Before this clicks
Supervised learning: a dataset tells you the right \(y\) for each \(x\). In RL, an agent chooses actions over time; feedback is a reward signal (possibly delayed), not a labeled correct action at every step. The goal is to maximize cumulative reward through trial and error (with structure from MDPs / policies / values).

title: Lecture 69 — Introduction to Reinforcement Learning (RL)
text:
Main ideas

1. Core objects







Object
Meaning




State \(s_t\)
What the agent knows about the world at time \(t\)


Action \(a_t\)
Choice the agent makes


Reward \(r_t\)
Scalar feedback after acting


Policy \(\pi\)
Behavior rule: \(\pi(a\mid s)\) or deterministic \(a=\pi(s)\)


Return \(G_t\)
Discounted sum of future rewards, e.g. \(G_t=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^k r_{t+k}\) with \(\gamma\in[0,1)\)





2. Interaction loop
\[
s_t \xrightarrow{a_t\sim\pi} r_t,\; s_{t+1}
\]
Repeat. The environment’s transition \(p(s_{t+1},r_t\mid s_t,a_t)\) is usually unknown; the agent must learn from samples.


3. Value functions (idea)
How good is it to be in \(s\) (and follow \(\pi\))?
\[
V^\pi(s)=\mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t\mid s_t=s].
\]
Action values \(Q^\pi(s,a)\) score taking \(a\) then following \(\pi\). Optimal policies maximize value. Many algorithms learn \(V\) or \(Q\) (TD, Q-learning) or optimize \(\pi\) directly (policy gradients).


4. Contrast with supervised learning









Supervised
RL




Feedback
Correct label \(y\)
Scalar reward (often sparse/delayed)


i.i.d. data?
Usually assumed
Trajectory data; actions change future states


Goal
Predict \(y\)
Maximize return



Imitation learning sits in between: demonstrate actions, then optionally improve with rewards.


5. Where RL shows up
Games, robotics, recommendation / bandits (simpler cousins), and aligning LLMs with preference rewards (high-level mention). The math foundations (MDPs, Bellman equations) are the long-term spine; this lecture is the vocabulary.

title: Lecture 69 — Introduction to Reinforcement Learning (RL)
text:
Worked mini-example
Grid world: states = cells, actions = \(\{\)N,S,E,W\(\}\), reward \(-1\) per step and \(+10\) at the goal. A random policy wanders; a good policy shortens paths. Delayed reward: only the goal gives a big bonus, so the agent must credit earlier moves (credit assignment) — unlike supervised labels on each move.

title: Lecture 69 — Introduction to Reinforcement Learning (RL)
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Reward = correct action label
Reward scores outcomes; many action sequences can be OK.


Policy = value
Policy chooses actions; value evaluates states/actions.


RL needs a full environment model
Model-free methods learn from interaction samples only.

title: Lecture 68 — Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
Learning goals

Frame an LLM as a next-token generative model over text.
Sketch why transformers (attention) scale to long context.
Distinguish pretraining, finetuning, and prompting at an intro level.
crumbs: Lecture 68 — Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs)

title: Lecture 68 — Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
Before this clicks
Text is a sequence of tokens \(w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T\) (subword pieces). A language model assigns probability
\[
p(w_1,\ldots,w_T)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(w_t\mid w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1}).
\]
Training on huge corpora to predict the next token teaches syntax, facts, and many skills as a side effect of compression / prediction. “Large” refers to scale: parameters, data, and compute.
crumbs: Lecture 68 — Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs)

title: Lecture 68 — Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
Main ideas

1. Next-token prediction
At each step the model outputs a softmax over the vocabulary. Loss is cross-entropy of the true next token (maximum likelihood for the autoregressive factorization). Generation: sample or greedily pick \(\hat w_t\), append, repeat.


2. Transformers (intuition)
Instead of processing tokens only left-to-right with a recurrent hidden state, self-attention lets each position form a weighted mix of other positions’ representations:
\[
\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)V
\]
(schematic). Stacked attention + feed-forward blocks yield deep contextual embeddings. Positional information is added so order matters.


3. Pretrain \(\to\) adapt







Stage
What happens




Pretrain
Next-token (or related) loss on broad unlabeled text


Finetune
Continue training on a narrower labeled / instruction dataset


Prompt
Freeze weights; steer behavior with carefully chosen input text (and optional few-shot examples)



Instruction tuning and RLHF-style preference optimization are common post-pretrain stages in modern chat models — course-level: adaptation need not always mean full retraining from scratch.


4. Capabilities and limits (honest intro)

Strengths: fluent text, translation-ish behavior, coding assist, tool use when wrapped in systems.
Limits: hallucinations (fluent wrong answers), context-window bounds, sensitivity to prompt wording, cost/latency, data bias.



5. Link to the course
LLMs are generative sequence models. Attention is a learned similarity-weighted combination — kin in spirit to kernels / soft lookup, but trained end-to-end at scale. Prompting is inference-time control of a conditional generative model \(p(w\mid\mathrm{context})\).
crumbs: Lecture 68 — Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs)

title: Lecture 68 — Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
Worked mini-example
Context: “The capital of France is”. The model’s next-token distribution should put high mass on “Paris”. Pretraining saw many such patterns; no explicit geography database is required for that particular fact to appear — but the same mechanism can invent plausible-sounding errors, which is why verification matters.
crumbs: Lecture 68 — Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs)

Confusion
Clarification




LLM = search engine
It generates tokens from \(p(w_t\mid\mathrm{past})\), not retrieve-by-default.


Prompting trains the model
Ordinary prompting does not update weights.


Bigger always true
Scale helps many benchmarks; it does not guarantee factuality.

title: Lecture 67 — Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text: Video: Lec 67 — Variational Auto Encoders : VAEs

title: Lecture 67 — Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
Learning goals

Pose a latent-variable model \(p(z)p_\theta(x\mid z)\) and why \(\log p_\theta(x)\) is hard.
Introduce the encoder (approximate posterior) \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\).
Decompose the ELBO into reconstruction + KL regularizer.

title: Lecture 67 — Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
Before this clicks
We want \(z\sim p(z)\) (often \(\mathcal{N}(0,I)\)) and a decoder \(p_\theta(x\mid z)\) (e.g. Gaussian or Bernoulli with NN means). The marginal
\[
p_\theta(x)=\int p_\theta(x\mid z)p(z)\,dz
\]
is typically intractable, so MLE is blocked. A VAE introduces a recognition network \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\) and optimizes a lower bound on \(\log p_\theta(x)\) — the ELBO — which is tractable with reparameterized sampling.

title: Lecture 67 — Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
Main ideas

1. Encoder and decoder

Encoder \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\): maps \(x\) to a distribution over latents (often diagonal Gaussian with mean/variance nets).
Decoder \(p_\theta(x\mid z)\): reconstructs \(x\) from \(z\).

Together they resemble an autoencoder, but both sides are probabilistic, and \(q\) is trained to match the true posterior in a variational sense.


2. ELBO
For each \(x\),
\[
\log p_\theta(x)\ge
\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]
-\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\big)
\;=\;\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;x).
\]

Reconstruction term: encourage \(z\sim q(\cdot\mid x)\) to decode back to \(x\).
KL term: keep \(q(z\mid x)\) close to the prior \(p(z)\) so latents stay well-behaved for ancestral sampling.

Maximize \(\mathcal{L}\) (equivalently minimize \(-\mathcal{L}\)) over \(\theta,\phi\).


3. Reparameterization (sketch)
For \(q_\phi(z\mid x)=\mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x),\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_\phi^2(x)))\), sample
\[
z=\mu_\phi(x)+\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),
\]
so gradients flow through \(\mu,\sigma\) into the encoder.


4. Generation after training
Drop the encoder: sample \(z\sim p(z)\), then \(x\sim p_\theta(x\mid z)\). The encoder is for training / representation; the prior+decoder is the generative model.


5. Contrast with GANs




VAE
GAN




Density
ELBO / approximate likelihood
Usually implicit


Training
Single ELBO objective
Adversarial min-max


Samples
Often blurrier
Often sharper


Encoder
Built-in \(q(z\mid x)\)
Not required

title: Lecture 67 — Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
Worked mini-example
MNIST digit \(x\). Encoder outputs \((\mu,\sigma)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^{16}\); sample \(z\); decoder outputs pixel Bernoulli probabilities. Reconstruction loss pushes decoded pixels toward \(x\); KL keeps \(q(z\mid x)\) from wandering arbitrarily far from \(\mathcal{N}(0,I)\). After training, \(z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\) through the decoder yields new digit-like images.

title: Lecture 67 — Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




ELBO = exact \(\log p(x)\)
It is a lower bound; gap is \(\mathrm{KL}(q\|p(z\mid x))\).


VAE is only an autoencoder
Prior + probabilistic decoder make it generative.


KL destroys all information in \(z\)
It trades compression vs fidelity; \(\beta\)-VAE tunes that tradeoff.

title: Lecture 66 — GAN (Generative Adversarial Networks)
text: Video: Lec 66 — GAN - Generative Adversarial Networks

title: Lecture 66 — GAN (Generative Adversarial Networks)
text:
Learning goals

Define the generator \(G(z)\) and discriminator \(D(x)\).
Write the classic min-max GAN objective.
Note training instability and mode collapse at an intuitive level.

title: Lecture 66 — GAN (Generative Adversarial Networks)
text:
Before this clicks
A GAN does not write down \(p_\theta(x)\) explicitly. Instead the generator turns noise \(z\sim p(z)\) into a fake sample \(G(z)\). A discriminator tries to tell real \(x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}\) from fake \(G(z)\). Training is adversarial: \(G\) learns to fool \(D\); \(D\) learns to catch \(G\).

title: Lecture 66 — GAN (Generative Adversarial Networks)
text:
Main ideas

1. Two players

Generator \(G_\theta\): \(\mathbb{R}^{k}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\), map latent noise to data space.
Discriminator \(D_\phi\): \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\to(0,1)\), probability that input is real.



2. Value function (Goodfellow et al.)
\[
\min_G\max_D\;
V(D,G)=
\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}[\log D(x)]
+\mathbb{E}_{z\sim p(z)}[\log(1-D(G(z)))].
\]

Inner \(\max_D\): better real-vs-fake classification.
Outer \(\min_G\): make \(D(G(z))\) large (fakes look real). In practice one often maximizes \(\log D(G(z))\) for stronger gradients early on.



3. Equilibrium intuition
If \(G\) perfectly matches \(p_{\mathrm{data}}\), the optimal \(D\) is \(1/2\) everywhere and \(G\) is indistinguishable from real data. Training rarely sits at a clean Nash equilibrium in deep nets — hence heuristics (architectures, losses, regularization).


4. Mode collapse
\(G\) may cover only a few modes of \(p_{\mathrm{data}}\) (same face pose, same digit style) that reliably fool \(D\). Samples look sharp but lack diversity. Mitigations are an active research area (alternative divergences, minibatch features, larger/better \(D\), etc.) — remember the failure mode even if details vary.


5. Pros / cons (beginner)



Pros
Cons




Often sharp samples
Unstable training


No explicit \(Z(\theta)\)
No easy likelihood


Flexible \(G\)
Mode collapse / evaluation hard

title: Lecture 66 — GAN (Generative Adversarial Networks)
text:
Worked mini-example
\(z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\), \(G\) a small MLP outputting 2D points, data = two Gaussian blobs. A healthy GAN spreads fakes across both blobs. Mode collapse: all \(G(z)\) pile on one blob that \(D\) currently struggles with — low \(V\) for \(G\) locally, but the other mode is missing.

title: Lecture 66 — GAN (Generative Adversarial Networks)
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Discriminator is the generator
\(D\) only judges; \(G\) creates.


GAN maximizes likelihood
Classic GANs optimize an adversarial game, not \(\log p(x)\).


Collapse = training NaNs only
Collapse can yield finite loss with low diversity.

title: Lecture 65 — Introduction to Generative Models
text: Video: Lec 65 — Introduction to Generative Models

title: Lecture 65 — Introduction to Generative Models
text:
Learning goals

Contrast generative models (\(p(x)\) or \(p(x,y)\)) with discriminative models (\(p(y\mid x)\) or \(f(x)\to y\)).
List what “generate” means: sample new \(x\sim\hat p\).
Preview major families: explicit density (VAE-like), implicit (GAN), and modern likelihood models (brief).

title: Lecture 65 — Introduction to Generative Models
text:
Before this clicks
A classifier only needs a decision boundary or \(p(y\mid x)\). A generative model aims at the data distribution itself: where probability mass lives in \(x\)-space (images, text tokens, audio). If you can sample from that model, you can create new examples that look like the training set.

title: Lecture 65 — Introduction to Generative Models
text:
Main ideas

1. Discriminative vs generative








Type
Models
Typical use




Discriminative
\(p(y\mid x)\) or score \(f(x)\)
Classification / regression


Generative
\(p(x)\) or \(p(x,y)\)
Sampling, density, imputation, …



Generative \(\Rightarrow\) discriminative is possible in principle via Bayes rule when \(p(x\mid y)\) and \(p(y)\) are modeled; the converse does not give you samples of \(x\).


2. Why generative models?

synthesize data (images, text)
fill missing parts / denoise
anomaly scoring via low \(p(x)\)
representation learning through latent \(z\)



3. Modeling styles (map)

Explicit normalized density — write \(p_\theta(x)\) and maximize likelihood (or ELBO when exact likelihood is hard): classical mixtures, autoregressive models, VAEs (variational bound).
Implicit models — define a sampler \(x=G_\theta(z)\), \(z\sim p(z)\), without a closed-form density: GANs.
Energy / score / diffusion families (course may only glance): learn how to move noise toward data.



4. Latent-variable intuition
Many deep generative models use
\[
z\sim p(z),\qquad x\sim p_\theta(x\mid z).
\]
Marginal \(p_\theta(x)=\int p_\theta(x\mid z)p(z)\,dz\) is often intractable — hence VAEs (bound) or GANs (avoid computing it).


5. Evaluation (beginner caution)

Likelihood on held-out data (when available)
Sample quality / diversity (FID-style metrics in vision)
Downstream usefulness of latents

Good samples \(\neq\) perfect density; good likelihood \(\neq\) always pretty samples.

title: Lecture 65 — Introduction to Generative Models
text:
Worked mini-example
Discriminative: given face pixels \(x\), predict age \(y\). Generative: learn \(p(x)\) over face images and draw new faces \(\tilde x\sim\hat p\). A conditional generative model \(p(x\mid y)\) could draw “faces that look age-\(y\).” Same pixels, different question.

title: Lecture 65 — Introduction to Generative Models
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Generative = always deep nets
Mixtures and PCA-Gaussian models are generative too.


Classifier samples new \(x\)
Discriminative models generally cannot.


One family wins forever
Tradeoffs: likelihood vs sample quality vs training stability.

title: Lecture 64 — NCE, InfoNCE, SimCLR, JEPA
text: Video: Lec 64 — NCE, Info-NCE, SimCLR, JEPA

title: Lecture 64 — NCE, InfoNCE, SimCLR, JEPA
text:
Learning goals

Lift NCE to InfoNCE: one positive vs many negatives in embedding space.
Sketch SimCLR: augmentations create positive pairs; contrastive loss trains the encoder.
State the JEPA high-level idea: predict in representation space, not pixel space.

title: Lecture 64 — NCE, InfoNCE, SimCLR, JEPA
text:
Before this clicks
NCE classified data vs noise to fit a density. Representation learning often does not need an explicit \(p(x)\). Instead: pull related views of the same object together in embedding space and push unrelated views apart. InfoNCE is the workhorse loss for that multi-negative contrast. JEPA is a different self-supervised family: predict missing/latent structure without reconstructing every pixel.

title: Lecture 64 — NCE, InfoNCE, SimCLR, JEPA
text:
Main ideas

1. InfoNCE (schematic)
Given a query embedding \(q\), one positive key \(k^+\) and negatives \(k_1,\ldots,k_m\),
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}=-\log\frac{\exp(\mathrm{sim}(q,k^+)/\tau)}{\exp(\mathrm{sim}(q,k^+)/\tau)+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\exp(\mathrm{sim}(q,k_j)/\tau)},
\]
where \(\mathrm{sim}\) is often cosine similarity and \(\tau>0\) a temperature. This is a softmax classifier that should pick the positive among the noise/negatives — the NCE spirit, now in feature space.


2. SimCLR (high level)

Sample an image \(x\); draw two random augmentations \(t,t'\) (crop, color jitter, …).
Encode \(z=f(t(x))\), \(z'=f(t'(x))\) (often with a projection head during training).
Treat \((z,z')\) as a positive pair; other batch embeddings as negatives.
Minimize InfoNCE (NT-Xent) so the two views of the same image match.

No class labels are required. The encoder \(f\) becomes a useful feature map for downstream linear probes / fine-tuning.


3. Why augmentations matter
Positives must share semantics but differ in nuisance factors. Weak augmentations \(\Rightarrow\) trivial shortcuts; strong, task-aligned augmentations \(\Rightarrow\) invariant features.


4. JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture) — idea level
Instead of reconstructing pixels (classic autoencoder) or only contrasting two views:

Encode context and a target region (or future) into embeddings.
Train a predictor so the context embedding predicts the target embedding.
Loss lives in representation space: focus on predictable structure, not high-frequency pixel noise.

This sits in the broader “predict in latent space” family (alongside related non-contrastive / predictive SSL methods). Course-level takeaway: self-supervision can mean contrast or latent prediction.


5. Map of ideas



Method
Core game




NCE
Data vs noise for densities


InfoNCE
Positive vs many negatives in embedding space


SimCLR
InfoNCE + strong image augmentations


JEPA
Predict target representations from context

title: Lecture 64 — NCE, InfoNCE, SimCLR, JEPA
text:
Worked mini-example
Batch of 4 images, two augmented views each \(\Rightarrow\) 8 embeddings. For view A of image 1, the positive is view B of image 1; the other 6 are negatives. InfoNCE raises \(\mathrm{sim}(q,k^+)\) relative to the negatives. After training, a linear classifier on frozen \(f(x)\) often works surprisingly well on labeled tasks — labels were never used in pretraining.

title: Lecture 64 — NCE, InfoNCE, SimCLR, JEPA
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




SimCLR needs ImageNet labels
Pretraining is unsupervised / self-supervised; labels are for evaluation.


InfoNCE = cross-entropy on semantic classes
Classes are instance / view identities in the batch, not object names.


JEPA reconstructs pixels
It predicts in embedding space by design.

title: Lecture 63 — NCE (Noise Contrastive Estimation)
text: Video: Lec 63 — NCE - Noise Contrastive Estimation

title: Lecture 63 — NCE (Noise Contrastive Estimation)
text:
Learning goals

See why normalizing a flexible model \(p_\theta(x)=u_\theta(x)/Z(\theta)\) is hard.
State NCE: turn density estimation into binary classification of data vs noise.
Read the logistic posterior that compares \(u_\theta\) to a known noise density \(p_n\).

title: Lecture 63 — NCE (Noise Contrastive Estimation)
text:
Before this clicks
A parametric density often has the form
\[
p_\theta(x)=\frac{u_\theta(x)}{Z(\theta)},\qquad Z(\theta)=\int u_\theta(x)\,dx.
\]
The unnormalized score \(u_\theta\) may be easy; the partition function \(Z(\theta)\) is often intractable. MLE needs \(Z\) (or its gradient). NCE sidesteps this by never requiring an exact normalized likelihood alone — it contrasts real samples with samples from a known noise distribution \(p_n\).

title: Lecture 63 — NCE (Noise Contrastive Estimation)
text:
Main ideas

1. Setup

Data samples \(x\sim p_d\) (unknown data distribution).
Noise samples \(x\sim p_n\) (you choose; easy to sample, known density).
Mix them and ask a classifier: “did this \(x\) come from data or noise?”



2. Posterior odds
Let prior odds of noise vs data be controlled by how many noise samples you draw (class balance). With equal mixture weight for intuition, Bayes says
\[
P(y=\mathrm{data}\mid x)=\frac{p_d(x)}{p_d(x)+p_n(x)}.
\]
NCE models \(p_d\) by \(p_\theta\) (or its unnormalized cousin) and fits \(\theta\) so that a logistic classifier matching these odds works well on the mixed sample.


3. Logistic form with unnormalized model
Using \(p_\theta(x)=u_\theta(x)/Z(\theta)\), the log-odds involve \(\log u_\theta(x)-\log Z(\theta)-\log p_n(x)\). Critically, \(Z(\theta)\) becomes just another parameter (or is absorbed), so you optimize a classification loss without integrating \(u_\theta\) over all \(x\).
Schematic binary loss on labels \(y\in\{0,1\}\) (data vs noise):
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}\big[y\log\sigma(s_\theta(x))+(1-y)\log(1-\sigma(s_\theta(x)))\big],
\]
where \(s_\theta(x)\) is a logit built from \(\log u_\theta(x)-\log p_n(x)\) (plus a bias for \(Z\)).


4. Intuition
If \(p_\theta\) matches \(p_d\), the optimal classifier recovers the true posterior above. If \(p_\theta\) is wrong, the classifier is imperfect and the loss pushes \(\theta\) to fix the density ratio \(p_d/p_n\).


5. Design choices

Noise \(p_n\): must overlap the data support; too far away makes the task trivial and uninformative.
Number of noise samples: more noise can improve estimation but costs compute.
NCE is a parent of later contrastive losses (InfoNCE) used in representation learning.

title: Lecture 63 — NCE (Noise Contrastive Estimation)
text:
Worked mini-example
Suppose data are 1D Gaussians concentrated near \(0\), and noise is Uniform\([-10,10]\). A flexible \(u_\theta\) that puts high mass near \(0\) makes “data vs noise” easy in the right way; a flat \(u_\theta\) cannot separate well. Fitting the logistic NCE loss raises \(u_\theta\) where real points lie relative to \(p_n\), shaping an estimated density without computing \(Z\) by quadrature.

title: Lecture 63 — NCE (Noise Contrastive Estimation)
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




NCE needs class labels of the task
Labels are only data vs noise, not semantic classes.


Noise can be anything
Poor \(p_n\) \(\Rightarrow\) useless or unstable learning.


NCE = GANs
Related spirit (contrast), different math (explicit \(p_n\), logistic NCE).

title: Lecture 62 — PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
text: Video: Lec 62 — PCA - Principal Component Analysis

title: Lecture 62 — PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
text:
Learning goals

Motivate PCA as variance maximization (and equivalent reconstruction error minimization).
Connect principal directions to eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.
Project, truncate, and reconstruct \(x\) from the top \(r\) components.

title: Lecture 62 — PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
text:
Before this clicks
Centered data: subtract the sample mean so \(\bar x=0\). A unit vector \(u\) (\(\lvert u\rvert=1\)) defines a 1D axis. The projected scalar is \(u^\top x\); its sample variance is \(u^\top\Sigma u\) where \(\Sigma\) is the empirical covariance. PCA finds axes that capture as much of that variance as possible, in order.

title: Lecture 62 — PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
text:
Main ideas

1. Covariance picture
With centered columns or rows as appropriate, the sample covariance is
\[
\Sigma=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i x_i^\top
\]
(up to the usual \(n\) vs \(n-1\) convention). \(\Sigma\) is symmetric PSD, so it has orthonormal eigenvectors \(u_1,\ldots,u_d\) and eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge 0\).


2. First principal component
Maximize variance of the projection:
\[
\max_{\|u\|=1} u^\top\Sigma u.
\]
The solution is the top eigenvector \(u_1\) of \(\Sigma\), with variance \(\lambda_1\). Next components solve the same problem in the subspace orthogonal to previous \(u\)’s: they are \(u_2,u_3,\ldots\).


3. Scores and truncation
Coordinates (scores) of \(x\) in the PC basis:
\[
z_j=u_j^\top x,\qquad j=1,\ldots,d.
\]
Keep only the top \(r\):
\[
z=(z_1,\ldots,z_r)^\top=U_r^\top x,\qquad U_r=[u_1\mid\cdots\mid u_r].
\]


4. Reconstruction
Approximate \(x\) by
\[
\hat x=U_r z=U_r U_r^\top x
\]
(with mean added back if you centered). The total reconstruction SSE equals the sum of discarded eigenvalues (trace identity): variance explained by the first \(r\) PCs is \((\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_r)/(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_d)\).


5. What PCA is / is not

Is: best linear \(r\)-dimensional subspace for squared reconstruction (among linear maps of this form).
Is not: a clustering method; not automatically “the semantically meaningful factors” if structure is nonlinear.

title: Lecture 62 — PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
text:
Worked mini-example
Points tightly scattered along the line \(x_2\approx 2x_1\) in \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\). Then \(u_1\) aligns with that diagonal, \(\lambda_1\gg\lambda_2\), and \(r=1\) reconstruction \(\hat x=u_1(u_1^\top x)\) recovers nearly every point; the second PC mainly holds noise.

title: Lecture 62 — PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




PCs are clusters
PCs are axes, not group labels.


Always keep variance \(>90\%\)
A heuristic, not a law; task needs matter.


PCA needs labels
Fully unsupervised; \(y\) is unused.

text:

title: Lecture 61 — \(k\)-Means Clustering
text: Video: Lec 61 — K-Means Clustering

title: Lecture 61 — \(k\)-Means Clustering
text:
Learning goals

State the \(k\)-means objective (sum of squared distances to cluster centers).
Run Lloyd’s algorithm: assign \(\to\) update centers \(\to\) repeat.
Recognize local minima and dependence on initialization / choice of \(k\).

title: Lecture 61 — \(k\)-Means Clustering
text:
Before this clicks
You are given points \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) and an integer \(k\). You want \(k\) groups. A center \(\mu_j\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) represents cluster \(j\). Similarity here means Euclidean distance \(\|x-\mu\|^2\). Soft / probabilistic cousins (mixtures, EM) appear elsewhere in the course; \(k\)-means is the hard-assignment workhorse.

title: Lecture 61 — \(k\)-Means Clustering
text:
Main ideas

1. Objective
Let \(z_i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) be the cluster index of \(x_i\), and \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\) the centers. Minimize
\[
J(\{z_i\},\{\mu_j\})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|x_i-\mu_{z_i}\|^2.
\]
Equivalently, with assignment indicators \(r_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\sum_j r_{ij}=1\),
\[
J=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{k} r_{ij}\,\|x_i-\mu_j\|^2.
\]


2. Lloyd iteration
Alternate two cheap steps from an initial \(\{\mu_j\}\):

Assign: for each \(i\), set \[
z_i=\arg\min_{j}\|x_i-\mu_j\|^2.
\]
Update: for each \(j\), set \(\mu_j\) to the mean of points with \(z_i=j\): \[
\mu_j=\frac{1}{|C_j|}\sum_{i:z_i=j}x_i,\qquad C_j=\{i:z_i=j\}
\] (skip empty clusters carefully in practice).

Each step does not increase \(J\); the algorithm stops when assignments stabilize (or after a max iteration count).


3. Why means?
For fixed assignments, the \(\mu_j\) that minimizes squared error for cluster \(j\) is exactly the sample mean of that cluster. So the update is optimal for that half of the problem.


4. Local minima and \(k\)
\(J\) is nonconvex in the joint \((z,\mu)\). Different initializations can yield different partitions and different final \(J\). Common practice: multiple random restarts; keep the lowest \(J\). Choosing \(k\) is a modeling decision (elbow / silhouette heuristics, domain knowledge) — not magically given by the data.


5. Limitations (honest)

Assumes roughly spherical, similar-scale clusters in Euclidean space.
Sensitive to outliers and feature scaling.
Soft memberships need mixtures / fuzzy variants.

title: Lecture 61 — \(k\)-Means Clustering
text:
Worked mini-example
Four points: \((0,0)\), \((0,1)\), \((10,0)\), \((10,1)\), and \(k=2\). Good init: centers near left and right pairs \(\Rightarrow\) clusters \(\{(0,0),(0,1)\}\) and \(\{(10,0),(10,1)\}\) with means \((0,0.5)\) and \((10,0.5)\). A bad init that puts both centers on the left can still recover the same partition after a few assign/update rounds, but pathological inits (and harder geometries) can trap Lloyd at a poor local minimum — hence restarts.

title: Lecture 61 — \(k\)-Means Clustering
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




\(k\)-means finds the global optimum
Only a local minimum of \(J\) in general.


Centers must be data points
Means need not coincide with any \(x_i\) (unlike \(k\)-medoids).


Larger \(k\) is always better
\(J\) falls as \(k\) grows; that alone does not mean a better model.

title: Lecture 61 — \(k\)-Means Clustering
text:

title: Lecture 60 — Unsupervised Learning
text: Video: Lec 60 — Un-Supervised Learning

title: Lecture 60 — Unsupervised Learning
text:
Learning goals

Contrast supervised learning (labels \(y\)) with unsupervised learning (only \(x\)).
Name the two big unsupervised goals: clustering and dimensionality reduction.
See unsupervised methods as tools for structure, compression, and representation learning.

title: Lecture 60 — Unsupervised Learning
text:
Before this clicks
In supervised learning you have pairs \((x_i,y_i)\) and want \(f(x)\approx y\). Here you only have \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\). There is no “correct label” to score against, so success means finding useful structure: groups, low-dimensional axes, or features that later help a supervised task.

title: Lecture 60 — Unsupervised Learning
text:
Main ideas

1. Supervised vs unsupervised



Setting
Data
Typical goal




Supervised
\((x_i,y_i)\)
Predict \(y\) from \(x\)


Unsupervised
\(x_i\) only
Discover patterns in \(x\)



Unsupervised objectives are often proxy losses (within-cluster variance, reconstruction error, contrastive scores) rather than a known true \(y\).


2. Clustering (overview)
Partition points into groups so that points in a group are similar and groups differ. Examples: customer segments, document topics (at a coarse level), image regions.
A classical algorithmic workhorse is \(k\)-means (next lecture): choose \(k\) centers and assign each \(x_i\) to the nearest center.


3. Dimensionality reduction (overview)
Map \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) to \(z\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\) with \(r\ll d\), keeping as much useful variation as possible. Reasons:

visualization (\(r=2\) or \(3\))
noise reduction / compression
cheaper downstream models

PCA (coming soon) finds linear directions of maximum variance. Nonlinear methods and autoencoders appear later in the course family of ideas.


4. Density and representation links
Unsupervised learning also includes density estimation \(p(x)\) and representation learning (features \(z=f(x)\) that make structure easier). Modern contrastive methods (NCE / SimCLR) sit in this last bucket: they never see class labels, yet learn embeddings that cluster related views.


5. Why it matters for ML
Labeled data are expensive; unlabeled data are plentiful. Unsupervised pretraining or clustering can:

reveal the shape of \(p(x)\)
initialize or regularize supervised models
reduce \(d\) before classification/regression

title: Lecture 60 — Unsupervised Learning
text:
Worked mini-example
Suppose you have 2D points forming two blobs, with no class labels. Clustering recovers the two blobs as groups. Separately, if the blobs lie along a thin diagonal strip in \(\mathbb{R}^{10}\), PCA can keep one or two axes that explain most variance and discard nearly constant coordinates — a form of unsupervised compression.

title: Lecture 60 — Unsupervised Learning
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Unsupervised = no algorithm / no loss
There is still an objective (e.g. within-cluster SSE); just no \(y\).


Clustering = classification
Classification predicts known labels; clustering invents groups.


Dimensionality reduction deletes information
It discards some variation by design; keep enough for the task.

title: Lecture 60 — Unsupervised Learning
text:
References

NPTEL: 106108841
Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning — unsupervised chapters
Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning — clustering / latent-variable overview

title: Lecture 59 — Cross Validation
text: Video: Lec 59 — Cross Validation

title: Lecture 59 — Cross Validation
text:
Learning goals

Separate train, validation, and test roles.
Define \(k\)-fold CV and the CV estimate of risk.
Use CV to choose hyperparameters; keep a final untouched test set when possible.

title: Lecture 59 — Cross Validation
text:
Before this clicks
Training error is optimistically biased: the model already saw those points. A single holdout validation set is honest but noisy if \(n\) is small, and wastes data. Cross-validation rotates which slice is held out so every point validates once, then averages the slice errors — a more stable estimate of generalization for model selection.

title: Lecture 59 — Cross Validation
text:
Main ideas

1. Holdout reminder
Split \(\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}\) (and ideally a final \(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}\)). Fit on train; score on val; report once on test after all choices freeze.


2. \(k\)-fold CV
Partition data into \(k\) folds \(F_1,\ldots,F_k\) of roughly equal size. For \(j=1,\ldots,k\):

Train on \(\mathcal{D}^{(-j)}=\bigcup_{i\neq j}F_i\).
Compute loss on \(F_j\): \(L_j\).

CV estimate:
\[
\widehat{R}_{\mathrm{CV}}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k} L_j
\]
(or the sample-weighted average if folds differ slightly in size). Common \(k=5\) or \(10\); \(k=n\) is leave-one-out (LOO).


3. Choosing hyperparameters
For each candidate \(\lambda\) (depth, \(\nu\), \(C\), …), compute \(\widehat{R}_{\mathrm{CV}}(\lambda)\) and pick
\[
\hat{\lambda}=\arg\min_\lambda \widehat{R}_{\mathrm{CV}}(\lambda).
\]
Then refit the model with \(\hat{\lambda}\) on all training data (excluding the final test set).


4. Bias–variance of the CV estimate








Scheme
Bias of error estimate
Cost




Large holdout
Higher variance of estimate
Cheap


\(k=5,10\)

\(k\) fits


LOO

\(n\) fits



Nested CV (outer test folds + inner selection folds) is the careful way when you must estimate the error of the whole selection pipeline.


5. Pitfalls

Leakage: preprocess (scaling, feature select) inside each train fold, not on the full set before splitting.
Do not tune on the final test fold.
Time series: use forward chaining, not random folds that peek at the future.

title: Lecture 59 — Cross Validation
text:
Worked mini-example
\(n=10\) points, \(k=5\) \(\Rightarrow\) folds of \(2\). Hyperparameter: tree depth \(d\in\{1,2,3\}\).
For \(d=2\), five models each train on \(8\) points; validation MSE on the two held-out points might be \((0.4,0.6,0.5,0.3,0.7)\). Then
\[
\widehat{R}_{\mathrm{CV}}(2)=\frac{0.4+0.6+0.5+0.3+0.7}{5}=0.5.
\]
If \(\widehat{R}_{\mathrm{CV}}(1)=0.7\) and \(\widehat{R}_{\mathrm{CV}}(3)=0.55\), pick \(d=2\), refit depth-\(2\) tree on all \(10\) (or on full train if a separate test exists).

title: Lecture 58 — Ada-Boosting
text: Video: Lec 58 — Ada-Boosting

title: Lecture 58 — Ada-Boosting
text:
Learning goals

Run AdaBoost: maintain sample weights, train a weak classifier, update weights.
Compute the stage weight \(\alpha_m\) from the weighted error.
See the final predictor as a signed weighted vote of the weak learners.

title: Lecture 58 — Ada-Boosting
text:
Before this clicks
Labels \(y_i\in\{-1,+1\}\). A weak classifier \(G_m\) need only beat chance (weighted error \(<1/2\)). AdaBoost raises weights on points \(G_m\) got wrong so the next learner focuses there, and assigns a larger vote \(\alpha_m\) to more accurate stages. The ensemble is \(\mathrm{sign}(\sum_m\alpha_m G_m(x))\).

title: Lecture 58 — Ada-Boosting
text:
Main ideas

1. Weights and weighted error
Start with \(w_i^{(1)}=1/n\). After training \(G_m\) with weights \(w_i^{(m)}\),
\[
\varepsilon_m=\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i^{(m)}\,\mathbf{1}\{G_m(x_i)\neq y_i\}
\]
(assume weights sum to \(1\); else normalize). Need \(\varepsilon_m<1/2\).


2. Stage coefficient
\[
\alpha_m=\frac12\log\frac{1-\varepsilon_m}{\varepsilon_m}.
\]
Smaller \(\varepsilon_m\) \(\Rightarrow\) larger \(\alpha_m\) (more trust).


3. Weight update
\[
w_i^{(m+1)}\propto w_i^{(m)}\exp\bigl(-\alpha_m y_i G_m(x_i)\bigr),
\]
then renormalize to sum to \(1\). Since \(y_i G_m(x_i)=+1\) on correct points and \(-1\) on errors, mistakes get multiplied by \(e^{\alpha_m}\) (upweighted) and correct points by \(e^{-\alpha_m}\).


4. Final classifier
\[
F(x)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\alpha_m G_m(x),\qquad
\hat{y}(x)=\mathrm{sign}\bigl(F(x)\bigr).
\]


5. Link to losses / GB
AdaBoost can be viewed as stagewise minimization of exponential loss \(\ell(y,F)=e^{-yF}\). Gradient boosting on that loss recovers a close cousin; AdaBoost’s classic presentation is the reweighting story above.

title: Lecture 58 — Ada-Boosting
text:
Worked mini-example
\(n=4\) points, equal weights \(w_i=1/4\). Weak rule \(G_1\) misses \(1\) point \(\Rightarrow\) \(\varepsilon_1=1/4\).
\[
\alpha_1=\frac12\log\frac{3/4}{1/4}=\frac12\log 3\approx 0.549.
\]
The missed point’s weight is multiplied by \(e^{\alpha_1}=\sqrt{3}\); each correct point by \(e^{-\alpha_1}=1/\sqrt{3}\); then renormalize. Next stump \(G_2\) is trained on the new weights and will try harder on that hard point. Final vote: \(\mathrm{sign}(\alpha_1 G_1+\alpha_2 G_2+\cdots)\).

title: Lecture 58 — Ada-Boosting
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Weights are model parameters \(w\) in \(w^\top x\)
Here \(w_i\) are training-sample importance weights


\(\varepsilon_m\ge 1/2\) is fine
Then \(\alpha_m\le 0\); flip the weak learner or stop — need \(\varepsilon_m<1/2\)


AdaBoost = gradient boosting on SSE
AdaBoost \(\leftrightarrow\) exponential loss / classification reweighting


Only works with trees
Any weak classifier API works; trees/stumps are common

title: Lecture 57 — Gradient Boosting Algorithm
text: Video: Lec 57 — Gradient Boosting Algorithm

title: Lecture 57 — Gradient Boosting Algorithm
text:
Learning goals

View boosting as stagewise minimization of an empirical loss.
For squared loss, see each step as fitting residuals.
State the generic gradient-boosting update with shrinkage.

title: Lecture 57 — Gradient Boosting Algorithm
text:
Before this clicks
We want \(F\) minimizing \(\sum_i \ell(y_i,F(x_i))\). Gradient boosting builds \(F\) as a sum of simple trees. At stage \(m\), treat the current prediction \(F_{m-1}(x_i)\) as fixed and add a tree \(f_m\) that points roughly in the direction that most reduces loss — the negative gradient of \(\ell\) w.r.t. the prediction at each training point. For \(\ell=(y-F)^{2}/2\), that direction is exactly the residual \(y-F\).

title: Lecture 57 — Gradient Boosting Algorithm
text:
Main ideas

1. Additive model
\[
F_M(x)=F_0(x)+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\nu\, f_m(x),
\]
with \(F_0\) a constant (e.g. \(\bar{y}\)), \(\nu\in(0,1]\) a learning rate (shrinkage), and each \(f_m\) a shallow regression tree.


2. Pseudo-residuals (functional gradient)
At points \(x_i\),
\[
r_{im}=-\left[\frac{\partial\ell(y_i,F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}\right]_{F=F_{m-1}}.
\]
Fit tree \(f_m\) to pairs \((x_i,r_{im})\) by least squares (CART regression). Then set \(F_m=F_{m-1}+\nu f_m\).


3. Squared loss \(\Rightarrow\) ordinary residuals
If \(\ell(y,F)=\frac12(y-F)^{2}\), then
\[
r_{im}=y_i-F_{m-1}(x_i).
\]
So gradient boosting literally fits the residuals of the current model, then adds a fraction \(\nu\) of that tree.


4. Algorithm sketch

Initialize \(F_0(x)=\arg\min_c\sum_i\ell(y_i,c)\).
For \(m=1,\ldots,M\): compute \(r_{im}\); fit \(f_m\) to \(\{r_{im}\}\); optionally line-search leaf values; \(F_m\leftarrow F_{m-1}+\nu f_m\).
Return \(F_M\).



5. Tuning knobs







Knob
Effect




\(M\)
More stages \(\to\) lower train loss; validate to stop


\(\nu\)
Smaller \(\Rightarrow\) need larger \(M\), often better test error


Tree depth
Depth \(1\)–\(3\) keeps base learners weak

title: Lecture 57 — Gradient Boosting Algorithm
text:
Worked mini-example
Points: \((x,y)\) with \(y=(1.0,\,2.0,\,3.0)\). \(F_0\equiv 2\). Residuals \(r=(1-2,\,2-2,\,3-2)=(-1,\,0,\,1)\).
A stump might predict \(f_1(x)\approx(-1,\,0,\,1)\) on those three rows. With \(\nu=0.5\),
\[
F_1=2+0.5\,f_1\;\Rightarrow\;\text{predictions }(1.5,\,2.0,\,2.5).
\]
New residuals \((1-1.5,\,2-2,\,3-2.5)=(-0.5,\,0,\,0.5)\). Next tree fits these; predictions march toward \(y\). Same loop, in high dimension, is gradient boosting.

title: Lecture 57 — Gradient Boosting Algorithm
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Always fit \(y\) again
After stage 0, trees fit gradients/residuals, not raw \(y\)


Same as AdaBoost
AdaBoost reweights classification errors; GB fits loss gradients


\(\nu=1\) is optimal
Full steps often overfit; shrinkage is standard


Need differentiable \(x\)
Gradients are w.r.t. predictions \(F(x_i)\), not features

title: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting
text: Video: Lec 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting
crumbs: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting

title: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting
text:
Learning goals

Motivate ensembles: reduce variance (and sometimes bias) by combining models.
Define bagging (bootstrap aggregating) and the random-forest idea.
Contrast bagging with boosting: sequential reweighting / residual fitting.
crumbs: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting

title: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting
text:
Before this clicks
A single deep tree is a low-bias, high-variance learner: change the sample a little, splits jump. Averaging many such trees trained on different bootstrap samples stabilizes predictions (bagging). Boosting instead builds models one after another, each fixing mistakes the current ensemble still makes. Same base learner (often a shallow tree); different collaboration pattern.
crumbs: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting

title: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting
text:
Main ideas

1. Ensemble prediction
Regression average / classification vote (or probability average):
\[
f_{\mathrm{ens}}(x)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} f_b(x)
\]
(with \(\mathrm{sign}\) or majority for \(\pm 1\) labels when appropriate).


2. Bagging
For \(b=1,\ldots,B\):

Draw a bootstrap sample \(\mathcal{D}_b\) (sample \(n\) rows with replacement from the training set).
Train tree \(f_b\) on \(\mathcal{D}_b\).

Aggregate as above. Trees are noisy but roughly unbiased; averaging cuts variance if errors are not perfectly correlated.
Random forest adds feature randomness: at each split, choose among a random subset of features — decorrelates trees further.


3. Boosting (big picture)
Fit \(f_1\), then \(f_2\) emphasizing points (or residuals) where \(f_1\) failed, then \(f_3\), … Final model is a weighted sum
\[
F_M(x)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\nu\, f_m(x)
\]
with small step size \(\nu\) (shrinkage) often helping generalization. Details differ for AdaBoost vs gradient boosting (next lectures).


4. Bagging vs boosting intuition









Bagging
Boosting




Order
Parallel / independent
Sequential


Focus
Equal-ish bootstrap draws
Hard examples / residuals


Typical trees
Deep, unpruned
Shallow (weak learners)


Main effect
Variance \(\downarrow\)
Bias \(\downarrow\) (risk of overfit if \(M\) huge)





5. Why trees ensemble so well?
Trees are unstable (good for bagging) and easy to make weak (good for boosting). Axis-aligned fragments combine into flexible surfaces without assuming linearity.
crumbs: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting

title: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting
text:
Worked mini-example
Three bootstrap trees vote on a test point: \(+1,+1,-1\) \(\Rightarrow\) bagged vote \(+1\). Separately, a boosted stack might be \(0.5\,f_1+0.3\,f_2+0.2\,f_3\) with each \(f_m\) correcting the previous weighted error — same base tree type, different combination logic.
Variance sketch: if \(B\) i.i.d. predictors each have variance \(\sigma^{2}\) and pairwise correlation \(\rho\),
\[
\mathrm{Var}\Bigl(\tfrac{1}{B}\sum_b f_b\Bigr)=\rho\sigma^{2}+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^{2}.
\]
Bagging helps through the \((1-\rho)/B\) term; forests try to shrink \(\rho\).
crumbs: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting

title: Lecture 56 — Ensemble Methods, Bagging and Boosting
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Bagging = boosting
Parallel average vs sequential correction


More trees always overfit in bagging
Bagging average usually plateaus; boosting can overfit with large \(M\)


Forest needs boosting
Random forest is bagging + feature subsets


Ensemble needs different algorithms
Same algorithm, different data/weights, is enough

title: Lecture 55 — Regression Trees
text: Video: Lec 55 — Regression Trees

title: Lecture 55 — Regression Trees
text:
Learning goals

Replace class impurity by squared-error cost for real-valued targets.
Derive that the optimal constant prediction on a region is the sample mean.
Split by minimizing weighted SSE of children (CART regression).

title: Lecture 55 — Regression Trees
text:
Before this clicks
Classification trees purify labels. Regression trees partition \(\mathcal{X}\) the same way, but each leaf predicts a number \(\hat{c}\) for \(y\in\mathbb{R}\). Under squared loss, the best constant on a fixed set of points is their average. Growing the tree means searching for a split that most reduces total squared error.

title: Lecture 55 — Regression Trees
text:
Main ideas

1. Leaf prediction under SSE
On a node \(S\) with targets \(\{y_i\}_{i\in S}\),
\[
\hat{c}_S=\arg\min_{c}\sum_{i\in S}(y_i-c)^{2}=\bar{y}_S=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}y_i.
\]
Node cost (sum of squares):
\[
\mathrm{SSE}(S)=\sum_{i\in S}(y_i-\bar{y}_S)^{2}.
\]


2. Choosing a split
For a candidate split into \(S_L,S_R\), score
\[
\mathrm{SSE}(S_L)+\mathrm{SSE}(S_R)
\]
and pick the feature/threshold with the smallest sum (largest SSE reduction vs parent). Same greedy recursion as classification CART; only the criterion changes.


3. Piecewise-constant function
The grown tree defines
\[
f(x)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\hat{c}_m\,\mathbf{1}\{x\in R_m\},
\]
where \(R_m\) are the leaf regions. Continuity is not required; jumps sit on split thresholds.


4. Stopping and smoothing cousins
Min leaf size, max depth, or cost-complexity pruning curb variance. (Ensembles of regression trees — bagging, random forests, boosting — come next lectures.)


5. Relation to classification trees




Classification
Regression




Leaf output
class vote / \(\hat{p}_k\)
mean \(\bar{y}\)


Split score
Gini / entropy gain
SSE reduction


Geometry
same axis-aligned partitions
same

title: Lecture 55 — Regression Trees
text:
Worked mini-example
Targets in \(S\): \(y=(1,2,6)\). Mean \(\bar{y}=3\),
\[
\mathrm{SSE}(S)=(1-3)^{2}+(2-3)^{2}+(6-3)^{2}=4+1+9=14.
\]
Split into \(\{1,2\}\) and \(\{6\}\):

Left mean \(1.5\), SSE \(=(1-1.5)^{2}+(2-1.5)^{2}=0.5\).
Right mean \(6\), SSE \(=0\).
Child total \(=0.5\) \(\ll\) \(14\) \(\Rightarrow\) strong split.

A worse split \(\{1\}\) vs \(\{2,6\}\): left SSE \(0\); right mean \(4\), SSE \(=(2-4)^{2}+(6-4)^{2}=8\); total \(8\) (still an improvement, but weaker than \(0.5\)).

title: Lecture 55 — Regression Trees
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Leaf should fit a line
Classic CART leaf is a constant; piecewise linear needs other models


Use Gini on \(y\)
Gini needs class labels; use SSE (or MAE variants) for regression


More splits always lower test MSE
Training SSE falls; test error can rise (overfit)


Split on \(y\) directly
Splits are on features \(x\); \(y\) only scores purity

title: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures
text: Video: Lec 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures
crumbs: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures

title: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures
text:
Learning goals

Describe a classification tree as a partition of \(\mathcal{X}\) into axis-aligned regions with constant class votes.
Define impurity via Gini and entropy; pick splits by information gain.
See greedy growing and the need to stop / prune to avoid memorizing noise.
crumbs: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures

title: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures
text:
Before this clicks
A decision tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions on features (e.g. “is \(x_1\le 3\)?”). Each leaf predicts by majority class (or class frequencies). Impurity measures how mixed the labels are in a node: pure node \(\Rightarrow\) impurity \(0\). A good split reduces average impurity of the children — that reduction is the gain.
crumbs: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures

title: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures
text:
Main ideas

1. Node class proportions
At a node \(S\) with \(n\) samples, let \(p_k\) be the fraction of class \(k\) (\(k=1,\ldots,K\)). Then \(\sum_k p_k=1\).


2. Impurity measures
Gini:
\[
G(S)=\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k(1-p_k)=1-\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k^{2}.
\]
Entropy:
\[
H(S)=-\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k\log p_k
\]
(with \(0\log 0:=0\)). Both are \(0\) if one \(p_k=1\), and largest when classes are balanced.


3. Information gain (impurity decrease)
Split \(S\) into \(S_L,S_R\) with sizes \(n_L,n_R\):
\[
\mathrm{Gain}(S;\text{split})
=I(S)-\frac{n_L}{n}I(S_L)-\frac{n_R}{n}I(S_R),
\]
where \(I\) is Gini or entropy. CART-style training picks the feature threshold maximizing gain (equivalently minimizing weighted child impurity).


4. Growing the tree
Recursively split leaves until pure, or hit a stop rule (max depth, min samples per leaf, gain too small). Deep trees fit training data almost perfectly \(\Rightarrow\) high variance; prune or constrain depth.


5. Prediction
Send \(x\) down the path of true/false answers; return the leaf’s majority label (or \(\arg\max_k p_k\)).
crumbs: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures

title: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures
text:
Worked mini-example
Node \(S\): 4 points, labels \([+,+,+,-]\) so \(p_+=3/4\), \(p_-=1/4\).
Gini:
\[
G(S)=1-\bigl((3/4)^2+(1/4)^2\bigr)=1-\bigl(9/16+1/16\bigr)=\frac{6}{16}=\frac{3}{8}.
\]
Entropy (nats, \(\ln\)):
\[
H(S)=-\frac{3}{4}\ln\frac{3}{4}-\frac{1}{4}\ln\frac{1}{4}.
\]
Suppose a split yields \(S_L\): \([+,+]\) (\(G=0\)) and \(S_R\): \([+,-]\) (\(G=1-(1/2)^2-(1/2)^2=1/2\)), sizes \(2,2\):
\[
\mathrm{Gain}=G(S)-\tfrac12\cdot 0-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\frac{3}{8}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8}.
\]
Any competing split with smaller gain loses.
crumbs: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures

title: Lecture 54 — Decision Trees and Impurity Measures
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Gini vs entropy
Both measure mix; splits usually similar in practice


Gain must use \(\log_2\)
Base only rescales entropy; argmax of gain unchanged


Trees are linear classifiers
Boundaries are piecewise constant, axis-aligned staircases


Pure leaves always best
On noisy data, purity can mean overfitting
