title: Lecture 31 — Bias–Variance Decomposition and Analysis
text: Video: Lec 31 — Bias - Variance Decomposition and Analysis

title: Lecture 31 — Bias–Variance Decomposition and Analysis
text:
Learning goals

State the generalization question: performance on a fresh sample from \(P_{X,Y}\).
Decompose (squared) risk into bias, variance, and irreducible noise.
Interpret bias as distance from the ideal risk minimizer; variance as sensitivity to the training set.

title: Lecture 31 — Bias–Variance Decomposition and Analysis
text:
Before this clicks
True risk \(R(h)=\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)\sim P}[L(h(X),Y)]\) is an expectation over the whole joint. ERM replaces that by an average on a finite sample \(\mathcal{D}\). Different draws of \(\mathcal{D}\) yield different \(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}\). Generalization asks whether \(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}\) still does well on new draws from the same \(P\).

title: Lecture 31 — Bias–Variance Decomposition and Analysis
text:
Main ideas

1. The generalization question
Given IID \(\mathcal{D}=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}\sim P_{X,Y}\), ERM returns a hypothesis \(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}\) in some class \(\mathcal{H}\).

Generalization: how well does \(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}\) perform on another sample from the same \(P_{X,Y}\)?

Doing well only on the training sample is not the goal (X-ray diagnosis on unseen patients, etc.).
If we could minimize true risk, any fresh sample from \(P\) would be fine. Trouble comes from the empirical surrogate at finite \(n\).


2. Squared-error setting (analysis template)
For \(L(h(x),y)=(h(x)-y)^2\), risk is
\[
R(h)=\mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\big[(h(X)-Y)^2\big].
\]
The ideal predictor (Bayes regressor under squared loss) is the conditional mean
\[
h^\star(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]
\]
(prove as homework: expand and use properties of conditional expectation).
Writing \(Y=h^\star(X)+\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon=Y-h^\star(X)\), the leftover \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2\mid X]\) is irreducible noise (label noise we cannot remove by choosing \(h\)).


3. Bias and variance of a learning algorithm
Think of the training set \(\mathcal{D}\) as random. Then \(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}\) is a random function. Roughly (pointwise intuition used in class):







Term
Meaning




Bias
How far the average learned predictor sits from \(h^\star\) (reality / true risk minimizer in \(\mathcal{H}\)’s sense)


Variance
How much \(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}\) jumps when \(\mathcal{D}\) is replaced by another draw


Noise
Uncontrollable label randomness



Algebraically, for squared loss, expected prediction error at a fixed \(x\) decomposes into bias\(^2\) + variance + noise. The lecture emphasizes the verbal meaning as much as the algebra:

Low bias: close to the true risk minimizer.
Low variance: stable across datasets.

Both must be small for small risk. In small-sample regimes they typically trade off (bias–variance dilemma). With huge \(n\) and huge capacity (modern GenAI scale), both can be driven down together.


4. Parameters vs hyperparameters (aside)
In a GMM, means / covariances / mixing weights are parameters fit by EM/MLE. The number of components \(K\) is a hyperparameter (chosen outside the inner optimizer). Bias–variance thinking applies to that outer choice too.


5. Bridge
Next lecture: a concrete 1-D regression picture of over-/underfitting, then regularization as a way to increase bias deliberately to cut variance.

title: Lecture 31 — Bias–Variance Decomposition and Analysis
text:
Worked mini-example
Suppose \(Y=f(X)+\varepsilon\) with \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid X]=0\), and two algorithms:

Always output the constant \(0\) (ignore data): high bias, zero variance.
Interpolate every training point with a wild high-degree fit: near-zero training bias, huge variance across draws of \(\mathcal{D}\).

Expected test error of (1) stays large even as \(n\to\infty\) if \(f\not\equiv 0\). Error of (2) can stay large at small \(n\) because a new sample of \(\varepsilon\) moves the interpolant a lot.

title: Lecture 31 — Bias–Variance Decomposition and Analysis
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Bias = “unfairness / ethics bias”
Here it is statistical approximation bias vs \(h^\star\).


Variance of \(Y\) = model variance
Model variance is variability of \(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}\) across datasets.


Training error \(=0\) means solved
Can be low bias + high variance (overfitting preview).


Decomposition only for classification
Lecture derives the clean form for squared loss; other losses have analogues with messier algebra.

title: Lecture 30 — Linear Models for Classification
text: Video: Lec 30 — Linear Models for Classification

title: Lecture 30 — Linear Models for Classification
text:
Learning goals

Adapt a linear hypothesis so its range matches labels (binary and \(K\)-class).
Recognize logistic regression as \(\sigma(\theta^\top x)\) / softmax of a linear map.
See why classification ERM usually needs gradient descent, and how cross-entropy fits the recipe.

title: Lecture 30 — Linear Models for Classification
text:
Before this clicks
ERM picks \(\theta\) by minimizing average loss of a hypothesis \(h_\theta\) on data. For regression we often used \(h_\theta(x)=\theta^\top x\) (or \(\theta^\top\phi(x)\)) with squared loss. Classification labels live in a discrete set (or one-hot vectors), so a raw linear score is the wrong type of output until we compose with a squash / normalize map.

title: Lecture 30 — Linear Models for Classification
text:
Main ideas

1. Range mismatch for classification
Data: \(\mathcal{D}=\{(x_i,y_i)\}\) with \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\).

Binary: \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) (or \(\{-1,+1\}\)).
\(K\)-class: often encode \(y\) as a one-hot vector in \(\{0,1\}^{K}\).

If \(h_\theta(x)=\theta^\top x\in\mathbb{R}\), the range is not \(\{0,1\}\) (or the simplex). Fix by composition.


2. Binary case: logistic / sigmoid link
\[
h_\theta(x)=\sigma(\theta^\top x),\qquad
\sigma(t)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-t}}.
\]
Then \(h_\theta(x)\in(0,1)\). A common classifier is thresholding:
\[
\hat{y}(x)=\mathbf{1}\{h_\theta(x)>\tau\}
\]
for a threshold \(\tau\) (a hyperparameter; ROC / false-positive tradeoffs appear in the tutorials). Same idea works with \(\sigma(\theta^\top\phi(x))\) (generalized linear features).
In class: any map that asymptotes to \(0\) on the left and \(1\) on the right is a sigmoid in Cybenko’s sense; the logistic is one popular choice.


3. \(K\)-class case: linear scores + softmax
Let \(\Theta\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d}\) and scores \(v=\Theta x\in\mathbb{R}^{K}\). Softmax:
\[
[\mathrm{softmax}(v)]_j
=\frac{e^{v_j}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}e^{v_k}}.
\]
Properties: each coordinate in \((0,1)\), and they sum to \(1\) (a discrete distribution over classes). Final decision: usually \(\arg\max_j\) of the softmax (or another rule you choose).
These models are the logistic classifiers / logistic regression family.


4. Loss + ERM: squared or cross-entropy
With one-hot \(y\) and probability vector \(h_\theta(x)\), squared error is possible but awkward. Cross-entropy (discrete) is the natural KL-style loss:
\[
L\big(h_\theta(x),y\big)
=-\sum_{k=1}^{K} y_k\log\big([h_\theta(x)]_k\big)
\]
(use the convention that puts the hard \(0/1\) label outside the \(\log\) so \(\log 0\) does not appear). Cross-entropy $= $ KL \(+\) entropy of the label distribution.
Exercise from class: which conditional \(P(Y\mid X)\) makes MLE match this loss?


5. No closed form \(\Rightarrow\) gradient descent
Unlike OLS, softmax + CE (or logistic + CE) generally has no closed-form \(\theta^\star\). Numerically:
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}=\theta^{(t)}-\alpha\,\nabla_\theta \widehat{R}(\theta^{(t)}).
\]

First-order methods dominate huge models (Hessian for \(10^{10}\) parameters is impossible).
Nonconvex surfaces: GD is not guaranteed to find a global minimum; the update comes from a first-order Taylor picture.
Logistic gradients can be hardcoded; deep nets need backpropagation (later).



6. Recipe (and teaser)
Choose \(h_\theta\), choose a loss, run GD on ERM. Same story as MLE / KL minimization under different packaging. Next lectures: bias–variance, then regularized ERM \(\leftrightarrow\) MAP.

title: Lecture 30 — Linear Models for Classification
text:
Worked mini-example
Binary \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\), \(\theta=(1,1)\), \(\tau=1/2\).
\[
\sigma(\theta^\top x)=\sigma(x_1+x_2).
\]

Point \((2,2)\): score \(4\), \(\sigma(4)\approx 0.98>1/2\) \(\to\) class \(1\).
Point \((-1,0)\): score \(-1\), \(\sigma(-1)\approx 0.27<1/2\) \(\to\) class \(0\).

Changing \(\tau\) moves the decision boundary in score-space and trades false positives vs false negatives (ROC).

title: Lecture 30 — Linear Models for Classification
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




“Logistic regression is a classifier with range \(\{0,1\}\)”
The model outputs a probability in \((0,1)\); the discrete label comes from a threshold.


Softmax outputs a one-hot
Softmax outputs a soft distribution; one-hot is for labels (or after \(\arg\max\)).


Squared loss for classification is “wrong”
It is a design choice with an implicit Gaussian-style story; CE matches a discrete conditional better.


GD always finds the global ERM optimum
Not for general nonconvex \(\widehat{R}\).

title: Lecture 29 — Generalized Least Squares (GLS)
text: Video: Lec 29 — Generalized Least Squares (GLS)

title: Lecture 29 — Generalized Least Squares (GLS)
text:
Learning goals

Lift raw \(x\) by a fixed transform \(\phi\) and run linear ERM in \(\phi\)-space.
Recognize polynomial / Fourier-style regression as generalized linear models.
Link choice of \(\phi\) to implicit class-conditional assumptions (Bayes view).
Preview: neural nets learn \(\phi\) instead of hand-designing it.

title: Lecture 29 — Generalized Least Squares (GLS)
text:
Before this clicks
Naive linear model: \(h_\theta(x)=\theta^\top x\). Real relationships may be quadratic, sinusoidal, etc. Idea: map \(x\mapsto\phi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^p\) with a user-chosen transform, then learn a linear model in the new coordinates.
(Playlist title says “GLS”; the lecture content is generalized linear models / least squares after feature transforms — classical “generalized least squares” with a noise covariance is a different topic.)

title: Lecture 29 — Generalized Least Squares (GLS)
text:
Main ideas

1. Fixed feature map
\[
\tilde x = \phi(x),\qquad \phi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^p.
\]
Coordinates of \(\phi\) may mix several input dimensions (design choice). Transform the whole training set, then solve OLS:
\[
\tilde\theta^\star = \arg\min_{\tilde\theta}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(\tilde\theta^\top\phi(x_i)-y_i\bigr)^2,
\]
with the usual normal-equation solution in the \(\phi\)-features.
Still “linear regression” in \(\tilde x\)-space; generally nonlinear in original \(x\).


2. Polynomial example
\(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \(\phi(x)=(1,x,x^2)^\top\). Then
\[
\tilde\theta^\top\phi(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2
\]
— polynomial regression = OLS after a polynomial feature map.
Fourier / sine–cosine expansions are the same pattern with trigonometric \(\phi\) (think Fourier series as ERM with those bases).


3. Design choices

What \(\phi\) to use (polynomial, wavelet, hand-crafted image/speech features, …).

Output dimension \(p\) (how many features).
Historically: entire careers spent on feature engineering. Deep nets later learn \(\phi\) jointly with the classifier.



4. Probabilistic / Bayes link (homework flavor from class)

Equal-covariance Gaussian class-conditionals \(\Rightarrow\) Bayes rule linear in \(x\).

Unequal covariances \(\Rightarrow\) quadratic decision boundary \(\Leftrightarrow\) quadratic features in an ERM story.
Choosing \(\phi\) reshapes the implicit distributional assumption behind the linear ERM in feature space.



5. Toward neural nets
If mixtures / complex densities need rich features, do not freeze \(\phi\): let a network represent \(\phi_\psi\) and train end-to-end. That is the “ignorance modeling” path previewed since Lecture 1.

title: Lecture 29 — Generalized Least Squares (GLS)
text:
Worked mini-example
Data roughly on a parabola. Linear OLS in raw \(x\) underfits. With \(\phi(x)=(1,x,x^2)\), OLS in 3-D feature space recovers a quadratic curve while still using the linear closed form in \(\tilde\theta\).

title: Lecture 29 — Generalized Least Squares (GLS)
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Linear in features \(\Rightarrow\) linear in \(x\)
Only if \(\phi\) itself is linear.


\(p\) must equal \(d\)
\(p\) is free; often \(p>d\).


Same as classical GLS (colored noise)
Here “generalized” means feature-lifted least squares / GLM-style maps.

Hastie et al., ESL — basis expansions & polynomials

title: Lecture 28 — Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
text: Video: Lec 28 — Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

title: Lecture 28 — Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
text:
Learning goals

Connect divergence / MLE estimation to empirical risk minimization (ERM).
See squared-loss ERM \(\Leftrightarrow\) Gaussian \(p(y\mid x)\) with mean \(h_\theta(x)\).
Solve linear regression / OLS in closed form via the pseudoinverse.

title: Lecture 28 — Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
text:
Before this clicks
Two cultures, one problem:







Probabilistic view
ERM view




Estimate distributions from \(\mathcal{D}\) via divergence / likelihood
Estimate a function \(h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\) by minimizing average loss



Claim in class: under matching assumptions, each divergence problem is an ERM with some loss, and each ERM is an MLE under some distributional assumption — checked case by case.

title: Lecture 28 — Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
text:
Main ideas

1. Equivalence example (squared loss)
Assume
\[
p_\theta(y\mid x) = \mathcal{N}\bigl(y;\, h_\theta(x),\, I\bigr).
\]
Maximizing likelihood (minimizing KL to the empirical conditional) reduces to
\[
\theta^\star = \arg\min_\theta \sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\|y_i - h_\theta(x_i)\bigr\|^2,
\]
i.e. ERM with squared error. Conversely, using squared loss implicitly assumes Gaussian noise around \(h_\theta(x)\).
The story “\(y=h_\theta(x)+\varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\)” is the same Gaussian conditional in generative clothing.


2. Linear family
\[
h_\theta(x) = \theta^\top x
\]
(with \(x\) optionally augmented by a trailing \(1\) so the bias sits inside \(\theta\)). Intuition: learn how much each measured feature contributes to the prediction.


3. OLS solution
ERM objective:
\[
\theta^\star = \arg\min_\theta \sum_{i=1}^{n}(\theta^\top x_i - y_i)^2.
\]
Stack rows \(x_i^\top\) into matrix \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) and targets into \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Normal equations yield
\[
\theta^\star = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y
\]
(when \(X^\top X\) is invertible). The map \(y\mapsto (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) uses the Moore–Penrose-style left pseudoinverse of \(X\).
This is linear regression because \(Y\) is continuous (not classification).

title: Lecture 28 — Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
text:
Worked mini-example
Two points \((x,y)=(1,1),(2,2)\), no bias term, scalar \(\theta\). OLS: \(\theta^\star=1\) (perfect line through origin). With bias via \(x\leftarrow(x,1)\), you can fit intercept as well.

title: Lecture 28 — Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




ERM ignores probability
Squared loss secretly assumes Gaussian \(p(y\mid x)\).


Pseudoinverse always needs invertibility
Use \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) when full rank; otherwise a generalized inverse / regularization.


Bias term forgotten
Augment \(x\) with a \(1\) coordinate or keep an explicit \(\theta_0\).

title: Lecture 27 — Nearest Neighbor Classifier
text: Video: Lec 27 — Nearest Neighbor Classifier

title: Lecture 27 — Nearest Neighbor Classifier
text:
Learning goals

Use the fix-\(K\), grow-\(V\) nonparametric density estimate.
Derive that \(k\)-NN classification is Bayes with that estimate.
Know the “at most twice Bayes risk” folklore bound and distance-metric role.

title: Lecture 27 — Nearest Neighbor Classifier
text:
Before this clicks
Parzen: fix volume, count neighbors.
Nearest-neighbor density: fix count \(K\), expand volume \(V\) around the query until \(K\) training points lie inside; then \(\hat p(x)=K/(nV)\).

title: Lecture 27 — Nearest Neighbor Classifier
text:
Main ideas

1. Density estimate
\[
\hat p(x) = \frac{K}{nV(x)},
\]
where \(V(x)\) is the volume needed to capture \(K\) neighbors of \(x\).


2. Bayes classifier with NN joint estimates
For \(M\)-class classification, grow a volume around query \(x\) until \(K\) labeled points are inside. Let \(K_i\) be how many of those have label \(i\) (\(\sum_i K_i=K\)).
Nearest-neighbor estimate of the joint:
\[
\widehat{p}(x,y=i) = \frac{K_i}{nV}.
\]
Posterior:
\[
\widehat{P}(Y=i\mid x) = \frac{K_i/(nV)}{\sum_j K_j/(nV)} = \frac{K_i}{K}.
\]
Bayes decision: choose \(i\) maximizing the posterior \(\Leftrightarrow\) choose the label with largest \(K_i\) among the \(K\) neighbors.
That is the \(k\)-nearest-neighbor classifier (here \(k=K\)).


3. Practical view

Pick distance metric (hyperparameter).

Pick \(k\).

Find \(k\) nearest training points to \(x\).

Majority vote (break ties somehow).

Special case \(k=1\): copy the label of the single nearest neighbor.


4. Theory highlight (stated without proof)
True risk of (suitable) nearest-neighbor rules is at most about twice the Bayes risk (classical result; see Duda–Hart). So a fancy method that loses to \(1\)-NN / \(k\)-NN on a problem is suspicious.


5. Course transition
This finishes the density-estimation arc. Next: return to ERM, linear models, then bias–variance / regularization (MAP in ERM clothing).

title: Lecture 27 — Nearest Neighbor Classifier
text:
Worked mini-example
\(k=3\), neighbors’ labels \(\{0,1,1\}\). Then \(\widehat{P}(Y=1\mid x)=2/3\), \(\widehat{P}(Y=0\mid x)=1/3\) \(\Rightarrow\) predict \(1\).

title: Lecture 27 — Nearest Neighbor Classifier
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




\(k\)-NN is “just a heuristic”
It is Bayes + NN nonparametric density estimates.


Volume is a free second knob
Choosing \(k\) implies a data-dependent volume.


Metric does not matter
Distance defines who the neighbors are — crucial.

title: Lecture 26 — Parzen Window
text: Video: Lec 26 — Parzen Window

title: Lecture 26 — Parzen Window
text:
Learning goals

Contrast parametric vs nonparametric density estimation.
Derive the histogram-style estimate \(\hat p(x)=K/(nV)\).
Write the Parzen-window (kernel) estimator with bandwidth \(h\).
Know soft kernels vs hard bins.

title: Lecture 26 — Parzen Window
text:
Before this clicks
Parametric path: assume a family \(p_\theta\), estimate \(\theta\) (MLE/MAP/EM). You get a whole function.
Nonparametric path: do not assume a global parametric form; only evaluate density at a query \(x\). For a Bayes classifier, evaluating \(p(x\mid y)\) at the test \(x\) is often enough.

title: Lecture 26 — Parzen Window
text:
Main ideas

1. Primitive estimate
Let \(R\) be a small region of volume \(V\) around \(x\). Then
\[
P(X\in R) = \int_R p(u)\,du \approx p(x)\,V
\]
if \(p\) is roughly constant on \(R\). With \(n\) i.i.d. samples, model “falls in \(R\)” as Bernoulli; MLE of that probability is \(K/n\) (\(K=\#\)points in \(R\)). Hence
\[
\hat p(x) = \frac{K}{nV}.
\]
This is the histogram idea.


2. Two nonparametric knobs

Fix \(V\), count \(K\) — Parzen window / kernel density estimate.

Fix \(K\), grow \(V\) — nearest-neighbor density estimate (next lecture).



3. Parzen window (hard cube)
Center a hypercube of side \(h\) at \(x\); volume \(V=h^d\). Define a unit-cube window \(\varphi(u)=1\) if \(|u_j|\le 1/2\) for all coordinates, else \(0\). Then
\[
\hat p(x) = \frac{1}{n h^d}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \varphi\!\left(\frac{x-x_i}{h}\right).
\]
(The sum counts how many \(x_i\) fall in the cube; divide by \(nV\).)


4. Soft kernels
Replace the hard indicator by a smooth kernel, e.g. a Gaussian bump. Then each point contributes a soft weight. Looks a bit like a mixture of Gaussians centered at data, but kernel parameters are fixed by the user, not learned like a GMM.
Bandwidth \(h\) (and kernel shape) are hyperparameters; theory studies when \(\hat p\to p\) as \(n\to\infty\).


5. Cost vs parametric models
Parametric: fit \(\theta\) once, evaluate quickly.
Parzen: for every new \(x\), sum over all training points — \(O(n)\) per query.

title: Lecture 26 — Parzen Window
text:
Worked mini-example
1-D data, \(h=2\), query \(x=0\). Hard window counts points in \([-1,1]\). If \(3\) of \(n=10\) fall inside, \(\hat p(0)=3/(10\cdot 2)=0.15\).

title: Lecture 26 — Parzen Window
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Parzen = GMM
Similar look with Gaussian kernels; GMM learns component parameters, Parzen does not.


One fit forever
Nonparametric estimate is query-dependent; recompute per \(x\).


Scale by \(h^d\) inside \(\varphi\)
Scale coordinates by \(h\); volume factor \(h^d\) sits outside (notation corrected in class).

title: Lecture 25 — MAP Estimate
text: Video: Lec 25 — MAP Estimate

title: Lecture 25 — MAP Estimate
text:
Learning goals

See when MLE fails with small \(n\).
Treat \(\theta\) as a random variable with a prior, form the posterior, take its mode (MAP).
Choose a conjugate prior; work the Bernoulli–Beta example.
Relate MAP \(\to\) MLE as \(n\to\infty\).

title: Lecture 25 — MAP Estimate
text:
Before this clicks
MLE treats \(\theta\) as an unknown constant and maximizes \(p(x\mid\theta)\). With tiny data, that can be silly: four coin tosses all heads \(\Rightarrow\hat\theta_{\mathrm{ML}}=1\) even if you know the coin is not two-headed.
Prior \(p(\theta)\): belief about \(\theta\) before seeing data. Posterior \(p(\theta\mid x)\propto p(x\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)\): updated belief.

title: Lecture 25 — MAP Estimate
text:
Main ideas

1. Bayesian parameter estimation (idea)
Assume \(\theta\sim p(\theta)\). After data \(x\),
\[
p(\theta\mid x) \;\propto\; p(x\mid\theta)\,p(\theta).
\]
You get a whole distribution over \(\theta\), not a single point. For building one Bayes classifier you often need one number: take the mode
\[
\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}} = \arg\max_\theta\, p(\theta\mid x) = \arg\max_\theta\, p(x\mid\theta)\,p(\theta).
\]
(Equivalently maximize \(\log p(x\mid\theta)+\log p(\theta)\).)


2. Conjugate priors
A prior is conjugate for a likelihood if the posterior stays in the same family as the prior. Motivation: parameter support/structure should not jump families just because you saw data (Bernoulli parameter stays on \((0,1)\); Beta\(\to\)Beta).


3. Example: Bernoulli with Beta prior
Likelihood (one flip): \(p(x\mid\theta)=\theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}\).
Beta prior:
\[
p(\theta) \propto \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1},\qquad \theta\in(0,1).
\]
Posterior \(\propto \theta^{x+\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-x}\) — still Beta (conjugate). Mode (for suitable \(\alpha,\beta\)):
\[
\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}} = \frac{x+\alpha-1}{\alpha+\beta-2}
\]
(for one sample; with \(n\) i.i.d. flips, replace \(x\) by \(\sum_i x_i\) and adjust the denominator with \(n\)).
Compare to \(\theta_{\mathrm{ML}}=\bar x\). Extra \(\alpha,\beta\) “pseudo-counts” pull the estimate toward the prior. As \(n\to\infty\), MAP \(\to\) MLE (data washes out the prior).
Uniform prior (special Beta) recovers MLE.


4. Full Bayes vs MAP (preview)
MAP collapses the posterior to one point. Fully Bayesian methods keep \(p(\theta\mid x)\) and push uncertainty into predictions (e.g. Bayesian neural nets). Later: MAP \(\leftrightarrow\) regularization in the ERM view.


5. Link to nonparametric next
Sometimes you only need \(p(x)\) at a query point, not a global parametric form — Parzen / nearest-neighbor density estimates.

title: Lecture 25 — MAP Estimate
text:
Worked mini-example
Fair-coin belief: Beta\((\alpha,\beta)\) peaked near \(1/2\). Data: three heads, one tail. MLE \(=3/4\). MAP pulls toward \(1/2\) depending on \(\alpha,\beta\). If all four are heads, MLE \(=1\) but MAP \(<1\) whenever \(\beta>1\).

title: Lecture 25 — MAP Estimate
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Prior comes from the training set
Prior is pre-data belief; data enters only through the likelihood.


Posterior family can be anything
Prefer conjugates so support/form stay coherent.


MAP uses the posterior mean
MAP = mode; for asymmetric posteriors mean \(\neq\) mode.

title: Lecture 24 — EM for GMMs
text: Video: Lec 24 — EM for GMMs

title: Lecture 24 — EM for GMMs
text:
Learning goals

Write a GMM as \(p(z)\,p(x\mid z)\) (dice then Gaussian).
Run the E-step: responsibilities via Bayes.
Set up the M-step objective for \((\alpha_j,\mu_j,\Sigma_j)\).
See why a fitted GMM is also a generative sampler.

title: Lecture 24 — EM for GMMs
text:
Before this clicks
A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) with \(M\) components:
\[
p_\theta(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{M} \alpha_j\,\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_j,\Sigma_j),\qquad \alpha_j\ge 0,\;\sum_j\alpha_j=1.
\]
Direct MLE hits \(\log\sum_j(\cdots)\) — hard. Introduce a discrete latent \(Z\in\{1,\ldots,M\}\) and use EM.

title: Lecture 24 — EM for GMMs
text:
Main ideas

1. Latent-variable story
\[
p_\theta(x,z) = p_\theta(z)\,p_\theta(x\mid z).
\]

\(Z\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_M)\) (roll an \(M\)-faced die).
\(X\mid Z=j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_j,\Sigma_j)\).

Marginalizing \(Z\) recovers the mixture. Parameters:
\[
\theta = \{\alpha_j,\mu_j,\Sigma_j\}_{j=1}^{M}.
\]


2. E-step (responsibilities)
With current \(\theta^{(t)}\),
\[
q^{(t+1)}(Z=j\mid x) = p_{\theta^{(t)}}(Z=j\mid x)
= \frac{\alpha_j^{(t)}\,\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_j^{(t)},\Sigma_j^{(t)})}{\sum_{k=1}^{M}\alpha_k^{(t)}\,\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_k^{(t)},\Sigma_k^{(t)})}.
\]
This is a discrete distribution over \(j\) for each data point (do it for every \(x_i\)).


3. M-step setup
Form
\[
F(\theta,q^{(t+1)}) = \mathbb{E}_{q^{(t+1)}}\!\left[\log\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q^{(t+1)}(z)}\right]
\]
and maximize in \(\theta\). For one point, the useful part is
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{M} q(Z=j\mid x)\Bigl[\log\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)+\log\alpha_j\Bigr],
\]
then sum over \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Closed forms (derived in Tutorial 8): weighted means, weighted covariances, and \(\alpha_j\) = average responsibility.


4. GMM as a generative model
After fitting: sample \(j\sim\alpha\), then sample \(x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_j,\Sigma_j)\). If the mixture matched the data distribution well (KL / likelihood), samples look like data. Course context: use GMMs to estimate class-conditionals for a Bayes classifier; generation is a bonus viewpoint.


5. Why EM works here
For mixture models the posterior \(p(z\mid x)\) is available in closed form via Bayes — so the “optimal variational \(q\)” is computable. Same idea extends to other latent-variable models when that posterior is tractable (HMMs mentioned as a historically notationally heavy example).


6. Bridge to MAP
MLE uses only data. With little data, MLE can be wild (e.g. five heads \(\Rightarrow\hat p=1\)). Next lectures put a prior on \(\theta\) (Bayesian / MAP).

title: Lecture 24 — EM for GMMs
text:
Worked mini-example (generative draw)
\(M=2\), \(\alpha=(0.7,0.3)\), \(\mu_1=-1\), \(\mu_2=2\), unit variances. Roll: with probability \(0.7\) draw from \(\mathcal{N}(-1,1)\), else from \(\mathcal{N}(2,1)\). The marginal density of \(X\) is the two-bump mixture.

text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




\(\alpha_j\) are free reals
They are mixture probabilities — simplex constraints.


E-step updates \(\mu_j\)
E-step only updates \(q\); M-step updates \(\theta\).


GMM \(\neq\) sampler
Fitting + ancestral sampling is generation.

title: Lecture 23 — Convergence of EM
text: Video: Lec 23 — Convergence of EM

title: Lecture 23 — Convergence of EM
text:
Learning goals

Restate the EM loop with clear \(\theta\) vs \(q\) bookkeeping.
Prove that \(\ell(\theta^{t+1})\ge \ell(\theta^t)\) (nondecreasing likelihood).
Know a practical stopping rule and a limitation of EM.

title: Lecture 23 — Convergence of EM
text:
Before this clicks
Evidence lower bound (ELBO): for a variational distribution \(q(z)\),
\[
F(\theta,q) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\log\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q(z)}\right] \;\le\; \log p_\theta(x)=\ell(\theta),
\]
with equality when \(q(z)=p_\theta(z\mid x)\) (posterior). EM maximizes the likelihood by iteratively tightening and raising this lower bound.
Key notational point: \(q\) and \(F(\theta,q)\) can be evaluated at different parameter values.

title: Lecture 23 — Convergence of EM
text:
Main ideas

1. EM algorithm (recall)
Initialize \(\theta^{(1)}\). For \(t=1,2,\ldots\) until convergence:
E-step. Set
\[
q^{(t+1)}(z) \;=\; p_{\theta^{(t)}}(z\mid x)
\]
and form the ELBO as a function of \(\theta\):
\[
F\bigl(\theta,\,q^{(t+1)}\bigr) = \mathbb{E}_{q^{(t+1)}}\!\left[\log\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q^{(t+1)}(z)}\right].
\]
M-step.
\[
\theta^{(t+1)} \;=\; \arg\max_\theta F\bigl(\theta,\,q^{(t+1)}\bigr).
\]


2. Convergence claim
\[
\ell(\theta^{(t+1)}) \;\ge\; \ell(\theta^{(t)}).
\]
Likelihood never decreases (may stay flat).


3. Proof chain

After the E-step, \(q^{(t+1)}=p_{\theta^{(t)}}(z\mid x)\), so the bound is tight at \(\theta^{(t)}\): \[
\ell(\theta^{(t)}) = F\bigl(\theta^{(t)},\,q^{(t+1)}\bigr).
\]
M-step maximizes \(F(\cdot,q^{(t+1)})\), so \[
F\bigl(\theta^{(t+1)},\,q^{(t+1)}\bigr) \;\ge\; F\bigl(\theta^{(t)},\,q^{(t+1)}\bigr).
\]
By Jensen / ELBO construction, for any \(\theta\), \[
\ell(\theta) \;\ge\; F\bigl(\theta,\,q^{(t+1)}\bigr).
\] In particular at \(\theta^{(t+1)}\): \[
\ell(\theta^{(t+1)}) \;\ge\; F\bigl(\theta^{(t+1)},\,q^{(t+1)}\bigr).
\]
Chain (3)+(2)+(1): \(\ell(\theta^{(t+1)})\ge\ell(\theta^{(t)})\).

Note: Equality in step 3 needs the posterior at \(\theta^{(t+1)}\), which we do not have yet — so we only use \(\ge\), not \(=\), at the new point.


4. Practice notes

Stopping: track \(\ell(\theta^{(t+1)})-\ell(\theta^{(t)})\); stop when improvement \(<\delta\) (user hyperparameter), or after a max iteration count.
Drawback: inequality is not strict — EM can stall at local maxima / saddle plateaus.
EM does not invent new likelihood; it guarantees monotone progress of the true \(\ell\) under this construction.

title: Lecture 23 — Convergence of EM
text:
Worked mini-example (logic only)
Start at \(\theta^{(t)}\). E-step makes ELBO touch \(\ell\) at that point. M-step climbs the ELBO surface in \(\theta\) with \(q\) frozen. The new \(\ell\) sits above the new ELBO value, which sits above the old ELBO value, which equals the old \(\ell\). Hence likelihood did not drop.

title: Lecture 23 — Convergence of EM
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




EM always finds the global MLE
No — only monotone improvement; local optima possible.


ELBO always equals likelihood
Only when \(q\) is the posterior at the same \(\theta\) you evaluate.


Stop when parameters stop moving
Equivalent in spirit; class emphasizes monitoring likelihood improvement.

title: Lecture 22 — Expectation Maximization Algorithm
text: Video: Lec 22 — Expectation Maximization Algorithm

title: Lecture 22 — Expectation Maximization Algorithm
text:
Learning goals

Prove the ELBO gap equals \(\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q(z)\,\|\,P_\theta(z\mid x)\bigr)\)
Conclude the tight choice \(q^\star(z)=P_\theta(z\mid x)\)
Write the EM iteration (E-step / M-step)
Know when EM applies vs when full variational inference over \(q\) is needed

title: Lecture 22 — Expectation Maximization Algorithm
text:
Before this clicks
ELBO: \(L(\theta)=\log P_\theta(x)\ge F(\theta,q)=\mathbb{E}_q[\log P_\theta(x,z)-\log q(z)]\).
KL divergence between two distributions on \(Z\). Posterior \(P_\theta(z\mid x)\).

title: Lecture 22 — Expectation Maximization Algorithm
text:
Main ideas

1. When is the ELBO tight?
Compute the gap (algebra in lecture):
\[
L(\theta)-F(\theta,q)=\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q(z)\,\|\,P_\theta(z\mid x)\bigr)\;\ge\; 0.
\]
Therefore \(F=L\) iff
\[
q(z)=P_\theta(z\mid x).
\]
Best variational distribution (for fixed \(\theta\)) is the true posterior of the latent given data.


2. Two-block view
In full generality one could optimize \(F\) over both \(q\) (function space — variational calculus) and \(\theta\). That is variational inference.
If \(P_\theta(z\mid x)\) is tractable, skip optimizing \(q\): just set \(q\leftarrow P_\theta(z\mid x)\) and optimize \(\theta\). GMMs sit in this tractable-posterior camp. VAEs / many deep models do not — estimate \(q\) explicitly (later courses).


3. EM algorithm (tractable posterior case)
Initialize \(\theta^{(0)}\). For \(t=0,1,2,\ldots\) until a stopping rule:

E-step (expectation): set \[
q^{(t)}(z)\;\leftarrow\; P_{\theta^{(t)}}(z\mid x)
\] and form the ELBO \(F(\theta,q^{(t)})\) as a function of \(\theta\) (expectation under fixed \(q^{(t)}\)).
M-step (maximization): \[
\theta^{(t+1)}\;\leftarrow\;\arg\max_\theta F\bigl(\theta,\,q^{(t)}\bigr).
\]

Then repeat: new \(\theta\) \(\Rightarrow\) new posterior \(\Rightarrow\) new bound \(\Rightarrow\) new \(\theta\).
(For \(n\) datapoints, apply with latents \(z_i\) and sum ELBO terms — same pattern.)


4. Why alternate?
The tight \(q\) depends on the current \(\theta\). After you move \(\theta\), the old \(q\) is no longer the posterior at the new parameter, so rebuild the bound and maximize again.


5. Correctness teaser (next lecture)
EM guarantees the observed likelihood does not decrease:
\[
L\bigl(\theta^{(t+1)}\bigr)\;\ge\; L\bigl(\theta^{(t)}\bigr).
\]
It need not strictly increase every time, and need not reach a global maximum — one reason “GMM is universal + EM exists” does not end all of ML.


6. Storyline reminder
Want Bayes classifier \(\Rightarrow\) estimate class-conditionals \(\Rightarrow\) those may be GMMs \(\Rightarrow\) GMM MLE via EM as latent-variable ELBO optimization with \(q=P(z\mid x)\).

title: Lecture 22 — Expectation Maximization Algorithm
text:
Worked mini-example (conceptual)
Two-component GMM: \(z\in\{1,2\}\) is “which Gaussian generated \(x\).”

E-step: compute responsibilities \(q(z=j\mid x)=P_{\theta^{(t)}}(z=j\mid x)\) (soft assignment).
M-step: re-estimate weights / means / covariances by maximizing the expected complete log-likelihood under those responsibilities (standard GMM updates — detailed in later EM-for-GMM lecture).

One iteration: soft-cluster points, then refit Gaussians to weighted points.

title: Lecture 22 — Expectation Maximization Algorithm
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




E-step maximizes something
E-step sets \(q\) to the current posterior (makes ELBO tight); M-step maximizes over \(\theta\)


EM always finds the global MLE
Guarantees non-decreasing likelihood; local optima possible


Always optimize \(q\) with gradients
Only when posterior is intractable; else plug in \(P_\theta(z\mid x)\)


ELBO gap is mysterious
It is exactly \(\mathrm{KL}(q\|P_\theta(z\mid x))\)

text:

title: Lecture 22 — Expectation Maximization Algorithm
text:

What likelihood monotonicity property does EM claim (preview)?

(Short answers are in self-check-answers.qmd.)

title: Lecture 21 — MLE for Latent Variable Models
text:
Learning goals

Write the observed-data log-likelihood with a latent sum/integral inside the \(\log\)
Introduce a variational distribution \(q(z)\) and apply Jensen to get a lower bound
Recognize the ELBO (evidence lower bound) and the new optimization target
crumbs: Lecture 21 — MLE for Latent Variable Models

title: Lecture 21 — MLE for Latent Variable Models
text:
Before this clicks
Latent model: \(P_\theta(x)=\sum_z P_\theta(x,z)\).
Want \(\max_\theta\log P_\theta(x)\) but have \(\log\sum_z\).
Jensen: for concave \(\log\), \(\log\mathbb{E}[U]\ge\mathbb{E}[\log U]\) (discrete expectations OK).
crumbs: Lecture 21 — MLE for Latent Variable Models

title: Lecture 21 — MLE for Latent Variable Models
text:
Main ideas

1. Likelihood with one datapoint (notation)
Class algebra uses a single \(x\) for clarity; for \(n\) points, add an outer sum over \(i\).
\[
L(\theta)=\log P_\theta(x)=\log\sum_z P_\theta(x,z)
\]
(discrete latent; continuous \(\mapsto\) integral).
Goal: maximize \(L(\theta)\), and also deal with unknown \(z\) by estimating a density/mass on \(Z\).


2. Insert \(q(z)\)
Let \(q(z)>0\) be any distribution on \(Z\) (mass function if discrete). Then
\[
P_\theta(x)=\sum_z q(z)\,\frac{P_\theta(x,z)}{q(z)},
\]
so
\[
L(\theta)=\log\mathbb{E}_{z\sim q}\Bigl[\frac{P_\theta(x,z)}{q(z)}\Bigr].
\]


3. Jensen \(\Rightarrow\) ELBO
Because \(\log\) is concave,
\[
L(\theta)\;\ge\; \mathbb{E}_{z\sim q}\Bigl[\log\frac{P_\theta(x,z)}{q(z)}\Bigr]
\;=\; F(\theta,q).
\]
\(F(\theta,q)\) is the evidence lower bound (ELBO) (“evidence” \(=\) log-likelihood). It replaces \(\log\)sum by an expectation of logs — much friendlier structure.


4. New optimization problem
Instead of maximizing \(L(\theta)\) directly (intractable for many latent models), maximize the lower bound \(F(\theta,q)\) over \(\theta\) (and, in full generality, over \(q\)).
Caveat stated in class: maximizing a lower bound does not automatically maximize \(L\); we need algorithms (EM next) that control the gap.


5. Link forward
Lecture 22 asks: which \(q\) makes the bound tight (\(F=L\))? Answer: \(q(z)=P_\theta(z\mid x)\). That choice yields the EM iteration when the posterior is tractable (e.g. GMMs).
crumbs: Lecture 21 — MLE for Latent Variable Models

title: Lecture 21 — MLE for Latent Variable Models
text:
Worked mini-example
Binary latent \(z\in\{0,1\}\), some joint \(P_\theta(x,z)\). Pick \(q(0)=q(1)=\tfrac12\). Then
\[
F(\theta,q)=\tfrac12\sum_{z=0}^{1}\log\frac{P_\theta(x,z)}{1/2}
=\tfrac12\sum_{z=0}^{1}\log\bigl(2P_\theta(x,z)\bigr),
\]
while \(L(\theta)=\log\bigl(P_\theta(x,0)+P_\theta(x,1)\bigr)\). Jensen guarantees \(L\ge F\); equality only for special \(q\) (next lecture).
crumbs: Lecture 21 — MLE for Latent Variable Models

title: Lecture 21 — MLE for Latent Variable Models
text:

Confusion
Clarification




ELBO replaces the true likelihood forever
It is a bound we optimize when \(L\) is hard; tightness matters


\(q\) must equal the prior \(P(z)\)
\(q\) is a free variational distribution on \(Z\)


Jensen gives an upper bound
For concave \(\log\), Jensen gives a lower bound on \(\log\mathbb{E}\)


Only neural VAEs use ELBO
EM for mixtures is the same ELBO idea with a special \(q\)

title: Lecture 20 — Latent Variable Models

title: Lecture 20 — Latent Variable Models
text:
Learning goals

Recall why mixture MLE is hard (\(\log\sum\)) and needs a new algorithm family
Motivate latent \(Z\) as compression / semantics / unobserved structure
Define a latent variable model via marginalization of \(P_\theta(x,z)\)
See mixtures / GMMs as latent-variable models (discrete component index)

title: Lecture 20 — Latent Variable Models
text:
Before this clicks
Mixture: \(P_\theta(v)=\sum_j\alpha_j P_{\theta_j}(v)\).
Log-likelihood has \(\log\sum_j\), blocking easy MLE. Joint / marginal / conditional densities for two RVs.

title: Lecture 20 — Latent Variable Models
text:
Main ideas

1. From mixtures to a broader family
EM will apply to a large class: latent variable models. Mixtures are members; so are many deep generative models (VAEs, diffusion — previewed as future course material). Same algorithmic skeleton, different choices of \(P(x,z)\).


2. Philosophy: information via compression
High-\(d\) \(x\) (pixels) often has lower-dimensional semantics (digit thickness, face attributes, …). Introducing an unobserved \(Z\) is a modeling way to talk about that compressed representation. Latent directions can carry editable semantics (style change stories in class).
We typically do not hand-label what each coordinate of \(Z\) means; the model discovers structure (representation learning). Dimensionality and distributional form of \(Z\) are design choices.


3. Mathematical definition
Observed data \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). Introduce unobserved \(z\) (often \(z\in\mathbb{R}^{k}\) with \(k<d\), but not required; for mixtures \(z\) is discrete).
Latent variable model: define a joint \(P_\theta(x,z)\) and set the observed model to the marginal
\[
P_\theta(x)=\sum_z P_\theta(x,z)
\quad\text{(discrete $z$)},
\]
or
\[
P_\theta(x)=\int P_\theta(x,z)\,dz
\quad\text{(continuous $z$)}.
\]
Once a joint exists, so do \(P_\theta(z)\), \(P_\theta(x\mid z)\), \(P_\theta(z\mid x)\), etc.


4. What we estimate
Still care about modeling \(P(x)\) (or whatever observed law). With latents we typically estimate both parameters \(\theta\) and structure over \(Z\) (a distribution on the latent) — because \(z\) values were never observed.


5. Mixture as latent variable model
Think of discrete \(Z\in\{1,\ldots,M\}\) with \(P(Z=j)=\alpha_j\) and \(P(x\mid Z=j)=P_{\theta_j}(x)\). Then
\[
P_\theta(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\alpha_j P_{\theta_j}(x),
\]
exactly the mixture. So GMM MLE is latent-variable MLE with a discrete component indicator.


6. Parameters for a GMM (bookkeeping)
Estimate \(\{\alpha_j,\mu_j,\Sigma_j\}_{j=1}^{M}\). \(M\) remains a hyperparameter. Outer sum in the log-likelihood is over data points; inner sum is over components — different roles.

title: Lecture 20 — Latent Variable Models
text:
Worked mini-example
Handwritten digit image \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\). Let discrete \(Z\in\{0,\ldots,9\}\) mean “which digit semantics.” Even without labels, a latent-variable model that recovers \(P(Z\mid x)\) is doing unsupervised discovery of digit identity — the lecture’s MNIST-style motivation.

title: Lecture 20 — Latent Variable Models
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Latent \(Z\) is in the dataset
By definition unobserved; we infer distributions over it


Must know what \(Z\) “means”
Usually unsupervised; interpretation is post hoc


Latent models replace density estimation
They are a way to parameterize \(P_\theta(x)\) via a joint


Continuous \(Z\) only
Mixtures use discrete \(Z\); transformers / VAEs often continuous

title: Lecture 19 — Density Estimation for Mixed Distribution

crumbs: Lecture 19 — Density Estimation for Mixed Distribution

title: Lecture 19 — Density Estimation for Mixed Distribution
text:
Learning goals

See the failure mode of unimodal models on multimodal data
Define a mixture density and the special case GMM
Treat \(M\) (number of components) as a hyperparameter
Understand why GMM log-likelihood is \(\log\sum\) (not analytically friendly)
crumbs: Lecture 19 — Density Estimation for Mixed Distribution

title: Lecture 19 — Density Estimation for Mixed Distribution
text:
Before this clicks
MLE needs a model family \(P_\theta\). If the family cannot get close to \(P_V\) in KL, no amount of optimizing \(\theta\) saves you (same energy as choosing a too-poor hypothesis class in ERM).
crumbs: Lecture 19 — Density Estimation for Mixed Distribution

title: Lecture 19 — Density Estimation for Mixed Distribution
text:
Main ideas

1. Bad model family \(\Rightarrow\) large KL floor
If truth is multimodal but \(P_\theta\) is a single Gaussian, you can only slide mean / inflate variance. KL stays large — analogous to fitting a line to a quadratic.
Mode: a point where the density’s derivative vanishes; multimodal \(=\) multiple such bumps (typical in practice).


2. Mixture density
For \(v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\),
\[
P_\theta(v)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\alpha_j\, P_{\theta_j}(v),
\]
with \(\alpha_j\in[0,1]\), \(\sum_j\alpha_j=1\), and each \(P_{\theta_j}\) a density. This is a convex combination of densities, not a combination of the random variable’s values.
Components need not share a family; often they do (homogeneous mixture).


3. Gaussian mixture model (GMM)
Each \(P_{\theta_j}=\mathcal{N}(\mu_j,\Sigma_j)\). Parameters: weights \(\alpha_j\), means \(\mu_j\), covariances \(\Sigma_j\).
Hyperparameter: \(M\) (and often the component family) — chosen, not usually optimized inside the same MLE step as \(\theta\).


4. Why GMMs are popular (theorem stated in class)
GMMs are universal density approximators for continuous densities: with enough components you can drive KL to the truth arbitrarily small in principle. (Linear combinations of Gaussians act like a basis for a rich function space — Fourier analogy in class.)


5. Why not “course ends at GMM + Bayes”?
In high dimension (curse of dimensionality), iterative MLE for GMMs can stick at poor local optima. Also many modern models need broader latent-variable / variational tools. Still: GMM + EM is a core algorithmic chapter.


6. The algebraic snag
For exponential-family singles, \(\log P_\theta\) cancels the exp and derivatives separate. For mixtures,
\[
\log P_\theta(v_i)=\log\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{M}\alpha_j P_{\theta_j}(v_i)\Bigr)
\]
— log of a sum. Setting derivatives to zero does not yield a clean closed form \(\Rightarrow\) need iterative methods (EM), previewed as optimizing a lower bound on the likelihood.
crumbs: Lecture 19 — Density Estimation for Mixed Distribution

title: Lecture 19 — Density Estimation for Mixed Distribution
text:
Worked mini-example
1-D data with two clear clumps near \(-2\) and \(+2\). A single \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})\) MLE puts mass in the middle valley. A \(2\)-component GMM can place one Gaussian on each clump with weights \(\approx\) clump sizes — much smaller KL to a two-mode truth.
crumbs: Lecture 19 — Density Estimation for Mixed Distribution

text:

Confusion
Clarification




Mixture \(=\) RV is sum of RVs
Mixture combines densities with weights \(\alpha_j\)


More components always better in practice
Extra capacity helps approximation but hurts optimization / overfitting concerns


Universal approximator \(\Rightarrow\) solved ML
Theory vs high-\(d\) optimization reality


Parameter \(=\) hyperparameter
\(\alpha,\mu,\Sigma\) estimated; \(M\) typically chosen

title: Lecture 18 — MLE for Generalized Discrete Random Variable
text:
Learning goals

Model a general discrete RV with \(M\) atoms and probabilities \(p_1,\ldots,p_M\)
Write its PMF using one-hot auxiliary codes
Solve constrained MLE \(\Rightarrow\) \(\hat p_j=\) empirical frequency of symbol \(a_j\)
crumbs: Lecture 18 — MLE for Generalized Discrete Random Variable

title: Lecture 18 — MLE for Generalized Discrete Random Variable
text:
Before this clicks
MLE maximizes \(\sum_i\log P_\theta(v_i)\).
Probabilities must satisfy \(p_j\ge 0\) and \(\sum_j p_j=1\) (constrained optimization / Lagrange).
crumbs: Lecture 18 — MLE for Generalized Discrete Random Variable

title: Lecture 18 — MLE for Generalized Discrete Random Variable
text:
Main ideas

1. Model
Each \(V_i\) takes values in \(\{a_1,\ldots,a_M\}\) with
\[
P(V=a_j)=p_j,\qquad \theta=(p_1,\ldots,p_M).
\]
(Coin = \(M=2\); die = \(M=6\).) Only \(M-1\) free parameters because of the simplex constraint.


2. One-hot representation
For each observation \(v_i\), define \(z_i\in\{0,1\}^{M}\) with
\[
z_{ij}=1 \iff v_i=a_j.
\]
Example (die): \(v=2\) \(\mapsto\) \((0,1,0,0,0,0)\).
Then the PMF compactly reads
\[
P_\theta(v_i)=\prod_{j=1}^{M} p_j^{z_{ij}}.
\]
(Only the matching \(p_j\) survives.)


3. Log-likelihood
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log P_\theta(v_i)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{M} z_{ij}\log p_j.
\]


4. Constraints matter
Without \(\sum_j p_j=1\) and bounds, maximizing \(\sum z_{ij}\log p_j\) drives some \(p_j\to\infty\). So optimize with
\[
p_j\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^{M}p_j=1.
\]
Lagrangian algebra (exercise in class) yields
\[
\hat p_j=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_{ij}=\frac{\#\{i:v_i=a_j\}}{n}.
\]
Moral: counting frequencies is MLE for this categorical model — again minimum KL under that assumption.


5. Estimator quality (pointer)
How close \(\hat p\) is to true \(p\) is a concentration / confidence question (analogous to generalization for ERM). Beyond this course’s depth, but the same spirit.
crumbs: Lecture 18 — MLE for Generalized Discrete Random Variable

title: Lecture 18 — MLE for Generalized Discrete Random Variable
text:
Worked mini-example
Die rolls: \(2,3,2,1,2\) (\(n=5\)). Then
\[
\hat p_1=\tfrac15,\; \hat p_2=\tfrac35,\; \hat p_3=\tfrac15,\; \hat p_4=\hat p_5=\hat p_6=0.
\]
(Zero estimates for unseen faces are allowed under plain MLE; smoothing is a later / other topic.)
crumbs: Lecture 18 — MLE for Generalized Discrete Random Variable

title: Lecture 18 — MLE for Generalized Discrete Random Variable
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




This is binomial / multinomial trials
One categorical draw’s PMF; multinomial is counts from many IID draws


Unconstrained MLE is fine
Without simplex constraints the optimum is nonsense


One-hot changes the experiment
Reparameterization for algebra; same data


Frequency estimator is “just heuristics”
It is the ML estimator for this model

title: Lecture 17 — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text: Video: Lec 17 — MLE for Gaussian Distribution

title: Lecture 17 — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text:
Learning goals

Reconnect Bayes optimality \(\Rightarrow\) “estimate densities from data”
Run MLE for \(V\sim\mathcal{N}(\theta,I)\) and get \(\hat\theta=\bar V\)
See this as an analytically solvable case before mixtures / EM

title: Lecture 17 — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text:
Before this clicks
MLE / min KL: \(\hat\theta=\arg\max_\theta\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\log P_\theta(v_i)\).
Bayes classifier needs posteriors / class-conditionals. Multivariate Gaussian density with mean \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) and covariance \(I\).

title: Lecture 17 — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text:
Main ideas

1. Why density estimation now?
To implement the Bayes classifier you need \(P(Y\mid X)\) or pieces that determine it: priors, class-conditionals \(p(x\mid y)\), etc. So the algorithmic stretch of the course focuses on estimating densities (evaluation, not yet sampling / generation).


2. MLE template (again)
IID sample \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) from unknown \(P_V\). Assume model \(P_\theta\), maximize
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log P_\theta(v_i).
\]


3. Gaussian mean model
Assume
\[
P_\theta(v)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\exp\Bigl(-\tfrac12\|v-\theta\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr),\qquad v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
\]
(covariance fixed to \(I\)). Parameters: \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\).
Up to additive constants independent of \(\theta\),
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta)\;\propto\; -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|v_i-\theta\|_{2}^{2}.
\]
Set \(\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}=0\) \(\Rightarrow\)
\[
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{ML}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_i.
\]
Moral: “take the sample average as the mean” is MLE / minimum KL under this Gaussian model — not a random habit.


4. Analytic vs numeric
Here differentiation works cleanly. Later (mixtures), \(\log\sum_j(\cdots)\) blocks that cancellation; we will need iterative methods (EM).


5. Link to class-conditionals
Example story: model pixel vectors of an X-ray class as high-\(d\) Gaussians; MLE mean \(=\) average image in that class (under this simplified covariance).

title: Lecture 17 — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text:
Worked mini-example
\(d=1\), data \(\{0,2,4\}\), model \(\mathcal{N}(\theta,1)\).
\[
\hat\theta=\frac{0+2+4}{3}=2.
\]
Same as minimizing \(\sum_i (v_i-\theta)^2\).

title: Lecture 17 — MLE for Gaussian Distribution
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Sample mean is always “the” mean estimate
It is ML for this Gaussian mean model (covariance fixed)


We estimated the full Gaussian
Covariance was fixed to \(I\); estimating \(\Sigma\) is a similar but matrix exercise


Density estimation \(=\) sampling
Here we care about evaluating \(P_\theta(v)\); generative sampling is a later topic


Only unsupervised
Same algebra estimates a class-conditional if you restrict to one class’s samples

text:

Bishop PRML Ch.2 — Gaussian MLE

title: Lecture 16 — Bayes Classifier
text: Video: Lec 16 — Bayes Classifier

title: Lecture 16 — Bayes Classifier
text:
Learning goals

State the Bayes classifier for binary (and \(K\)-class) \(0\)–\(1\) loss
Sketch why its risk is minimal among all classifiers
See that implementing Bayes \(\Rightarrow\) density / posterior estimation
Preview: under squared loss, the risk minimizer is \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\)

title: Lecture 16 — Bayes Classifier
text:
Before this clicks
True risk \(R(h)=\mathbb{E}[L(h(X),Y)]\).
For \(0\)–\(1\) loss, \(L(h(x),y)=\mathbf{1}\{h(x)\neq y\}\).
Posteriors \(P(Y=y\mid X=x)\); class-conditionals \(P(X\mid Y)\).

title: Lecture 16 — Bayes Classifier
text:
Main ideas

1. Binary Bayes rule (\(0\)–\(1\) loss)
Define
\[
h_B(x)=
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } P(Y=0\mid X=x) > P(Y=1\mid X=x),\\
1 & \text{otherwise (ties broken arbitrarily).}
\end{cases}
\]
Equivalently: predict the label with largest posterior. This is the Bayes classifier.
Claim: for binary classification with \(0\)–\(1\) loss, \(R(h_B)\le R(h)\) for every classifier \(h\).


2. Proof sketch (partition view)
For any \(h\), partition \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) into
\[
S_i(h)=\{x: h(x)=i\},\quad i\in\{0,1\}
\]
(disjoint, union all space). Under \(0\)–\(1\) loss,
\[
R(h)=P\bigl(h(X)\neq Y\bigr).
\]
Split the error event into “predict \(1\) when \(Y=0\)” and “predict \(0\) when \(Y=1\)”, rewrite with class-conditionals, and integrate densities over \(S_1(h)\) and \(S_0(h)\).
For each \(x\), only one of the two integrand pieces is active (whichever region \(h\) assigns \(x\) to). The Bayes rule always picks the region so that the smaller of the two non-negative contributions is kept. Integrating the pointwise minimum yields the smallest possible risk.


3. Practice: you rarely know the posteriors
Bayes optimality is theoretical until you can compute \(P(Y\mid X)\). So “build the best classifier” becomes estimate the needed densities (posterior directly, or priors + class-conditionals via Bayes’ rule).


4. Extensions stated in class

\(K\)-class, \(0\)–\(1\) loss: \(h_B(x)=\arg\max_{k} P(Y=k\mid X=x)\) (same “pick largest posterior” idea; homework-style proof).
Regression, squared loss: true-risk minimizer is the conditional mean \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]\) (standard probability result).

Optimal \(h\) depends on the loss.


5. Why this lecture matters in the course arc
ERM \(\leftrightarrow\) distribution estimation was about matching problems. Bayes shows matching solutions: the true-risk minimizer is a functional of \(P(Y\mid X)\). Next lectures develop estimation tools (MLE examples, mixtures, EM, MAP, …) so you can approximate that posterior / those densities.

title: Lecture 16 — Bayes Classifier
text:
Worked mini-example
At a fixed \(x\), suppose \(P(Y=0\mid x)=0.7\), \(P(Y=1\mid x)=0.3\). Bayes predicts \(0\).
Any rule that predicts \(1\) at this \(x\) pays conditional error probability \(0.7\) instead of \(0.3\). Averaging over \(x\) cannot beat always taking the locally better choice — that is the Bayes idea in one point.

title: Lecture 16 — Bayes Classifier
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Bayes classifier uses a Bayesian prior on \(\theta\)
Here “Bayes” means decision theory / Bayes risk; it uses class posteriors


We can ship \(h_B\) without data
We need estimates of the distributions


Same \(h^\star\) for every loss
Squared loss \(\Rightarrow\) conditional mean, not \(0\)–\(1\) Bayes rule


Empirical risk minimizer \(=\) Bayes
Only in the limit / under conditions; finite samples differ

title: Lecture 15 — Risk Minimization Framework

title: Lecture 15 — Risk Minimization Framework
text:
Learning goals

Define loss, true risk, and empirical risk (ERM)
See why true risk is intractable and what ERM actually optimizes
Connect ERM \(\leftrightarrow\) MLE / KL minimization (same algorithms, two languages)
State the generalization question: minimizers, not only objectives, must track

title: Lecture 15 — Risk Minimization Framework
text:
Before this clicks
Supervised data \(\mathcal{D}=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}\) drawn IID from unknown \(P_{X,Y}\).
Hypothesis \(h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\). Lecture 14 already showed MSE ERM \(=\) Gaussian conditional MLE.

title: Lecture 15 — Risk Minimization Framework
text:
Main ideas

1. Hypothesis and loss
A hypothesis \(h\) is a candidate map from features to labels (classifier or regressor).
A loss \(L:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[0,\infty)\) scores one prediction against one true label. Examples:

Squared error: \(L(h(x),y)=\|h(x)-y\|_{2}^{2}\)
\(0\)–\(1\) loss: \(L(h(x),y)=0\) if \(h(x)=y\), else \(1\)



2. True risk = expected loss
\[
R(h)=\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)\sim P_{X,Y}}\bigl[L(h(X),Y)\bigr].
\]
Ideal ML problem:
\[
h^\star \in \arg\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}} R(h).
\]
This is the risk minimization framework.


3. Empirical risk (what we can compute)
\(P_{X,Y}\) is unknown \(\Rightarrow\) true risk cannot be evaluated. Surrogate:
\[
\hat R(h)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} L\bigl(h(x_i),y_i\bigr).
\]
Empirical risk minimization (ERM):
\[
\hat h \in \arg\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}} \hat R(h).
\]
IID + LLN \(\Rightarrow\) \(\hat R(h)\to R(h)\) for fixed \(h\). That does not automatically mean \(\hat h\to h^\star\). Whether the minimizer converges is the generalization question (statistical learning theory; overfitting / underfitting live here).


4. ERM example \(=\) previous MLE example
Regression, parametric \(h_\theta\), squared loss:
\[
\hat\theta\in\arg\min_\theta\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(h_\theta(x_i)-y_i\bigr)^{2}.
\]
Same as MLE with \(P_\theta(y\mid x)=\mathcal{N}(y; h_\theta(x), I)\).


5. Two languages, one problem








Lens
You choose…
You optimize…




Density estimation
Family \(P_\theta\) + divergence (KL)
Parameters of \(P_\theta\)


ERM
Hypothesis class + loss
\(h\) (or \(\theta\) in \(h_\theta\))




GPT-style training is often described as ERM with cross-entropy.
GMMs / many generative models are described as explicit KL / MLE on a density.

They are algorithmically the same story when the loss \(\leftrightarrow\) distributional assumption match.


6. Cliffhanger for Lecture 16
For binary \(Y\) and \(0\)–\(1\) loss, what \(h\) minimizes true risk? (Answer next lecture: the Bayes classifier.)

title: Lecture 15 — Risk Minimization Framework
text:
Worked mini-example
Three points, \(0\)–\(1\) loss, hypotheses that always predict \(0\) vs always predict \(1\). Labels: \(0,0,1\).
\[
\hat R(h\equiv 0)=\tfrac13,\qquad \hat R(h\equiv 1)=\tfrac23.
\]
ERM picks \(h\equiv 0\). True risk depends on the unknown prior \(P(Y=1)\); with tiny \(n\), empirical and true minimizers can disagree — that is the generalization gap in miniature.

title: Lecture 15 — Risk Minimization Framework
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




\(\hat R\to R\) implies \(\hat h\to h^\star\)
Not automatically; need conditions / bounds


ERM and MLE are rivals
Matching loss \(\leftrightarrow\) model makes them the same optimization


Loss must be \(0\)–\(1\)
Design choice; different losses \(\Rightarrow\) different optimal \(h\)


Only supervised
Framework extends; unsupervised = no \(Y\), different hypothesis/loss story

title: Lecture 14 — Example of ML Estimate
text: Video: Lec 14 — Example of ML Estimate

title: Lecture 14 — Example of ML Estimate
text:
Learning goals

Split MLE practice into: (A) choose \(P_\theta\) and (B) solve the optimization
See NLL as the probabilistic reading of a loss
Work a supervised regression example: Gaussian \(P(Y\mid X)\) with mean \(h_\theta(x)\) \(\Rightarrow\) least squares

title: Lecture 14 — Example of ML Estimate
text:
Before this clicks
Lecture 13: minimizing forward KL \(\Leftrightarrow\) maximizing \(\sum_i\log P_\theta(V_i)\).
Hypothesis / model function \(h_\theta\): a map from features to the parameter(s) of a conditional density.

title: Lecture 14 — Example of ML Estimate
text:
Main ideas

1. Two design questions

How to choose \(P_\theta\)? Pick a parametric family (often via a “canonical” function approximator \(h_\theta\)).
How to optimize? Sometimes closed form (derivative \(=0\)); often numerical (e.g. neural nets).

Slogan from class: vector calculus + probability + optimization cover a huge fraction of engineering ML.


2. NLL is a loss
\[
\mathrm{NLL}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log P_\theta(V_i).
\]
People call the summand (or average) a loss. Deterministic “pick a loss and minimize” stories are usually a distributional assumption in disguise.


3. Choosing \(P_\theta\) via \(h_\theta\)
Example pattern: assume \(P_\theta\) is Gaussian, and let the mean be \(h_\theta(x)\) (neural net, linear map, …). Then estimating \(P_\theta\) reduces to estimating the parameters of \(h_\theta\).


4. Concrete case: supervised regression
Data \((x_i,y_i)\) with \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\), \(y_i\in\mathbb{R}\). Goal: estimate \(P(Y\mid X)\).
Model assumption:
\[
P_\theta(y\mid x)=\mathcal{N}\bigl(y;\, h_\theta(x),\, I\bigr)
\]
(mean \(=h_\theta(x)\), variance fixed to identity / \(1\) in 1-D). Here \(h_\theta:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\).
Log-likelihood algebra (constants dropped) yields
\[
\hat\theta \in \arg\min_\theta \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl(y_i-h_\theta(x_i)\bigr)^{2}.
\]
Mic-drop statement from class:

Least-squares / MSE ERM is MLE under a Gaussian conditional with mean \(h_\theta(x)\).



5. Broader moral (preview)







You pick…
You are assuming…




Squared error loss
Gaussian noise around \(h_\theta(x)\)


Cross-entropy (binary)
Bernoulli with parameter \(h_\theta(x)\) (next threads)


A hypothesis class \(h_\theta\)
How the distribution’s parameters depend on \(x\)



All of this is still “minimize KL / maximize likelihood” under those assumptions. Usefulness (generalization) is a later question — “all models are wrong…”

title: Lecture 14 — Example of ML Estimate
text:
Worked mini-example
Heights / lifestyle features \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{5}\), lifespan \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), \(N=100\) people. Assume \(Y\mid X=x\sim\mathcal{N}(h_\theta(x),1)\) with \(h_\theta(x)=\theta^{\top}x\).
Then MLE for \(\theta\) is ordinary least squares:
\[
\hat\theta=\arg\min_\theta\sum_{i=1}^{100}(y_i-\theta^{\top}x_i)^{2}.
\]
If instead \(h_\theta\) is a neural net, the objective is still MSE, but optimization is numerical (gradients), not a closed-form normal equation.

title: Lecture 14 — Example of ML Estimate
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




MSE is “just engineering”
Under Gaussian conditional mean \(h_\theta\), it is MLE


Fixing variance to \(I\) is mandatory
Example choice; you can also learn variance / other forms


\(h_\theta\) must be linear
Design choice: linear, nonlinear, NN, …


Useful model = true model
We ask usefulness / generalization later, not “truth”

title: Lecture 13 — Minimization of KL Divergence
text: Video: Lec 13 — Minimization of KL Divergence

title: Lecture 13 — Minimization of KL Divergence
text:
Learning goals

Turn “estimate \(P_V\) from IID samples” into minimize \(\mathrm{KL}(P_V \| P_\theta)\)
Drop the entropy-of-data term and replace the expectation by a sample average (weak LLN)
See that this is exactly maximum likelihood (MLE) / minimizing negative log-likelihood

title: Lecture 13 — Minimization of KL Divergence
text:
Before this clicks
You need the KL recipe from Lectures 11–12: given a true density \(P_V\) and a model density \(P_\theta\),
\[
\mathrm{KL}(P_V \| P_\theta) = \int P_V(v)\,\log\frac{P_V(v)}{P_\theta(v)}\,dv
\]
(continuous case). Also: IID samples, law of large numbers, and “likelihood = density evaluated at a point.”

title: Lecture 13 — Minimization of KL Divergence
text:
Main ideas

1. Setup (works for any ML problem shape)
Let
\[
\mathcal{D}=\{V_1,\ldots,V_N\}
\]
be IID from unknown \(P_V\). Here \(V\) is a placeholder: it might be \(X\), \((X,Y)\), \(Y\mid X\), etc. Goal: estimate \(P_V\) by a parametric model \(P_\theta\).


2. Minimize forward KL
Choose
\[
\theta^\star \in \arg\min_\theta \mathrm{KL}(P_V \| P_\theta).
\]
Expand:
\[
\mathrm{KL}(P_V \| P_\theta) = \underbrace{\int P_V\log P_V\,dv}_{\text{entropy of data (no }\theta\text{)}} - \int P_V(v)\,\log P_\theta(v)\,dv.
\]
Drop the first term. Equivalent problem:
\[
\theta^\star \in \arg\min_\theta \Bigl(-\mathbb{E}_{V\sim P_V}[\log P_\theta(V)]\Bigr)
= \arg\max_\theta \mathbb{E}_{V\sim P_V}[\log P_\theta(V)].
\]


3. Approximate the expectation with data (weak LLN)
We do not know \(P_V\), so we cannot compute the expectation exactly. With IID samples,
\[
\mathbb{E}_{P_V}[\log P_\theta(V)] \;\approx\; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log P_\theta(V_i).
\]
So the practical estimator is
\[
\hat\theta \in \arg\max_\theta \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log P_\theta(V_i)
= \arg\min_\theta \Bigl(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log P_\theta(V_i)\Bigr).
\]
The second form is negative log-likelihood (NLL) minimization. Large \(N\) is why “more data helps”: the LLN approximation gets better.


4. Same thing as maximum likelihood
Under IID,
\[
L(\mathcal{D};\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{N} P_\theta(V_i),\qquad
\log L = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\log P_\theta(V_i).
\]
Maximizing \(\log L\) is identical to the sample-average KL recipe. The instructor prefers the story “minimal KL estimator”; the field’s name is maximum likelihood.


5. Forward vs reverse KL

Forward: \(\mathrm{KL}(P_V \| P_\theta)\) — expectation under \(P_V\), approximable by samples from data.
Reverse: \(\mathrm{KL}(P_\theta \| P_V)\) — introduces terms involving \(\log P_V\) under \(P_\theta\) that we cannot compute the same way.

That is why the course uses forward KL for this estimator.


6. LOTUS reminder
\(\log P_\theta(V)\) is a function of the RV \(V\). LOTUS says you may take \(\mathbb{E}_{P_V}[\log P_\theta(V)]\) without first building the law of the transformed RV — justifying the sample-mean approximation above.

title: Lecture 13 — Minimization of KL Divergence
text:
Worked mini-example
Suppose \(N=3\) discrete points and a 1-parameter model \(P_\theta(v)=\theta^v(1-\theta)^{1-v}\) for \(v\in\{0,1\}\) (Bernoulli). Data: \(1,1,0\).
\[
\frac{1}{3}\sum_i\log P_\theta(V_i)=\frac{1}{3}\bigl(2\log\theta+\log(1-\theta)\bigr).
\]
Maximize \(\Rightarrow\) \(\hat\theta=2/3\), the usual MLE frequency. Same answer as minimizing empirical forward KL to a Bernoulli model.

title: Lecture 13 — Minimization of KL Divergence
text:
Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




“We need \(P_V\) to compute KL”
True for the population KL; after dropping entropy we only need samples + a computable \(P_\theta\)


MLE ≠ KL minimization
Under this forward-KL + IID setup they are the same optimization


Reverse KL is “just as easy”
Not for this data-driven recipe — wrong expectation measure


Likelihood is a probability
Likelihood is a density value at a point (continuous case), not \(P(V=v)\)

title: Lecture 12 — Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
text: Video: Lec 12 — Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence

title: Lecture 12 — Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
text:
1. Cross-entropy
Let \(p\) and \(q\) be two distributions on the same space. Define
\[
H(p,q)
=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}\bigl[-\log q(x)\bigr].
\]
Story: samples are truly drawn from \(p\), but you score surprise with \(-\log q\). Average that surprise under the true \(p\).

If \(q=p\), cross-entropy collapses to ordinary entropy \(H(p)\).
If \(q\) is a wrong model (e.g. Gaussian mean \(3\) while truth has mean \(0\)), cross-entropy measures how costly that wrong assumption is on average under the truth.

Not symmetric: \(H(p,q)\neq H(q,p)\) in general.
Discrete form:
\[
H(p,q)=-\sum_{i} p(x_i)\log q(x_i).
\]

title: Lecture 12 — Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
text:
2. KL divergence = extra surprise
Class definition (after fixing the algebra live):
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)
=H(p,q)-H(p).
\]
Expand:
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)
&=\mathbb{E}_{p}[-\log q]-\mathbb{E}_{p}[-\log p]\\
&=\mathbb{E}_{p}\bigl[\log p(X)-\log q(X)\bigr]\\
&=\mathbb{E}_{p}\Bigl[\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
Discrete:
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sum_{i} p(x_i)\log\frac{p(x_i)}{q(x_i)}.
\]
Continuous (densities):
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\int p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\,dx.
\]
Reading: entropy is average information in \(p\); cross-entropy is average information when coding / scoring with \(q\) under true \(p\). Their difference is the extra bits (nats) you pay for using \(q\) instead of \(p\).
Because cross-entropy is at least entropy (Gibbs inequality / Jensen on \(-\log\)), this difference is non-negative.

title: Lecture 12 — Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
section: 3. Properties you should prove as homework
text:
3. Properties you should prove as homework

Non-negativity: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\ge 0\).
Identity of indiscernibles (one side): \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=0\) iff \(p=q\) (almost everywhere).
Asymmetry: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\neq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\) in general.
Not a metric: asymmetry alone already means it fails to be a metric; triangle inequality also fails.

Still: when \(p\) and \(q\) match, KL is \(0\); when they diverge, KL grows — exactly the kind of training signal Lecture 10 asked for.

title: Lecture 12 — Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
text:
4. Tiny concrete example
Two Bernoullis on \(\{0,1\}\):
\[
p(1)=\tfrac12,\quad q(1)=\tfrac34.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)
&=
\tfrac12\log\frac{1/2}{3/4}
+
\tfrac12\log\frac{1/2}{1/4}
=
\tfrac12\log\frac{2}{3}
+
\tfrac12\log 2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Swap \(p\leftrightarrow q\) and the number changes — asymmetry in one line.

title: Lecture 12 — Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
text:
5. Role in the ML recipe
With model \(p_{\theta}\) playing the role of \(q\),
\[
\theta^{\star}=\arg\min_{\theta}\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(p\,\|\,p_{\theta}\bigr)
\]
is a canonical training goal. Later lectures connect this to maximum likelihood (minimizing KL is tightly linked to maximizing likelihood of the data under \(p_{\theta}\)).

title: Lecture 12 — Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
text:
6. Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




KL is a distance like Euclidean
Directed divergence; not symmetric.


\(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\) vs \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\)
Different numbers; pick the order that matches “truth vs model.”


Cross-entropy = KL
KL \(=\) cross-entropy \(-\) entropy (entropy depends only on \(p\)).


Continuous KL uses probabilities at points
Uses densities inside the log ratio; still integrates against \(p\).

title: Lecture 12 — Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
text:
7. References

Course playlist: MFML
Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory — KL divergence chapter
Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning — KL and MLE connection
Bishop, PRML — KL in variational / approximation settings (optional)

title: Lecture 12 — Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
text:
8. Self-check

(Answers: self-check-answers.qmd.)

title: Lecture 11 — Entropy
text: Video: Lec 11 — Entropy

title: Lecture 11 — Entropy
text:
1. Why information theory here?
To train, we need a number that says how far \(p\) is from \(p_{\theta}\). A classical family of such numbers comes from information theory (originally: communicate as much meaning as possible under bandwidth limits).
This lecture builds entropy; the next builds cross-entropy and KL divergence.

title: Lecture 11 — Entropy
text:
2. Information content of one event
For an event \(A\) with probability \(P(A)>0\), define
\[
I(A)=-\log P(A).
\]
Called information or surprisal of \(A\).

Design requirements (intuition → formula)

Likely events carry little information. “Sun rises in the east” is unsurprising. Rare events (“you win the lottery”) are highly informative / surprising. So \(I\) should decrease as \(P(A)\) increases → the minus sign in front of \(\log\).
The sure event \(\Omega\) carries zero information. \(P(\Omega)=1\Rightarrow I(\Omega)=-\log 1=0\).
The empty event is infinitely surprising. \(P(\emptyset)=0\Rightarrow I(\emptyset)=+\infty\) (limit).
Independence adds information. If \(A,B\) independent, \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\), so

\[
I(A\cap B)=I(A)+I(B).
\]
\(-\log P(A)\) hits all four.

title: Lecture 11 — Entropy
section: 3. From one event to a whole distribution: entropy
text:
3. From one event to a whole distribution: entropy
Let \(X\) be discrete with PMF \(p\) on values \(\{x_i\}\). Surprisal of the outcome \(x_i\) is \(-\log p(x_i)\).
Average surprisal under \(p\) is an expectation:
\[
H(p)
=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}\bigl[-\log p(x)\bigr]
=-\sum_{i} p(x_i)\log p(x_i).
\]
This number \(H(p)\) is the entropy of \(p\).
Interpretation: how much uncertainty / average surprise lives in draws from \(p\).
(Continuous analogue is differential entropy \(\int -p\log p\); similar algebra, slightly different interpretation — flagged for KL next time.)

title: Lecture 11 — Entropy
text:
4. Tiny concrete example
Fair coin: \(p(H)=p(T)=1/2\). Using \(\log_2\),
\[
H(p)=-2\cdot\Bigl(\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac12\Bigr)=1\text{ bit}.
\]
Two-headed coin: \(p(H)=1\), \(p(T)=0\). Using the convention \(0\log 0:=0\),
\[
H(p)=0.
\]
No uncertainty — every toss is heads.

title: Lecture 11 — Entropy
text:
5. Link forward
Entropy alone does not compare two different distributions \(p\) and \(q\). Next lecture: cross-entropy \(H(p,q)\) and
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=H(p,q)-H(p)
\]
(the extra surprise from using \(q\) when truth is \(p\)).

title: Lecture 11 — Entropy
text:
6. Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Entropy is only physics / thermodynamics
Same math; here it is average surprisal of a PMF.


High probability \(\Rightarrow\) high information
Opposite: high \(P(A)\) \(\Rightarrow\) low \(I(A)\).


Entropy compares two models
Entropy is a property of one distribution; KL compares two.


Continuous entropy = discrete entropy
Differential entropy is analogous but not identical in meaning.

title: Lecture 11 — Entropy
text:

MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (free) — friendly entropy
Bishop, PRML — information-theoretic losses (optional peek)

title: Lecture 10 — Challenge With ML
text: Video: Lec 10 — Challenge With ML

title: Lecture 10 — Challenge With ML
text:
1. Central problem (again)
\[
\mathcal{D}=\{x_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\ \text{i.i.d. from unknown density }p.
\]
(Writing “sample from a density” is slight abuse — sampling is from the distribution — but this is the course’s working language.)
Whether we write \(p(x)\), \(p(x,y)\), \(p(y\mid x)\), … the estimation task is the same shape.
Challenge: we know nothing a priori about \(p\). We are not totally blind only because we have samples.

title: Lecture 10 — Challenge With ML
text:
2. What is a “model”?
Any algorithm’s estimate of the unknown density is called a model.
Large language models, classifiers, GMMs, … — in this worldview they are density (or conditional-density) estimators.

All models are wrong; some are useful.
(All estimators are imperfect; usefulness is judged by a metric / task.)

There is no single correct density estimator; we compare them by how well they serve a chosen divergence / downstream goal.

title: Lecture 10 — Challenge With ML
text:
3. Three-step recipe for density estimation

Step 1 — Model choice: pick a parametric family
Assume
\[
p \approx p_{\theta}
\]
for some parameter \(\theta\) in a family you choose.
Examples of families:







Family
Typical \(\theta\)




Linear / logistic-style forms
weights \(w\)


Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)\)
\((\mu,\Sigma)\)


Mixture models, kernels, neural nets, transformers
their internal parameters



Neural nets are popular because they are universal approximators: with enough capacity they can approximate very broad classes of functions. Choosing the family is still a leap of faith: if truth is quadratic and you only allow lines, you are stuck with a bad model class. The optimizer will only find the best line, not invent a parabola.
Correction noted in a later lecture: for \(w_1^{\top}x+w_2\), if \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{D}\) then \(w_1\in\mathbb{R}^{D}\) and \(w_2\) is a scalar (dimensions must match).


Step 2 — Choose a “distance” between \(p\) and \(p_{\theta}\)
Need a function
\[
d(p,p_{\theta})\ \ge\ 0
\]
measuring how far the model is from truth.
Quotes around “distance”: many ML divergences are not metrics (not symmetric, may fail triangle inequality). They are still useful. KL divergence (Lectures 11–12) is the star example in this course.
Apparent paradox: \(d\) seems to need the unknown \(p\). Later tools (likelihoods, empirical averages, LLN, …) let us optimize without writing \(p\) explicitly.


Step 3 — Train: optimize parameters
\[
\theta^{\star}
=\arg\min_{\theta}\, d\bigl(p,\,p_{\theta}\bigr).
\]
Finding \(\theta^{\star}\) is what people call training the model.
Different algorithms = different \((p_{\theta},\ d,\ \text{optimizer})\) triples.

title: Lecture 10 — Challenge With ML
text:
4. Why hundreds of algorithms?
If density estimation were one easy closed form, we would not need so many methods. The hardness is:

unknown \(p\),
high-dimensional \(x\),
choice of family and divergence,
computational optimization.

The rest of the course instantiates this recipe many times.

title: Lecture 10 — Challenge With ML
text:
5. Tiny concrete example
Suppose scalar data and we choose the family of 1D Gaussians
\[
p_{\theta}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Bigr),\quad
\theta=(\mu,\sigma^{2}).
\]
Step 1 fixes “truth is somehow Gaussian.”
Step 2 might use KL or equivalently maximize likelihood (later).
Step 3 returns \((\hat\mu,\hat\sigma^{2})\) — e.g. sample mean and variance.
If the true density is a two-peak mixture, every Gaussian is wrong; some Gaussians are still “least bad” under your divergence.

title: Lecture 10 — Challenge With ML
text:
6. Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




Training invents the model class
Training only fits \(\theta\) inside the class you chose.


One correct model
Estimators are approximations; usefulness is relative.


Divergence must be a mathematical metric
KL & friends often are not; still OK.


\(p(x)\) vs \(p(y\mid x)\) are different problems
Same estimation template; different target density.
