title: Lecture 9 — Density Function
text: Video: Lec 09 — Density Function

title: Lecture 9 — Density Function
text:
1. Definition (continuous case)
Let \(X\) be continuous with distribution (CDF) \(P_{X}\). A density \(p_{X}\) is a function
\[
p_{X}:\ \text{range of }X\ \to\ [0,\infty)
\]
such that (in 1D)
\[
P_{X}(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x} p_{X}(t)\,dt
\]
when this makes sense. In \(\mathbb{R}^{D}\), the same idea uses a \(D\)-dimensional integral over the “southwest” region used for the multivariate CDF.
Properties to lock in:

Densities are non-negative.
They are not required to lie in \([0,1]\).
\(\int p_{X}=1\) over the whole space (normalization).

Course notation habit (approximate): fancy / double-stroke \(P\) for distributions; plain \(p\) for densities. From here on, algorithms mostly manipulate densities.

title: Lecture 9 — Density Function
section: 2. Evaluating a density \(\neq\) getting a probability
text:
2. Evaluating a density \(\neq\) getting a probability
Plug a number \(x_0\) into \(p_{X}\): you get a non-negative real number. That number is not \(P(X=x_0)\) in continuous models.
Probabilities come from integrating the density over a set:
\[
P(X\in A)=\int_{A} p_{X}(x)\,dx.
\]
Integrals over regions recover the distribution (a true probability measure). Point evaluations do not.
People still call \(p_{X}(x_0)\) a likelihood (of the parameter / model at that observation) — useful language later, still not “probability of the singleton.”

title: Lecture 9 — Density Function
text:
3. Interview trap: uniform on \([0,1/2]\)
If \(X\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0,1/2]\), then
\[
p_{X}(x)=2\quad\text{for }x\in[0,1/2].
\]
The density equals 2, which cannot be a probability (probabilities \(\le 1\)). Yet
\[
\int_{0}^{1/2} 2\,dx=1,
\]
so as a density it is perfectly valid. This kills the myth “PDF values are probabilities because Gaussians look \(\le 1\).”

title: Lecture 9 — Density Function
text:
4. Discrete case: mass functions
For a discrete RV, the object analogous to a density is a probability mass function (PMF). Evaluating a PMF at a point is a probability:
\[
p_{X}(x)=P(X=x).
\]
Same letter \(p\) is often overloaded — always ask: continuous or discrete?
Not every continuous law has a density (pathological cases exist). In this course we assume practical data can be modeled with RVs that do have densities.

title: Lecture 9 — Density Function
text:
5. Problem statement, updated
Earlier: given \(\mathcal{D}\), estimate the distribution.
Working form from now:
\[
\text{Given }\mathcal{D},\ \text{estimate the density }p\quad
\text{(joints / marginals / conditionals as needed)}.
\]
We speak of distributions when we mean the probability measure; we compute with densities for mathematical ease, assuming a one-to-one link in the well-behaved cases we care about.

title: Lecture 9 — Density Function
text:
6. Tiny concrete example
Let
\[
p(x)=\begin{cases}6x(1-x), & 0\le x\le 1,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
Check normalization:
\[
\int_{0}^{1}6x(1-x)\,dx=6\int_{0}^{1}(x-x^{2})\,dx=6\Bigl[\tfrac{1}{2}-\tfrac{1}{3}\Bigr]=1.
\]
Then \(p(0.5)=6\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.5=1.5\), which is fine for a density, not a probability. But
\[
P(0.4\le X\le 0.6)=\int_{0.4}^{0.6}6x(1-x)\,dx
\]
is a probability.

title: Lecture 9 — Density Function
text:
7. Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




\(p(x)\in[0,1]\) always
False — see uniform on a short interval.


\(p(x_0)=P(X=x_0)\) continuously
False for continuous RVs.


Density = distribution
Density describes many continuous distributions; the distribution is the measure / CDF.


No density \(\Rightarrow\) useless data
Rare pathologies; we assume nice densities exist for our data.

title: Lecture 8 — Distribution Estimation
text: Video: Lec 08 — Distribution Estimation

title: Lecture 8 — Distribution Estimation
text:
1. Starting point
\[
\mathcal{D}=\bigl\{(x_i,y_i)\bigr\}_{i=1}^{n}
\sim_{\text{i.i.d.}} P_{X,Y}\ \text{(unknown)}.
\]

\(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{D}\) — features / inputs / “data”
\(y_i\in\mathbb{R}^{K}\) or discrete categories — outputs / “labels” (optional)

Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are RVs on one \(\Omega\). Labels may be absent; then we only have \(\{x_i\}\).
Data is the raw material — algorithms are only as good as the samples they see.

title: Lecture 8 — Distribution Estimation
text:
2. Foundational problem
\[
\text{Given }\mathcal{D}\text{ from unknown }P,\quad
\text{estimate }P,\quad\text{and/or learn to sample from }P.
\]







Focus
Common name




Estimate useful laws / conditionals; sampling secondary
Discriminative methods


Emphasize generating new samples
Generative methods



This course leans on estimation; a later course goes deep on generative sampling.
Sometimes we do not need the full law — only a moment (expectation, second moment, …). That is still “learning about \(P\).”

title: Lecture 8 — Distribution Estimation
section: 3. Which distribution? Depends on the question
text:
3. Which distribution? Depends on the question
Fix a dataset of images with disease labels. Different questions pick different targets:



Real question
Target




Given this image, how likely is disease?
\(P(Y\mid X)\)


How common is disease in the population (ignore pixels)?
\(P_{Y}\)


How do pixels look in general (ignore labels)?
\(P_{X}\)


How do pixels look among diseased cases?
\(P(X\mid Y=y)\)


Full coupled story of image and label
\(P_{X,Y}\)



Classification / regression (conventional names): estimate \(P(Y\mid X)\).

discrete \(Y\) \(\to\) classification

continuous \(Y\in\mathbb{R}^{K}\) \(\to\) regression

Boundaries are thin; inpainting can be “\(P(Y\mid X)\)” where \(Y\) is just masked pixels of \(X\).

title: Lecture 8 — Distribution Estimation
text:
4. Conditioning reminder
When we write \(P(X\mid Y)\) or \(p(x\mid y)\):

the conditioned variable is fixed to a value,
the object is a distribution over the other variable,
changing the fixed value changes the conditional law.

So conditionals are functions of the conditioning value.

title: Lecture 8 — Distribution Estimation
text:
5. Supervised vs unsupervised (know the words)



Conventional phrase
Meaning in industry talk




Supervised
Labels present; used in the algorithm


Unsupervised
No labels



Mathematically in this course: labels are just another RV / dimensions. Human labeling is costly — that is why “supervised” feels expensive — but the abstract problem is still distribution estimation.
Self-supervised learning: carve fake labels out of \(X\) itself.

title: Lecture 8 — Distribution Estimation
text:
6. Preview: densities next
Class mostly writes density functions (for continuous RVs) for algorithmic convenience, while conceptually we still mean the underlying distribution / measure. Lecture 9 makes that precise.

title: Lecture 8 — Distribution Estimation
text:
7. Tiny concrete example
\(n=10{,}000\) chest X-rays, \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\).

Screen a new scan \(\to\) need \(\widehat{P}(Y\mid X=x_{\text{new}})\).

Report prevalence \(\to\) need \(\widehat{P}(Y=1)\) (can ignore images).

Build a “disease look” synthesizer \(\to\) need something like \(\widehat{P}(X\mid Y=1)\) plus a sampler.

Same \(\mathcal{D}\); three different estimation targets.

title: Lecture 8 — Distribution Estimation
text:
8. Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




\(P_Y\) vs \(P(X\mid Y)\)
\(P_Y\) never looks at pixels; \(P(X\mid Y)\) is the law of images for a fixed label.


Estimating \(P_{X,Y}\) always means generative sampling
You can estimate a joint without shipping a sampler.


One true supervised/unsupervised split in math
Naming; both are distribution estimation.


IID is an English vibe
It is a precise product / same-law assumption used by algorithms.

title: Lecture 8 — Distribution Estimation
text:

title: Lecture 7 — IID Assumption
text: Video: Lec 07 — IID Assumption

title: Lecture 7 — IID Assumption
text:
1. Identically distributed
Think of the \(n\) pairs as coming from \(n\) random variables (each vector-valued), all with the same law \(P_{X,Y}\).
Equivalently: the experimental conditions do not change across the \(n\) draws (same hospital protocol, same population story, … — intuition only; the math is “same distribution”).
If you train on lung X-rays and test on brain MRI without rebuilding the model story, the identical-distribution assumption is broken.

title: Lecture 7 — IID Assumption
text:
2. Independent (statistical sense)
Events \(A,B\) independent \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\).
For RVs: joint = product of marginals. For the dataset viewed as \(n\) RVs \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) (each \(Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)\)),
\[
P_{Z_1,\ldots,Z_n} = P_{Z_1}\cdots P_{Z_n}
\]
when they are independent (and with identical laws, each factor equals the same \(P_Z\)).

title: Lecture 7 — IID Assumption
section: 3. Two viewpoints of the same dataset
text:
3. Two viewpoints of the same dataset








View
Story
Need the words “i.i.d.”?




A
\(n\) realizations of one RV \(Z\)
“i.i.d.” is almost redundant — one law, many trials


B
One realization of \(n\) RVs \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\)
Yes: identical laws + mutual independence



Textbooks write \(\mathcal{D}\sim P\) with a tilde for “sampled from.” Sampling means repeating the underlying random experiment.

title: Lecture 7 — IID Assumption
section: 4. Critical: independence across points, not pixels
text:
4. Critical: independence across points, not pixels
IID does not say that the \(D\) coordinates inside one vector \(x_i\) are independent.

Image 1 independent of image 2: yes (the usual IID claim).
Pixel \((1,1)\) independent of pixel \((1,2)\) inside the same image: not assumed in general (nearby pixels are dependent).

Some algorithms add a stronger assumption of independence across dimensions; that is a separate modeling choice.

title: Lecture 7 — IID Assumption
text:
5. What breaks when IID breaks?
Algorithms we build will use independence and identical laws in their math. If test points come from a different experiment / different law, those algorithms are not entitled to work.
Whether faces and buildings are “one experiment” or two is a design choice. Merge them into one giant dataset and you can call them one law; train on faces only and test on buildings and you violated the identical-distribution story you baked into training.

title: Lecture 7 — IID Assumption
text:
6. Supervised / unsupervised / self-supervised (nomenclature)
Class view: everything is estimating laws of RVs on \(\Omega\).







Name people use
Rough meaning




Supervised
Some coordinates called “labels” \(Y\) exist


Unsupervised
Only \(X\); no separate \(Y\)


Self-supervised
Mask / split some dimensions of \(X\) and treat them as a fake \(Y\) (e.g. inpainting)



Labels often come from human judgment; that is why supervised data is expensive — not because the math is different.

title: Lecture 7 — IID Assumption
section: 7. Formal problem statement of ML (this course)
text:
7. Formal problem statement of ML (this course)
\[
\text{Given }\mathcal{D}\text{ sampled from unknown }P,\quad
\text{estimate }P\text{ (or conditionals / marginals)}.
\]
Often write \(P_{X}\) and allow \(Y\) to be folded into \(X\).

Estimating \(P(Y\mid X)\) with discrete \(Y\): classification

Estimating \(P(Y\mid X)\) with continuous \(Y\): regression

Estimating joints / marginals and learning to sample: generative modeling

Discriminative methods in this course mostly estimate useful conditionals without insisting on a full generative sampler.

Slogan from class: All machine learning is: given \(\mathcal{D}\), estimate \(P\).

title: Lecture 7 — IID Assumption
text:
8. Tiny concrete example
Three coin tosses recorded as \(1=\)heads, \(0=\)tails: \((1,0,1)\).

IID view B: three Bernoulli RVs, same \(p\), independent, so

\[
P(1,0,1)=p\cdot(1-p)\cdot p.
\]

Not claimed: nothing about “coordinates of a vector image” here — each toss is already a full data point.

If the coin secretly changes after toss 2, identical distribution fails and that product formula is the wrong model.

title: Lecture 7 — IID Assumption
text:
9. Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




IID = pixels independent
No — samples independent.


“Independent” in English
Means the product rule for joints / events.


Train and test can be any domains
Test should match the law you estimated under.


Supervised ≠ unsupervised mathematically
Same distribution-estimation game; different which coordinates you name.

text:

title: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
text: Video: Lec 06 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
crumbs: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution

title: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
text:
1. An image is a \(D\)-dimensional vector
Take an image of size \(P\times Q\) pixels. In software it is a \(P\times Q\) grid of numbers. Stack the rows into one long list and you get a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^{PQ}\). Write
\[
D = PQ.
\]
So every image is a point in \(\mathbb{R}^{D}\). The same story holds for any tabular feature vector: a data point is a \(D\)-dimensional vector.
crumbs: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution

title: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
section: 2. That vector sits in the range of a random variable
text:
2. That vector sits in the range of a random variable
In the probabilistic view:
\[
X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{D},
\]
and the image you store on disk is one value \(x\) in the range of \(X\) (one realization / observation).
Behind \(X\) sit:

an underlying random experiment with sample space \(\Omega\),
a probability measure \(P\) on events,
a pushforward distribution \(P_{X}\) on (Borel) sets in \(\mathbb{R}^{D}\).


Take-home line from class: every data point is an element of the range space of a random variable.

What is \(\Omega\) for “patients get X-rayed”? That is a modeling choice — you invent a coherent story for the experiment that produces the images (and later the labels).
crumbs: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution

title: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
text:
3. Pixel values are not probabilities
A common confusion (asked in class): pixel intensities lie in \(\{0,\ldots,255\}\) or \([0,1]\) after normalization — so are they probabilities?
No.

A data point \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{D}\) is just a real vector (an outcome in the range).
Probability lives on events (sets), via \(P\) or the pushforward \(P_{X}\).
The distribution tells you the likelihood of observing (sets of) such vectors under the experiment — not that the vector entries themselves are probabilities.

Uniform-on-\([0,1/2]\) density equals \(2\) everywhere on its support: that number is clearly not a probability (Lecture 9 will hammer this again for densities).
crumbs: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution

title: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
section: 4. What the distribution is telling you
text:
4. What the distribution is telling you
For continuous models you talk about subsets of the range, not single points. Roughly:

subsets of images \(\leftrightarrow\) inverse-image events in \(\Omega\) \(\leftrightarrow\) values of \(P_{X}\).

Intuition used in class: \(P_{X}\) quantifies how likely it is to obtain that kind of image under the experiment.
Key slogan:

The distribution function completely specifies what we need to know about the underlying experiment (for the purposes of this course).

That is why the whole course is about estimating distributions from samples.
crumbs: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution

title: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
section: 5. Labels = another random variable on the same \(\Omega\)
text:
5. Labels = another random variable on the same \(\Omega\)
The X-ray story is not only “get an image”; a clinician also assigns a label (disease / no disease, or a bounding box, …).
Model:
\[
X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{D},\qquad Y:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{K}
\]
(or \(Y\) discrete with a finite set of categories). Both sit on the same sample space. Calling \(Y\) a “label” is nomenclature; mathematically it is just another RV.



Task
Typical \(Y\)




Binary disease
\(Y\in\{0,1\}\)


Multi-class
\(Y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\)


Tumor box (center, height, width)
\(Y\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\)



Because both exist, there is a joint \(P_{X,Y}\).
crumbs: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution

title: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
section: 6. The dataset notation that appears next
text:
6. The dataset notation that appears next
A supervised dataset is a set of pairs
\[
\mathcal{D}=\bigl\{(x_i,y_i)\bigr\}_{i=1}^{n},
\]
said to be sampled i.i.d. from the unknown joint \(P_{X,Y}\) (tilde notation \(\sim\)). What “i.i.d.” means is the next lecture.
crumbs: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution

title: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
text:
7. Tiny concrete example
Suppose \(2\times 2\) grayscale patches, so \(D=4\). One observed patch might be
\[
x = (0.1,\ 0.8,\ 0.2,\ 0.7)\in\mathbb{R}^{4}.
\]
A binary label \(y=1\) (“abnormal”) is not a fifth pixel of \(x\); it is a value of a second RV \(Y\) defined on the same experiment “patient imaged and labeled.” The object we want later is often \(P(Y\mid X)\) — likelihood of the label given the image — which needs the joint world of \((X,Y)\).
crumbs: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution

title: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
text:
8. Common confusions







Confusion
Clarification




“The image is the random variable.”
Loosely said in class; precisely: the image is a point in the range of an RV.


Pixel values = probabilities
No — they are coordinates in \(\mathbb{R}^{D}\).


Supervised vs unsupervised are totally different math
Both are distribution estimation; “label” is just another coordinate / RV.


Knowing one sample tells you \(P_{X}\)
One point is not a distribution; we need many samples + structure (later lectures).
crumbs: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution

title: Lecture 6 — Understanding a Chest X-Ray as Sample from Distribution
text:

title: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2
text: Video: Lec 05 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2
crumbs: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2

title: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2
text:
1. Quick recall
What we observe in practice are vectors living in the range of a random variable. Behind them sit:
\[
\text{experiment}\ \to\ \Omega\ \to\ X\ \to\ \text{data in }\mathbb{R}^{d},\quad\text{with distribution }P_{X}.
\]
crumbs: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2

title: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2
text:
2. Vector-valued random variables (two equivalent views)
View A — one function
\[
X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{d}.
\]
View B — \(d\) scalar functions on the same \(\Omega\)
\[
X_1:\Omega\to\mathbb{R},\quad \ldots,\quad X_d:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}.
\]
These views are the same idea written differently: a \(d\)-dimensional observation is \(d\) numbers that came from one underlying experiment (or jointly modeled experiments).
crumbs: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2

title: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2
section: 3. Several RVs on one sample space → joints
text:
3. Several RVs on one sample space → joints
You can define many functions on the same \(\Omega\). Example: two scalars \(X_1,X_2\) on one \(\Omega\).
Each has its own distribution. Because inverse images land back in \(\mathcal{F}\), and \(\mathcal{F}\) is closed under intersections/unions, we can talk about combined events → joint distribution.

Joint CDF intuition (1D×1D)
For numbers \(a,b\),
\[
P_{X_1,X_2}(a,b)
= P\bigl(\{\omega: X_1(\omega)\le a\text{ and }X_2(\omega)\le b\}\bigr).
\]
That event is the intersection of the two inverse-image events. Extend to \(d\) variables with a Cartesian product of half-lines (Lecture 4).
crumbs: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2

title: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2
text:
4. Conditional probability → conditional distributions
For events \(A,B\) with \(P(B)>0\),
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.
\]
English: given that \(B\) happened, how likely is \(A\)?
Push this idea through random variables to get conditional distributions.
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are RVs (possibly vector-valued) on the same space, write \(P_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\) for the distribution of \(X\) when \(Y\) is fixed to a value \(y\).
For continuous variables (when densities exist — next lectures),
\[
p(x\mid y)=\frac{p(x,y)}{p(y)},
\]
where \(p(y)\) is the marginal of \(Y\).

What “marginal” means
Integrate (or sum) the joint over the variable you want to remove:
\[
p(y)=\int p(x,y)\,dx.
\]
Name origin (discrete case): write the joint as a table; summing along a margin of the table gives the marginal.
Important: when we write \(p(x\mid y)\), the conditioning variable is fixed; the sample space of interest is “shrunk” to that evidence.
crumbs: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2

title: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2
text:
5. Why ML cares (X-ray example)

\(X\): image vector (range of an imaging RV)
\(Y\): label diseased / not (another RV, possibly on a related experiment)

Diagnosis asks for something like \(P(Y\mid X=x)\) — the conditional distribution of the label given the observed image.
That is exactly why joints / conditionals appear before “learning algorithms.”
crumbs: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2

title: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2
text:
6. Common confusions







Confusion
Clear version




“Random variable is a random number”
It is a function \(\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\)


Joint vs conditional
Joint: both vary; conditional: one is fixed


Marginal “throws away” info
It describes one RV after averaging out the other


\(X\) and \(Y\) need the same dimension
Ranges can be \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) and \(\mathbb{R}^{k}\)
crumbs: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2

title: Lecture 5 — Recap of Probability Theory Part 2
text:

Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis, Introduction to Probability — clean event-based view

text:

Give two views of a vector-valued RV.

In words: what does \(P(A\mid B)\) ask?

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text: Video: Lec 04 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
1. Setup from Lectures 2–3
We have the probability triplet \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and a random variable
\[
X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}
\]
(or later \(X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{d}\)).
Question of this lecture: what happens to the measure \(P\) when we pass to the range of \(X\)?
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
section: 2. Which subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\) do we use? Borel sets
text:
2. Which subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\) do we use? Borel sets
Not every subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) is treated as an “event” in the range. We use a standard family: the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\).
Intuition used in class: building blocks are half-lines of the form
\[
(-\infty,\ x]
\]
(and the \(\sigma\)-algebra they generate). In \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\), the analogous building blocks are Cartesian products of such half-lines (rectangles unbounded toward \(-\infty\) in each coordinate).
Random variables are defined so that inverse images of these Borel sets land back in \(\mathcal{F}\) (measurability) — so probabilities remain well-defined.
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
3. Pushforward measure = distribution of \(X\)
\(X\) maps outcomes in \(\Omega\) to numbers in \(\mathbb{R}\). Subsets of \(\Omega\) map (via inverse images) to subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\).
Because \(P\) lives on events in \(\Omega\), there is an induced measure on (Borel) subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\). That induced measure is called:



Name used in class
Same idea




Pushforward measure
\(P\) “pushed” through \(X\)


Distribution of \(X\)
law of \(X\)


Distribution function / CDF
common 1-D encoding of that law



Picture: one measurable space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)\) + a map \(X\) \(\Rightarrow\) a new measure space on the range side.

Course notation
Script / calligraphic \(P\) with a mark for \(X\) means the distribution of the random variable \(X\). In these notes we write \(P_{X}\).
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
4. Definition in one dimension (CDF view)
For \(X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) and a real number \(x\),
\[
P_{X}(x) \;=\; P\bigl( X^{-1}((-\infty,\ x]) \bigr) \;=\; P\bigl(\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le x\}\bigr).
\]
In words:

Build the Borel set \((-\infty,\ x]\) in \(\mathbb{R}\).
Take its inverse image under \(X\) (a subset of \(\Omega\)).
Evaluate the original probability measure \(P\) on that event.

That value is the distribution function (CDF) at \(x\).
Endpoint convention: the interval is typically closed at \(x\) and open toward \(-\infty\), i.e. \((-\infty,\ x]\).

Probability is always assigned to a set (an event). Evaluating the distribution at \(x\) is still “probability of a set” — the set \(\{\omega : X(\omega)\le x\}\).
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
section: 5. How is \(P\) “assigned” in the real world?
text:
5. How is \(P\) “assigned” in the real world?
Class answer: nature / the labeling process assigns the underlying measure. A radiologist’s intuition is hard to put into equations — we treat it as given by the problem.
Our engineering job (central theme of the course):

Given samples from the range of random variables, estimate the underlying distribution / measure.

That is the probabilistic formulation of ML that the next lectures will connect to function approximation.
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
section: 6. The working triplet from now on
text:
6. The working triplet from now on
Pushing forward gives a new triplet on the observation side, schematically
\[
\bigl(\mathbb{R},\ \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}),\ P_{X}\bigr).
\]
Once data are vectors from sensors, we mostly talk and compute in this pushforward world, while remembering that an underlying \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)\) and map \(X\) sit behind it.
That is why random variables were invented: not decoration — the device that moves us from abstract \(\Omega\) to numbers with a well-defined distribution.
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
7. Vector-valued random variables
In ML, usually
\[
X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{d}.
\]
(“Vector-valued RV” just means: the range consists of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\).)

Borel building blocks in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)
Cartesian products of half-lines, e.g. in \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\):
\[
(-\infty,\ x_1] \times (-\infty,\ x_2].
\]
Geometrically: everything “southwest” of the point \((x_1,x_2)\) in the plane (with the usual closed/open conventions on edges).


Distribution at a vector \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\)
Input to \(P_{X}\) is an element of the range of \(X\). For vector \(X\),
\[
P_{X}(x) \;=\; P\Bigl( X^{-1}\bigl( (-\infty,x_1]\times\cdots\times(-\infty,x_d] \bigr) \Bigr).
\]
Again: inverse image under \(X\), then apply \(P\).
Notation clash warning (from class): capital \(X\) for the RV vs small/bold \(x\) for a point in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) — same letter family, different objects.
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
8. Distribution vs density (preview)

The distribution function / pushforward is a valid probability measure (on Borel sets).
A density (when it exists) is not itself a probability: evaluating a density at a single point does not give \(P(X=x)\) in continuous models.

Formal density discussion continues later; do not confuse “PDF value at a point” with “probability of an event.”
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
section: 9. Multiple random variables (setup for next class)
text:
9. Multiple random variables (setup for next class)
There can be several random variables (hence possibly several experiments / sample spaces, or one joint experiment — your modeling choice).

X-ray + disease (two views)







View
Meaning




One experiment
“Get disease and get imaged” as a single process \(\to\) one \(\Omega\), maybe vector-valued \(X\)


Two experiments
Disease outcome vs imaging outcome as separate RVs that may be correlated



Both are allowed; random experiments are chosen by the modeler.


Vector RV vs many scalars
A Gaussian vector in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) can be seen as:

one RV with range \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\), or

\(d\) correlated scalar RVs (covariance / correlation matrix).

Same mathematics, two stories.


Discriminative vs generative (preview)
In this worldview they can look unified: the label is simply another coordinate of a vector-valued random variable; conditioning corresponds to restricting to appropriate events (set operations on the underlying spaces).
Next lectures: joint / conditional distributions more carefully, then ML as learning distributions (linked back to function approximation).
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
section: 10. What to refresh before next class
text:
10. What to refresh before next class

Joint distributions of several RVs

Conditional distributions (ask: which events am I conditioning on?)

Discrete vs continuous RVs

Always relate formulas back to sets in \(\Omega\) and inverse images under \(X\)
crumbs: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3

title: Lecture 4 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 3
text:
11. Self-check

What is a pushforward measure in one sentence?

Why do we care about Borel half-lines \((-\infty,x]\)?
In \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\), what geometric region does \((-\infty,x_1]\times(-\infty,x_2]\) describe?

(Answers: self-check-answers.qmd.)

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
text: Video: Lec 03 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
text:
1. Where we left off
Lecture 2 gave us:

Sample space \(\Omega\)
Events \(\mathcal{F}\) (suitable subsets of \(\Omega\))
Probability measure \(P : \mathcal{F} \to [0,1]\)

Question for ML: where does this fit, and what do we do next?
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
text:
2. The probability triplet
The package
\[
(\Omega,\ \mathcal{F},\ P)
\]
is the probability triplet (probability space).

Useful analogy



Abstract probability
Concrete geometry on the line




\(\Omega\)
\(\mathbb{R}\)


events \(\mathcal{F}\)
(nice) subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\)


\(P\)
length (Lebesgue) measure



Same pattern: a ground set, a family of subsets, a measure on those subsets.
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
section: 3. Why we cannot stop at the triplet
text:
3. Why we cannot stop at the triplet
\(\Omega\) is often abstract and non-numeric (heads/tails; “someone got imaged and labeled”).
Engineers need numbers — we add, subtract, run algorithms, store arrays.
Slogan from class: think abstract, act concrete.

Thinking: probability space / experiment
Acting: concrete observations (vectors on a computer)

So we need a bridge from abstraction \(\to\) something we can compute with.

Sensors / observations (X-ray story)
Part of \(\Omega\): the whole story (nodule develops, person visits, imaging happens, …).
What we actually store: an X-ray image \(\to\) a vector on disk.
We work with vectors; we started from an abstract sample space. What connects them?
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
text:
4. Random variable = the bridge
A random variable is a function
\[
X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}
\]
(or, more useful for ML, \(X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{d}\)).
It maps each abstract outcome \(\omega \in \Omega\) to a number (or vector) we can manipulate.

Why we need it







Without \(X\)
With \(X\)




Only abstract outcomes (H/T, “process happened”)
Concrete numbers / vectors


Hard to do algebra / ML
Can compute, fit models, store data



You cannot stop at \(\Omega\) if you want engineering work. The extra map \(X\) is not optional decoration — it is why RVs were defined.


Famous misnomer

A random variable is neither random nor a variable.
It is a deterministic function \(\Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) (or \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)).

(Name is historical; treat it as a function.)


Range need not be all of \(\mathbb{R}\)

Can be integers, a finite set, etc.
In practice for images / features: range is \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)
Lecture generalizes: think \(X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{d}\)
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
section: 5. What is a data point? (two layers of truth)
text:
5. What is a data point? (two layers of truth)

Deterministic language (Lecture 1)
An image is a point / vector in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\).


Probabilistic language (this lecture)
Still a point in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\), but that \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) is the range of a random variable \(X\) defined on an underlying sample space \(\Omega\) from a random experiment we do not fully observe.
Mental checklist whenever you see a datapoint \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\):
random experiment
      |
      v
sample space Omega
      |
      v
random variable X : Omega -> R^d
      |
      v
observed vector x  (element of the range of X)
Folder of images = many such range elements (realizations / observations of \(X\)).
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
text:
6. Preview: what happens to \(P\)? (next ideas)
Defining \(X\) raises the natural question:

We had \(P\) on subsets of \(\Omega\). Under \(X\), what becomes of that measure on subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)?

Answer (named in class, developed next): pushforward measure, which becomes the distribution of \(X\).
Also mentioned: the image of the event \(\sigma\)-algebra under \(X\) relates to the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) (measure-theoretic detail — intuition: “nice” subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)).
This lecture stopped as that transition began; later parts fill in distribution / density.

Exercise left in class
Is a random variable necessarily bijective? (Think carefully; not required for this course’s main path.)
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
text:
7. One-page summary







Object
Role




\((\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)\)
Probability triplet — abstract uncertainty


Sensor / measurement
How we observe the world


\(X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\)
Random variable — bridge to numbers


Datapoint \(x\)
Element of the range of \(X\)



ML connection: classical “vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\)” sit inside a probabilistic story: experiment \(\to\) \(\Omega\) \(\to\) \(X\) \(\to\) data.
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2
text:
8. Self-check

Write down the probability triplet and one analogy with length on \(\mathbb{R}\).
Why is \(\Omega\) alone not enough for ML engineering?
Define a random variable formally (domain and codomain).
Why is “random variable” a misnomer?
In the X-ray example, what is abstract (\(\Omega\)) vs what is concrete (range of \(X\))?

(Answers: self-check-answers.qmd.)
crumbs: Lecture 3 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 2

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text: Video: Lec 02 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
1. Bridge from Lecture 1
Last time: ML = function approximation.

Data: pairs from two sets
Assume unknown \(f\) maps domain \(\to\) range
Goal: estimate \(f\) (so we can predict on new inputs)

Prediction means: for a new \(x\) with unknown \(y\), use \(\hat{f}\) to guess \(y\).
Example: X-ray \(\to\) \(\{0,1\}\) (diseased / not).
How (abstractly): guess a model family \(\to\) refine with data.
Why that is not enough alone: for many problems you cannot derive \(f\) from physics (coin toss; reflectance \(\to\) “disease”). So we use a statistical / probabilistic approach: many observations, infer structure from data.

The gap this lecture closes







Familiar language
Probabilistic language (feels harder at first)




Learn / estimate a function \(f\)
Estimate an underlying distribution (e.g. via divergence minimization later)



Same spirit — different math language. Today: foundations so that link becomes natural.
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
2. Why probability theory?
We must decide under uncertainty.
Irony stressed in class:

Inputs / world: uncertain
Final decisions (e.g. diagnosis): must be deterministic (A doctor cannot usefully stop at “60% diseased” without a decision rule.)

So we need a mathematical framework for uncertainty that still ends in decisions.
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
section: 3. Random experiment (where “random” starts — and almost ends)
text:
3. Random experiment (where “random” starts — and almost ends)
Probability begins with a random experiment:

An experiment whose outcomes we treat as uncertain / not fully predictable from our model of the world.

Important points from lecture:

“Randomness” itself is not rigorously defined — we assume we know what a random experiment is, then proceed with set theory / measure theory.
After fixing the experiment and its outcomes, almost nothing else is “random” — including random variables (coming soon): they are deterministic maps.
The designer chooses what counts as the experiment.

One toss of a coin
Five tosses of a coin Both are valid random experiments — different sample spaces.



Classic examples



Random experiment
Typical outcomes




Coin toss
\(\{H, T\}\)


Die roll
\(\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\)





ML examples (see every datapoint this way)







Task
What is the “random experiment”? (intuition)




X-ray diagnosis
Person gets ill / seeks care \(\to\) imaging \(\to\) image on disk \(\to\) clinician label


Spam filter
Someone drafts/sends email \(\to\) someone labels spam / not


Brain measurement \(\to\) prediction
Person + protocol \(\to\) recorded signal



Punchline for ML: every training point is an outcome of an underlying random experiment. That is the probabilistic starting point.
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
4. Sample space \(\Omega\)
Once the random experiment is fixed:
\[
\Omega = \{\text{all possible outcomes of the experiment}\}
\]
This set is the sample space.

Critical reminders

\(\Omega\) need not be numeric. Coin: \(\Omega = \{H,T\}\) — no numbers yet. X-ray pipeline: outcomes are abstract “whole process happened this way” objects — still not vectors until we define random variables (next lectures).
Sample space = enumerate outcomes in a set. Set theory begins here.


Don’t ask “what is randomness?” — collect outcomes into \(\Omega\), then work mathematically.

(Side joke from class: “random number generators” are deterministic algorithms \(\to\) pseudo-random.)
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
5. Why measures? Comparing subsets
Having \(\Omega\) alone does not let us predict. We need to talk about how large / how likely subsets are.

Analogy: real numbers and length
On \(\mathbb{R}\), to say which of two intervals is “bigger,” we use length (Lebesgue measure on nice sets).

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\): area
In \(\mathbb{R}^3\): volume
In \(\mathbb{R}^d\): \(d\)-dimensional volume

General idea: given a set, form subsets, assign a measure so we can compare / quantify them.
A measure is a mathematical function on (certain) subsets with formal properties (non-negativity, additivity for disjoint unions, etc.). This course gives the intuition; a full measure-theory course makes it airtight.


Back to \(\Omega\)
Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a suitable collection of subsets of \(\Omega\) (events). Goal: assign a measure on members of \(\mathcal{F}\).
(In full rigor \(\mathcal{F}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra — named in the lecture goals; formal axioms continue in the next parts.)
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
6. Probability measure \(P\)
One special measure on events is the probability measure
\[
P : \mathcal{F} \to [0,1]
\]

Properties (as stated in class)
For events \(A,B \in \mathcal{F}\):

Non-negativity: \(P(A) \ge 0\)
Normalized on \(\Omega\): \(P(\Omega) = 1\)
Empty set: \(P(\emptyset) = 0\)
Additivity for disjoint events: if \(A \cap B = \emptyset\), then

\[
P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)
\]

Values lie in \([0,1]\) (unlike raw length, which can be arbitrarily large)

Analogy: think of \(P\) like “length,” but scaled so the whole sample space has measure 1.


Vocabulary



Term
Meaning




Outcome
An element of \(\Omega\)


Event
A subset of \(\Omega\) (element of \(\mathcal{F}\))


\(P(A)\)
Probability measure of event \(A\)
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
section: 7. Meaning of \(P(A)\): optional until the end
text:
7. Meaning of \(P(A)\): optional until the end
Mathematically, \(P\) is just a measure with those axioms.
Common interpretation: \(P(A)\) = “likelihood” that event \(A\) occurs (e.g. \(P(A)=0.7\) \(\to\) “70% chance” in ordinary speech).
Lecture philosophy:

You can run almost all of the math of ML treating \(P\) as a pure abstraction.
Assign human meaning (diagnosis language, business risk, etc.) at the end, when a decision must be communicated.
Same measure, different stories in different applications — like “area under a curve” meaning different physical things in different sciences.

Abstraction payoff for ML: once data = values of random variables with an underlying \(P\), the same algorithms apply to images, text, time series, brain signals — all are vectors in the range of those maps. That is why a “generalist” ML view is possible.
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
8. Link back to “ignorance modeling”
If you were omniscient about all physics of a coin toss, the outcome would be deterministic. Because we are not, we use the probabilistic apparatus: experiment \(\to\) \(\Omega\) \(\to\) events \(\to\) \(P\).
There need not be “true metaphysical randomness” for the framework to be useful.
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
9. One-page map (so far)
Random experiment  (assumed)
        |
        v
Sample space Omega  (set of outcomes; may be non-numeric)
        |
        v
Events  (subsets in F)
        |
        v
Probability measure P : F -> [0,1]
        |
        v
(Next lectures) Random variables, distributions
        |
        v
ML as estimating structure of P  (parallel to estimating f)
(In prose we write the sample space as \(\Omega\).)
crumbs: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1

title: Lecture 2 — Recap of Probability Theory - 1, Part 1
text:
10. What comes next
This part stopped at sample space + probability measure. Still ahead (as previewed): random variables, pushforward measures, distribution / density functions — and the explicit parallel between estimating \(f\) and estimating distributions.

text:

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
text: Video: Lec 01 — Overview of Function Approximation

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
text:
1. What this course is for
This is the first of a two-course series:







Course
Role




This one
Mathematical / probabilistic foundations of ML


Next semester
State-of-the-art algorithms (esp. generative models)



Goal: move from “internet data scientist” (drive the car) to someone who can build and reason about algorithms (design the engine).
Analogy used in class:

You don’t need to know how an internal combustion engine works to drive a car.
You do need that knowledge if you want to build a better one.

By the end, reading an ML paper should feel closer to reading a novel than decoding opaque jargon.
Teaching style: mostly chalk-and-board (no slides). Mathematics is treated as a language of precision — English is too ambiguous for engineering implementation.
Viewpoint: almost everything will be developed from a probabilistic standpoint (with deterministic parallels pointed out along the way).

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
text:
2. The central problem: function approximation
Most problems in science and engineering can be cast as function approximation.

Classical motivation
Kepler / Gauss-era question: observe planet positions at some times → predict positions at other times.

Independent variable: time → call this \(x\)
Dependent variable: position → call this \(y\)



Formal setup
Two sets:

Domain set \(\mathcal{X}\) (often called “input”; here we keep it abstract)
Range set \(\mathcal{Y}\) (often called “output”)

We are given a dataset of paired observations:
\[
\mathcal{D} = \bigl\{(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)\bigr\}
\]
where each \(x_i \in \mathcal{X}\) and \(y_i \in \mathcal{Y}\).
Assumption: there exists a function
\[
f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}
\]
such that the observations are (related to) evaluations of \(f\).
Problem: \(f\) is unknown.

Machine learning in one line (deterministic view):
Given \(\mathcal{D}\), find / estimate \(f\).

This is an ill-posed / “blind” problem: we only have samples, not a description of \(f\).

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
section: 3. How humans solve blind problems (the philosophy)
text:
3. How humans solve blind problems (the philosophy)
If you know nothing about \(f\), you cannot magically recover “truth.” The workable philosophy is:

Start with an initial guess on \(f\) (a model family)
Refine that guess using data \(\mathcal{D}\) (a learning algorithm)


Example: planetary motion
Kepler assumed orbits are ellipses. That does not finish the job — there are infinitely many ellipses. Data tells you which ellipse (among the family) fits.


Vocabulary that will stick for the whole course







Everyday phrase
ML meaning




Initial guess / family of candidates
Model / model family


Procedure that improves the guess with \(\mathcal{D}\)
Learning algorithm


Dataset \(\mathcal{D}\)
Data (“data is the new oil” — quality of \(\mathcal{D}\) limits quality of \(\hat{f}\))



Famous proverb cited in lecture:

All models are wrong, but some are useful.

We never have access to “true reality”; we only get estimates. The course will define what “useful” means rigorously later (error, risk, generalization, etc.).


Model families you will meet later
Different guesses on \(f\):

Linear models

Quadratic / polynomial families

Kernel machines

Decision trees

Neural networks

Different refinement algorithms (examples):

Least squares

Error backpropagation (for neural nets)

“Learning” = choosing a family + refining it with data. Both will be formalized later.


Overfitting (preview)
A bad “solution”: define \(\hat{f}(x_i) = y_i\) only at observed points and invent nonsense elsewhere.
That memorizes \(\mathcal{D}\) but fails the real goal: predict for unseen \(x\).
This idea will later be formalized as overfitting.

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
section: 4. Domains need not be scalars — think vectors
text:
4. Domains need not be scalars — think vectors
Nothing forces \(x\) or \(y\) to be single numbers. We often work with vector-valued inputs/outputs.

Running example: chest X-ray diagnosis

\(x_i\): an X-ray image

\(y_i \in \{0,1\}\): diseased / not diseased

In a computer, an image is a \(P \times Q\) matrix of pixel intensities (e.g. \(0\)–\(255\) for 8-bit).
Stack columns into one long vector of length \(PQ\). Then:
\[
x_i \in \mathbb{R}^{PQ}
\]
Abstractly, for the rest of the course:
\[
x \in \mathbb{R}^{d}
\]
(a point in \(d\)-dimensional Euclidean space).
The unknown \(f\) maps a high-dimensional image to a label \(\{0,1\}\).
In the real world, that \(f\) is roughly “what a radiologist does.”
ML tries to mimic such maps — this is the universal function approximation ambition: learn useful maps between complicated spaces.

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
text:
5. Why a probabilistic viewpoint?
Many ML methods can be told in a deterministic “fit a curve” language. That is not enough for the hard cases.

Measurable physics vs abstract human constructs
Easy (Newtonian) maps:

Force ↔︎ acceleration (linear, few parameters)

Enough to fly an aircraft with a small model

Hard maps:

Pixel reflectance → gender, disease, intent

Microphone pressure waveform → phoneme / meaning

A microphone measures pressure gradients. A camera measures reflected/absorbed radiation.
Why those numbers should equal an abstract label like “gender” or “phone /ah/” is not a simple physics formula with 5 parameters. Human semantics are complex; models may need millions of parameters.
Thought experiment (assignment-style): take MNIST digits and randomly shuffle labels. You can still train a model that fits those random labels. Semantics are subtle; memorization is possible; meaning is not automatic.


Historical lesson: speech recognition
For decades, speech scientists tried physics-first inversion:

Model vocal tract as waveguides / constrictions

Invert from waveform → articulatory configuration → phone

Hard and brittle.
In the late 1980s, statistical methods solved practical digit / speech recognition by:

Making many observations

Estimating patterns from data

Physics-first researchers sometimes called this “ignorance modeling.”
Engineers replied: but it works.
Modern deep learning sits in that lineage: systems that work at scale, even when full interpretability lags behind.


Takeaway
When \(f\) is too complex to derive from first-principles physics:

Make repeated observations and estimate \(f\) with statistical / probabilistic methods.

That is why this course is grounded in probability theory.

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
section: 6. From deterministic sets to random variables
text:
6. From deterministic sets to random variables
Deterministic view: \(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}\) are sets; \(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\); given \(\mathcal{D}\), estimate \(f\).
Probabilistic view: \(\mathcal{X}\) and \(\mathcal{Y}\) are (supports of) random variables.
Function approximation becomes closely related to distribution / density estimation.
There will be one-to-one parallels between:







Deterministic language
Probabilistic language




Estimate unknown \(f\)
Estimate distributions / conditionals involving \(X,Y\)


Model family
Parametric / structured distributions


Fit with data
Inference / learning from samples



Generative models, in particular, are most natural in the probabilistic language. That language is broad enough to cover both discriminative and generative formulations (terms to be defined soon).

title: Lecture 1 — Overview of Function Approximation
text:
7. Preparation for Lecture 2+
Refresh thoroughly before the next class:

Random experiment & sample space

Random variable (as a measurable function from sample space → \(\mathbb{R}\))

Probability measure

Distribution functions

Density functions (and that densities do not always exist)

Familiarity with measure-theoretic language (σ-algebras, etc.) will help — the course gets rigorous

Next lectures connect today’s function-approximation story to random variables and distribution estimation.

title: Lecture 1 — Self-check answers

text:

title: Lecture 1 — Beginner tutorial
text:
Course: Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning (Prof. Prathosh A.P.)
Based on: Lec 01 — Overview of Function Approximation



Create a tiny dataset (like observations in the lecture)
Make an initial guess for the unknown function (a model family)
Refine that guess using data
See overfitting (memorizing data)
See that a flexible model can even fit random labels
Turn a small “image” into a vector (X-ray idea from class)





Read each markdown cell (the text explanations).
Run the code cell right below it (Shift + Enter).
Do not skip cells — later cells need earlier ones.


You do not need to know ML already. If a line of code is new, the text above it explains what it does.




We need two libraries:



Library
Job




numpy
Work with numbers and arrays (lists of numbers)


matplotlib
Draw plots



If the next cell fails with ModuleNotFoundError, run this once in a cell:
%pip install numpy matplotlib
Then run the import cell again.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print("Imports OK. numpy version:", np.__version__)




In class we said:

We have pairs (x, y). We assume there is an unknown function f such that y ≈ f(x).
Goal: estimate f from data.

In this notebook we will pretend the true function is a sine wave:
\[
f(x) = \sin(2\pi x)
\]
In real ML we do not know f. Here we keep it secret from the “learner”, but we plot it as a dashed line so you can see the truth.

def true_f(x):
    """The unknown reality. In real problems we do NOT know this."""
    return np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)

# Try it on a few numbers
print("f(0.0) =", true_f(0.0))
print("f(0.25) =", true_f(0.25))  # should be about 1
print("f(0.5) =", true_f(0.5))    # should be about 0




Lecture notation:
\[
\mathcal{D} = \{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\}
\]
We will: 1. Pick random x values between 0 and 1 2. Compute y = true_f(x) 3. Add a little noise (real measurements are never perfect)
New words - seed: makes “random” numbers repeatable (same result every run) - noise: small random error added to y

def make_dataset(n=15, noise=0.15, seed=0):
    """Make n noisy observations from true_f."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)          # random number generator
    x = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 1, size=n))      # n random x in [0,1], sorted
    y = true_f(x) + rng.normal(0, noise, size=n)  # true value + noise
    return x, y

x_train, y_train = make_dataset()

print("Number of points:", len(x_train))
print("First 5 x values:", x_train[:5])
print("First 5 y values:", y_train[:5])




Red dots = what we observed (D)
Black dashed curve = true f (unknown in real life)

Notice: the dots are near the curve, but not exactly on it, because of noise.

x_grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 400)  # many x values for a smooth curve

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.plot(x_grid, true_f(x_grid), "k--", label="true f (unknown in real ML)")
plt.scatter(x_train, y_train, c="red", label="data D", zorder=3)
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("y")
plt.title("Observations vs the unknown function")
plt.legend()
plt.show()





From class:

Start with a guess for f (choose a model family)
Refine using data D

Our simple guess family: polynomials



Degree
Example shape




1
straight line: \(a + bx\)


2
parabola: \(a + bx + cx^2\)


3
cubic: \(a + bx + cx^2 + dx^3\)


high
can wiggle a lot



np.polyfit = refine the guess (find best coefficients for that degree)
np.polyval = use the fitted polynomial to predict y at new x

def fit_and_predict(x_train, y_train, x_query, degree):
    """
    Guess family: polynomials of this degree.
    Refine: least squares fit to the data.
    """
    coeffs = np.polyfit(x_train, y_train, degree)  # learn coefficients from D
    y_hat = np.polyval(coeffs, x_query)            # predict on new x
    return y_hat

# Quick test: fit a line (degree 1) and predict at x=0.5
y_at_half = fit_and_predict(x_train, y_train, 0.5, degree=1)
print("Degree-1 model prediction at x=0.5:", float(y_at_half))




We try three model families on the same data:



Degree
What usually happens




1
Too simple → underfitting (misses the curve)


3
Often a reasonable compromise


12
Too flexible → overfitting (chases noise, wild wiggles)

title: Lecture 1 — Beginner tutorial
text:
In class we said:

We have pairs (x, y). We assume there is an unknown function f such that y ≈ f(x).
Goal: estimate f from data.

In this notebook we will pretend the true function is a sine wave:
\[
f(x) = \sin(2\pi x)
\]
In real ML we do not know f. Here we keep it secret from the “learner”, but we plot it as a dashed line so you can see the truth.

def true_f(x):
    """The unknown reality. In real problems we do NOT know this."""
    return np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)

# Try it on a few numbers
print("f(0.0) =", true_f(0.0))
print("f(0.25) =", true_f(0.25))  # should be about 1
print("f(0.5) =", true_f(0.5))    # should be about 0

title: Lecture 1 — Beginner tutorial
text:
Lecture notation:
\[
\mathcal{D} = \{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\}
\]
We will: 1. Pick random x values between 0 and 1 2. Compute y = true_f(x) 3. Add a little noise (real measurements are never perfect)
New words - seed: makes “random” numbers repeatable (same result every run) - noise: small random error added to y

def make_dataset(n=15, noise=0.15, seed=0):
    """Make n noisy observations from true_f."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)          # random number generator
    x = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 1, size=n))      # n random x in [0,1], sorted
    y = true_f(x) + rng.normal(0, noise, size=n)  # true value + noise
    return x, y

x_train, y_train = make_dataset()

print("Number of points:", len(x_train))
print("First 5 x values:", x_train[:5])
print("First 5 y values:", y_train[:5])




Red dots = what we observed (D)
Black dashed curve = true f (unknown in real life)

Notice: the dots are near the curve, but not exactly on it, because of noise.

x_grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 400)  # many x values for a smooth curve

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.plot(x_grid, true_f(x_grid), "k--", label="true f (unknown in real ML)")
plt.scatter(x_train, y_train, c="red", label="data D", zorder=3)
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("y")
plt.title("Observations vs the unknown function")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

text:
From class:

Start with a guess for f (choose a model family)
Refine using data D

Our simple guess family: polynomials



Degree
Example shape




1
straight line: \(a + bx\)


2
parabola: \(a + bx + cx^2\)


3
cubic: \(a + bx + cx^2 + dx^3\)


high
can wiggle a lot



np.polyfit = refine the guess (find best coefficients for that degree)
np.polyval = use the fitted polynomial to predict y at new x

def fit_and_predict(x_train, y_train, x_query, degree):
    """
    Guess family: polynomials of this degree.
    Refine: least squares fit to the data.
    """
    coeffs = np.polyfit(x_train, y_train, degree)  # learn coefficients from D
    y_hat = np.polyval(coeffs, x_query)            # predict on new x
    return y_hat

# Quick test: fit a line (degree 1) and predict at x=0.5
y_at_half = fit_and_predict(x_train, y_train, 0.5, degree=1)
print("Degree-1 model prediction at x=0.5:", float(y_at_half))

title: Lecture 3 — Beginner tutorial
text:
Based on Lec 03.


Sample space can be abstract (H / T).
A random variable is a function that turns those outcomes into numbers.
Run cells with Shift+Enter.




import numpy as np

print('Ready')





Omega = sample space

Events = subsets

P = probability measure

Example: fair coin, Omega = {H, T}.

Omega = {"H", "T"}

def P(event):
    event = set(event)
    return sum(0.5 for o in event if o in Omega)

print("Omega =", Omega)
print("P({H}) =", P({"H"}))




We cannot do much arithmetic with the labels H and T.
Define a map X: Omega -> real numbers, for example:

X(H) = 1

X(T) = 0

That map is the random variable (a deterministic function!).

def X(omega):
    """Random variable: abstract outcome -> number."""
    return 1 if omega == "H" else 0

for outcome in sorted(Omega):
    print(f"X({outcome}) = {X(outcome)}")




When we “observe” many coin tosses, we store numbers (0/1), not the letters.
Those numbers are elements of the range of X.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
# simulate abstract outcomes, then map through X
abstract = rng.choice(["H", "T"], size=10)
data = np.array([X(o) for o in abstract])

print("Abstract outcomes:", abstract)
print("Observed data (range of X):", data)
print("Mean of data ≈ P(H) for fair coin:", data.mean())




For images, X maps Omega -> R^d (a long vector of pixels).
Tiny demo: pretend each outcome maps to a 2-D “feature vector”.

def X_vec(omega):
    # toy features: [is_heads, bias_term]
    return np.array([1.0, 1.0]) if omega == "H" else np.array([0.0, 1.0])

print("X_vec(H) =", X_vec("H"))
print("X_vec(T) =", X_vec("T"))
print("shape:", X_vec("H").shape)  # like a mini R^2 datapoint





# Exercise A: redefine X so X(H)=+1 and X(T)=-1 (common coding).
# Compute the average of 5000 simulated values. What do you expect for a fair coin?

def X_pm(omega):
    return 1 if omega == "H" else -1

sim = rng.choice(["H", "T"], size=5000)
vals = np.array([X_pm(o) for o in sim])
print("sample mean:", vals.mean())  # expect near 0


# Exercise B: die Omega = {1,...,6}, X(omega)=omega (identity).
# This is already numeric — but still formally a random variable Omega -> R.

Omega_die = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}

def X_die(omega):
    return float(omega)

print([X_die(o) for o in sorted(Omega_die)])







Lecture idea
Here




Probability triplet
Omega, events, P


Need numbers
cannot stop at H/T labels


Random variable
function X: Omega -> R or R^d


Datapoint
value in the range of X



Next lectures: pushforward measure / distribution of X (what happens to P).
